drugs.name: Acetazolamide
drugs.mechanism: Reversibly inhibits both membrane-bound and cytosolic carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule, so H+ is unavailable for NHE3 and bicarbonate plus sodium escape reabsorption
drugs.indication: Acute mountain sickness (prevention and treatment), open-angle glaucoma, and metabolic alkalosis — including loop-diuretic-induced hypokalemic alkalosis
drugs.adverseEffects: Mild hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, calcium phosphate kidney stones from alkaline urine, paresthesia, somnolence, dizziness and ataxia

drugs.name: Aliskiren
drugs.mechanism: Potent selective competitive renin inhibition that blocks angiotensinogen from reaching the active site, so no angiotensin I is ever formed
drugs.indication: An alternative agent for hypertension only — never first-line, and never combined with an ACE inhibitor or ARB
drugs.adverseEffects: Hyperkalemia and hypotension, worse below a creatinine clearance of 30 mL/min; only about 3% bioavailable and sensitive to P-glycoprotein inducers and inhibitors

drugs.name: Amiloride
drugs.mechanism: Blocks luminal ENaC in principal cells so the lumen-negative potential is neutralized and ROMK can no longer secrete potassium; it enters the nephron by organic cation transporters rather than OATs
drugs.indication: Potassium-sparing adjunct to a thiazide or loop, lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus where it blocks lithium entry and preserves AQP2, and Liddle syndrome
drugs.adverseEffects: Hyperkalemia, especially with advanced age, renal impairment, hypoaldosteronism, RAS inhibitors, NSAIDs or potassium supplements

drugs.name: Amlodipine
drugs.mechanism: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockade with slow absorption and a 30-50 hour half-life, so plasma peaks and troughs are minimal
drugs.indication: First-line once-daily hypertension, where the flat concentration curve avoids the sympathetic reflex surges of short-acting agents
drugs.adverseEffects: Ankle edema — the most common side effect, caused by pre-capillary dilation with post-capillary reflex constriction, so diuretics do not help it

drugs.name: Bosentan
drugs.mechanism: Antagonizes endothelin receptors, blocking the most potent endogenous vasoconstrictor the endothelium produces
drugs.indication: Pulmonary arterial hypertension
drugs.adverseEffects: Hepatotoxicity requiring liver monitoring; teratogenic

drugs.name: Bumetanide
drugs.mechanism: NKCC2 blockade in the thick ascending limb with a longer duration of action than furosemide
drugs.indication: An alternative loop diuretic when a longer-acting agent is wanted; otherwise interchangeable with furosemide
drugs.adverseEffects: Loop-class electrolyte losses — sodium, potassium, chloride, calcium and magnesium — with ototoxicity at high doses

drugs.name: Captopril
drugs.mechanism: Competitively inhibits ACE, so angiotensin I is not converted to angiotensin II and bradykinin is not degraded; it is one of the two ACE inhibitors that is not a prodrug
drugs.indication: Hypertension, HFrEF, post-MI remodeling and proteinuric chronic kidney disease — though its short half-life forces 2-3 times daily dosing
drugs.adverseEffects: Dry cough in 5-20%, angioedema, hyperkalemia, first-dose hypotension and a fall in GFR; absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy

drugs.name: Carvedilol
drugs.mechanism: Third-generation non-selective beta blockade plus alpha-1 antagonism, calcium entry blockade and antioxidant activity
drugs.indication: HFrEF, where it is one of the four agents with proven mortality benefit; also hypertension
drugs.adverseEffects: Orthostatic hypotension from the alpha-1 component, bradycardia, and bronchospasm from non-selective beta blockade

drugs.name: Chlorthalidone
drugs.mechanism: Thiazide-like NCC blockade without a benzothiadiazine ring, with a 40-60 hour half-life giving 24-72 hours of action
drugs.indication: Hypertension when smoother 24-hour blood pressure control is wanted; cardiovascular outcomes equal those of hydrochlorothiazide
drugs.adverseEffects: A higher rate of hypokalemia than hydrochlorothiazide, driven by the much longer duration of action

drugs.name: Clevidipine
drugs.mechanism: Ultra-short-acting intravenous dihydropyridine with a 1-minute half-life, allowing minute-to-minute titration
drugs.indication: Hypertensive emergency where tight, rapidly reversible control is needed; duration is only 5-15 minutes
drugs.adverseEffects: Rebound hypertension on abrupt discontinuation; lipid emulsion vehicle

drugs.name: Clonidine
drugs.mechanism: Alpha-2 agonism at brainstem receptors — postsynaptic alpha-2 inhibits sympathetic neurons while presynaptic alpha-2 cuts norepinephrine release — lowering sympathetic and raising parasympathetic tone while preserving baroreceptor sensitivity, renal blood flow and GFR
drugs.indication: Refractory hypertension after ACE inhibitor, diuretic and CCB; also epidural pain control, ADHD, opioid and alcohol withdrawal, and menopausal vasomotor symptoms
drugs.adverseEffects: Sedation, dry mouth, constipation and bradycardia; abrupt cessation gives a catecholamine surge with rebound hypertension, so the beta blocker must be tapered off several days first

drugs.name: Desmopressin
drugs.mechanism: A vasopressin analogue that triggers release of stored von Willebrand factor and factor VIII from endothelial cells
drugs.indication: Von Willebrand disease and mild hemophilia A — and, at the V2 receptor, central diabetes insipidus
drugs.adverseEffects: Hyponatremia from excessive free water retention; facial flushing and headache

drugs.name: Digoxin
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits the myocyte Na+/K+ ATPase, so intracellular sodium rises, the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger slows, cytoplasmic calcium accumulates and more calcium binds troponin
drugs.indication: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, shifting a depressed Frank-Starling curve back to the left; also rate control in atrial fibrillation
drugs.adverseEffects: A narrow therapeutic window — hypokalemia leaves fewer K+ ions competing at the pump, so diuretics precipitate arrhythmia; verapamil raises levels by blocking P-glycoprotein

drugs.name: Diltiazem
drugs.mechanism: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockade with intermediate potency — less vasodilation than the dihydropyridines but real nodal effects, with an IV onset around 3 minutes
drugs.indication: Rate control in supraventricular tachyarrhythmia, hypertension and angina when some nodal effect is wanted
drugs.adverseEffects: Bradycardia and AV block; contraindicated with an IV beta blocker, in ventricular dysfunction, or with systolic pressure below 90 mmHg

drugs.name: Dobutamine
drugs.mechanism: Beta-1 dominant agonism that raises contractility and cardiac output — an inotrope, not a vasopressor
drugs.indication: Cardiogenic shock, where the primary insult is failing contractility rather than lost vascular tone
drugs.adverseEffects: Can cause hypotension, because beta-2 mediated vasodilation drops systemic vascular resistance

drugs.name: Dopamine
drugs.mechanism: A dose-dependent mix of D1, beta-1, alpha-1 and beta-2 activity, which is why the lecturer calls it a messy drug
drugs.indication: Not first line for any shock state; occasionally used when bradycardia accompanies hypotension
drugs.adverseEffects: Arrhythmias and tissue ischemia progressing to gangrene

drugs.name: Dorzolamide / Brinzolamide
drugs.mechanism: Topical carbonic anhydrase inhibition in the ciliary epithelium reduces bicarbonate formation, so aqueous humor secretion falls
drugs.indication: Open-angle glaucoma as eye drops, avoiding the systemic acidosis of oral acetazolamide
drugs.adverseEffects: Local ocular stinging and bitter taste, with minimal systemic effect

drugs.name: Doxazosin
drugs.mechanism: Alpha-1 selective blockade cleared by CYP3A4 with a 22-hour half-life and over 24 hours of action
drugs.indication: Once-daily therapy for hypertension with coexisting BPH
drugs.adverseEffects: Orthostatic hypotension, compensatory sodium and water retention that calls for a companion diuretic, and floppy iris syndrome

drugs.name: Enalapril
drugs.mechanism: A prodrug hydrolyzed by hepatic and intestinal esterases to enalaprilat, the active ACE inhibitor — and the only member of the class with an intravenous form
drugs.indication: Once-daily hypertension and heart failure therapy, with enalaprilat available when the intravenous route is required
drugs.adverseEffects: Class effects of cough, angioedema, hyperkalemia and reduced GFR; fetal hypotension, anuria, oligohydramnios and skull malformation in pregnancy

drugs.name: Epinephrine
drugs.mechanism: Alpha-1 greater than beta-1 greater than beta-2 agonism, raising heart rate, systemic vascular resistance and cardiac output together
drugs.indication: First line for anaphylaxis, given intramuscularly, and for cardiac arrest
drugs.adverseEffects: Tachyarrhythmias, hyperglycemia and lactic acidosis

drugs.name: Eplerenone
drugs.mechanism: Selective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism that spares androgen and progesterone receptors, cleared by CYP3A4 to inactive metabolites over a 7-9 hour duration
drugs.indication: Heart failure and hypertension in a patient who cannot tolerate the endocrine effects of spironolactone
drugs.adverseEffects: Hyperkalemia, and interaction with CYP3A4 inhibitors and grapefruit juice, but no gynecomastia

drugs.name: Esmolol
drugs.mechanism: Beta-1 selective blockade with a 9-minute half-life, given only as an intravenous infusion
drugs.indication: Hypertensive emergency and intraoperative tachycardia, where the drug must be able to disappear within minutes
drugs.adverseEffects: Hypotension and bradycardia that resolve quickly on stopping the infusion

drugs.name: Ethacrynic Acid
drugs.mechanism: The one loop diuretic that lacks a sulfonamide moiety, blocking NKCC2 without the N4-aromatic amine implicated in sulfonamide hypersensitivity
drugs.indication: Reserved for the patient with a documented severe sulfonamide allergy — the board answer, though clinical cross-reactivity is now considered insignificant
drugs.adverseEffects: The highest ototoxicity risk of the loop diuretics, with no efficacy or pharmacokinetic advantage, very expensive and often unavailable

drugs.name: Fenoldopam
drugs.mechanism: Dopamine D1 receptor agonism coupled through Gs to adenylyl cyclase and cAMP, dilating peripheral arterioles while producing natriuresis and diuresis
drugs.indication: Severe hypertension for up to 48 hours, particularly useful when renal function is compromised and in pediatric patients
drugs.adverseEffects: Reflex tachycardia, headache and flushing; a 5-minute half-life makes it fully titratable

drugs.name: Finerenone
drugs.mechanism: Nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist with a tissue distribution different from the steroidal agents
drugs.indication: Chronic kidney disease, particularly with type 2 diabetes, to slow progression
drugs.adverseEffects: Hyperkalemia, requiring potassium monitoring at initiation

drugs.name: Furosemide
drugs.mechanism: Blocks NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, preventing reabsorption of up to 25% of the filtered sodium load, and uniquely stimulates intrarenal PGE2 and PGI2 secretion
drugs.indication: Edema from any cause — acute pulmonary edema, chronic heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, cirrhotic ascites, acute kidney injury
drugs.adverseEffects: Hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia, ototoxicity and hyperuricemia; oral absorption is only 50-60% and unreliable in gut edema

drugs.name: Hydralazine
drugs.mechanism: Relaxes arteriolar smooth muscle only, by a mechanism that has never been defined; it undergoes NAT2 acetylation, so effect varies with acetylator status
drugs.indication: Moderate to severe hypertension, HFrEF paired with isosorbide dinitrate, and hypertensive emergency in pregnancy or postpartum
drugs.adverseEffects: Reflex tachycardia plus salt and water retention — because veins are untouched — so it needs a beta blocker and a diuretic alongside

drugs.name: Hydrochlorothiazide
drugs.mechanism: Blocks the Na+-Cl- cotransporter (NCC) in the distal convoluted tubule, preventing reabsorption of 5-10% of the filtered sodium load
drugs.indication: First-line for hypertension — an acute fall in ECF and cardiac output gives way to a sustained drop in peripheral vascular resistance
drugs.adverseEffects: Hyponatremia (the classic diuretic cause), hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, hyperuricemia, hyperglycemia and hypercalcemia, over a 6-12 hour duration

drugs.name: Labetalol
drugs.mechanism: Combined non-selective beta and alpha-1 blockade, available intravenously with a half-life around 5 hours
drugs.indication: Hypertensive emergency, and the recommended agent for hypertension in pregnancy
drugs.adverseEffects: Orthostatic hypotension, scalp tingling, bradycardia and bronchospasm

drugs.name: Lisinopril
drugs.mechanism: ACE inhibition without prodrug conversion, given once daily with a half-life that lengthens in the elderly
drugs.indication: First-line hypertension, HFrEF alongside a beta blocker and loop diuretic, and slowing progression of proteinuric CKD
drugs.adverseEffects: Dry cough from accumulated bradykinin, substance P and prostaglandins in the lung; angioedema; hyperkalemia

drugs.name: Losartan
drugs.mechanism: Competitive high-affinity antagonism at the AT1 receptor, leaving angiotensin II free to stimulate the vasodilating, natriuretic AT2 receptor and raising renin release
drugs.indication: Hypertension and proteinuric CKD in the patient who cannot tolerate an ACE inhibitor cough
drugs.adverseEffects: Hyperkalemia and reduced GFR as with ACE inhibitors, but little cough; angioedema rates no higher than non-RAS drugs

drugs.name: Mannitol
drugs.mechanism: An inert sugar distributed through the ECF that is freely filtered and never reabsorbed, holding water osmotically in the proximal tubule and descending limb
drugs.indication: Raised intracranial pressure with cerebral edema, dropping ICP within 15-30 minutes for 1.5-6 hours, and raised intraocular pressure; IV bolus only
drugs.adverseEffects: Pulmonary edema from the preload surge, hyponatremia in renal impairment, then dehydration with hypernatremia and hyperkalemia

drugs.name: Methyldopa
drugs.mechanism: Converted by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase and dopamine beta-hydroxylase to alpha-methylnorepinephrine, a false transmitter that replaces norepinephrine in vesicles and acts on alpha-2 receptors
drugs.indication: Hypertension in pregnancy — the long-standing agent of choice
drugs.adverseEffects: Sedation and depression; onset takes 4-6 hours but the effect lasts 24-48 hours

drugs.name: Metoprolol
drugs.mechanism: Second-generation relatively beta-1 selective blockade, with selectivity that is dose-dependent and lost at higher doses
drugs.indication: One of only four beta blockers with proven mortality benefit in stable heart failure, plus post-MI and rate control
drugs.adverseEffects: Excessive bradycardia, delayed recovery from insulin-induced hypoglycemia with blunted warning symptoms, decreased insulin sensitivity

drugs.name: Minoxidil
drugs.mechanism: Its active metabolite minoxidil sulfate opens K-ATP channels, hyperpolarizing arteriolar smooth muscle so it cannot contract
drugs.indication: Severe hypertension as a last-line agent, with a very strong antihypertensive effect lasting about 3 days
drugs.adverseEffects: Marked reflex tachycardia and fluid retention requiring a beta blocker and loop diuretic, plus hypertrichosis and pericardial effusion

drugs.name: Nebivolol
drugs.mechanism: Third-generation beta-1 selective blockade that also stimulates nitric oxide production for vasodilation
drugs.indication: Hypertension and heart failure — one of the four beta blockers with proven mortality benefit
drugs.adverseEffects: Headache and fatigue; the vasodilating agents avoid the insulin-resistance penalty of the non-vasodilating ones

drugs.name: Nicardipine
drugs.mechanism: Intravenous dihydropyridine producing arteriolar dilation with a rapid alpha-phase of about 3 minutes
drugs.indication: Hypertensive emergency, usually paired with labetalol or esmolol
drugs.adverseEffects: Hypotension with reflex tachycardia; the terminal half-life stretches to 14 hours after a long infusion

drugs.name: Nifedipine
drugs.mechanism: Dihydropyridine blockade of L-type channels in arteriolar smooth muscle only, with no effect on AV nodal conduction or the rate of channel recovery
drugs.indication: Hypertension and angina in extended-release form; also tocolysis for preterm labor at 24-34 weeks, limited to 48 hours
drugs.adverseEffects: Peripheral edema, headache and flushing; the immediate-release form causes reflex tachycardia and is contraindicated in unstable angina and STEMI

drugs.name: Nimodipine
drugs.mechanism: Dihydropyridine with selectivity for cerebral arteries, available orally only with 13% bioavailability
drugs.indication: Subarachnoid hemorrhage, to limit vasospasm
drugs.adverseEffects: Hypotension; must never be given intravenously

drugs.name: Nitroprusside
drugs.mechanism: Taken up by red cells and split into nitric oxide and cyanide; the nitric oxide activates guanylyl cyclase and raises cGMP, dilating arteries and veins alike
drugs.indication: Acute severe hypertension, acute decompensated heart failure, and controlled hypotension during surgery — onset under 2 minutes, duration 1-10 minutes
drugs.adverseEffects: Cyanide and thiocyanate accumulation, since detoxification by rhodanese is saturable and thiocyanate clearance takes about 3 days, longer still in renal failure

drugs.name: Norepinephrine
drugs.mechanism: Alpha-1 agonism far outweighing beta-1 and beta-2, so systemic vascular resistance rises with a modest inotropic boost to cardiac output
drugs.indication: The usual first-choice vasopressor in distributive, cardiogenic and mixed shock
drugs.adverseEffects: Tachyarrhythmias and digital ischemia; extravasation causes tissue necrosis

drugs.name: Olmesartan
drugs.mechanism: AT1 receptor blockade with once-daily oral dosing and no intravenous form available in the class
drugs.indication: Hypertension
drugs.adverseEffects: A sprue-like enteropathy unique to this ARB — severe chronic diarrhea and weight loss — on top of the class hyperkalemia

drugs.name: Phenoxybenzamine
drugs.mechanism: Irreversible non-selective alpha blockade favoring alpha-1 over alpha-2, so recovery requires synthesis of new receptors
drugs.indication: Pheochromocytoma — pre-operative alpha blockade before any beta blocker is added — and urinary outlet obstruction
drugs.adverseEffects: Reflex tachycardia from alpha-2 autoreceptor block releasing unregulated norepinephrine, miosis, and 3 or more days of effect after a dose

drugs.name: Phentolamine
drugs.mechanism: Competitive non-selective alpha blockade with equal alpha-1 and alpha-2 affinity, given intravenously with a 19-minute half-life
drugs.indication: Vasopressor extravasation, and reversal of the vasoconstrictor in dental local anesthesia
drugs.adverseEffects: Marked reflex tachycardia and hypotension over its 10-30 minute duration

drugs.name: Phenylephrine
drugs.mechanism: Pure alpha-1 agonism raising systemic vascular resistance with no beta activity at all
drugs.indication: Distributive or hypovolemic shock in the patient whose tachyarrhythmia makes a beta agonist unattractive
drugs.adverseEffects: Reflex bradycardia as the baroreflex answers the rise in afterload

drugs.name: Prazosin
drugs.mechanism: Selective alpha-1 antagonism relaxing both resistance arterioles and capacitance veins, so preload falls along with peripheral vascular resistance
drugs.indication: Add-on therapy for mild to moderate refractory hypertension; not initial therapy because it offers less cardiovascular mortality protection
drugs.adverseEffects: First-dose orthostatic hypotension and syncope, worst at initiation or dose increase; give a small first dose at bedtime

drugs.name: Propranolol
drugs.mechanism: First-generation non-selective competitive antagonism of beta-1 and beta-2 receptors, with high lipid solubility and CNS penetration
drugs.indication: Angina, arrhythmia, hyperthyroid symptom control, and low-dose use an hour before performance anxiety
drugs.adverseEffects: Bronchospasm from beta-2 blockade in asthma or COPD, peripheral vascular insufficiency, fatigue, insomnia and nightmares

drugs.name: Sacubitril-Valsartan
drugs.mechanism: Pairs neprilysin inhibition, which raises natriuretic peptides, bradykinin and substance P, with AT1 receptor blockade
drugs.indication: HFrEF, where the combined natriuretic and RAS-blocking effect outperforms an ACE inhibitor alone
drugs.adverseEffects: Hypotension and hyperkalemia, with angioedema risk that forbids overlapping it with an ACE inhibitor

drugs.name: Sildenafil
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits phosphodiesterase-5, the enzyme that degrades cGMP, so the nitric oxide signal in vascular smooth muscle is sustained rather than created
drugs.indication: Pulmonary arterial hypertension and erectile dysfunction
drugs.adverseEffects: Profound hypotension when combined with nitrates, since both arms of the same cGMP pathway are being pushed at once

drugs.name: Spironolactone
drugs.mechanism: Crosses the basolateral membrane to antagonize the cytosolic mineralocorticoid receptor, blocking transcription of ENaC, Na+/K+ ATPase and ROMK, with an effect proportional to the prevailing aldosterone level
drugs.indication: Primary aldosteronism, HFrEF and HFpEF, cirrhotic ascites, resistant hypertension, and acne or hirsutism through its antiandrogen activity
drugs.adverseEffects: Hyperkalemia plus off-target steroid receptor effects — gynecomastia, impotence, loss of libido, and falsely elevated digoxin assays

drugs.name: Terazosin
drugs.mechanism: Alpha-1 selective blockade with near-100% bioavailability and a 12-hour half-life supporting once-daily dosing
drugs.indication: Hypertension with benign prostatic hyperplasia, where relaxing bladder neck and prostatic smooth muscle improves urine flow
drugs.adverseEffects: Orthostatic hypotension, nasal stuffiness from loss of mucosal vasoconstriction, and intraoperative floppy iris syndrome

drugs.name: Torsemide
drugs.mechanism: NKCC2 blockade delivered with nearly 100% oral bioavailability and a 3-5 hour half-life, so the block is predictable even when the gut wall is edematous
drugs.indication: The rational switch in refractory edema when high-dose oral furosemide fails in a heart failure patient with gut edema
drugs.adverseEffects: The same electrolyte profile as furosemide — hypokalemia, alkalosis, hypomagnesemia — with a longer duration of diuresis around 12 hours

drugs.name: Triamterene
drugs.mechanism: Direct ENaC blockade in the cortical collecting duct, abolishing the electrical gradient that drives potassium secretion
drugs.indication: Combined with a thiazide to offset hypokalemia in hypertension and edema
drugs.adverseEffects: Hyperkalemia, triamterene stones, and a risk of interstitial nephritis

drugs.name: Vasopressin
drugs.mechanism: V1 and V2 receptor agonism raising vascular tone through a pathway entirely independent of adrenergic receptors
drugs.indication: The second agent added to norepinephrine in septic shock when a single pressor is not enough
drugs.adverseEffects: Arrhythmias and cardiac ischemia; splanchnic and digital hypoperfusion

drugs.name: Verapamil
drugs.mechanism: Non-dihydropyridine L-type calcium channel blockade acting on vessels and heart alike, depressing sinus node automaticity and slowing AV conduction with the strongest frequency-dependent block of the class
drugs.indication: Supraventricular tachyarrhythmia in a hemodynamically stable patient, hypertension, and angina
drugs.adverseEffects: Bradycardia, worsened cardiac output and marked constipation; blocks P-glycoprotein so digoxin levels rise toward toxicity

transporters.name: 11-beta-HSD Type 2
transporters.location: Cytosol of the principal cell, alongside the mineralocorticoid receptor
transporters.function: Converts cortisol to inactive cortisone so that cortisol, which binds the mineralocorticoid receptor as well as aldosterone does, cannot activate it
transporters.regulation: Overwhelmed by very high cortisol, or blocked pharmacologically, producing apparent mineralocorticoid excess
transporters.inhibitor: Licorice (glycyrrhetinic acid)

transporters.name: AQP1 (Aquaporin-1)
transporters.location: Both apical and basolateral membranes of the proximal tubule and the descending thin limb
transporters.function: A constitutively open water pore, so water follows sodium osmotically for the roughly 65% isosmotic reabsorption of the proximal tubule and the further 10% that concentrates fluid in the descending limb
transporters.regulation: Always present and not hormonally gated — this is why proximal reabsorption is obligatory rather than adjustable
transporters.inhibitor: None used clinically

transporters.name: AQP2 (Aquaporin-2)
transporters.location: Apical membrane of collecting duct principal cells
transporters.function: The gated water exit of the nephron — water can only leave the collecting duct down the medullary osmotic gradient through this pore, so it sets final urine concentration
transporters.regulation: Vasopressin acting at V2 receptors translocates it into the apical membrane; without ADH the tubule stays water-impermeable and urine is dilute
transporters.inhibitor: Lithium impairs its insertion, producing nephrogenic diabetes insipidus

transporters.name: Band 3 Anion Exchanger
transporters.location: Red blood cell membrane
transporters.function: Carries out the chloride shift — bicarbonate generated inside the red cell leaves in exchange for chloride entering, preserving electroneutrality so CO2 carriage can continue
transporters.regulation: Runs in the opposite direction in the lung, where the whole sequence reverses to blow off CO2
transporters.inhibitor: Not a clinical target; carbonic anhydrase is the only red-cell-bound piece of the bicarbonate buffer system

transporters.name: Calcium-Sensing Receptor (CaSR)
transporters.location: Basolateral membrane of the thick ascending limb
transporters.function: Senses plasma calcium and dials down paracellular divalent reabsorption when it rises
transporters.regulation: Activated by high plasma calcium or magnesium — and because it discriminates poorly between them, either one reduces reabsorption of both
transporters.inhibitor: Cinacalcet activates it; loop diuretics mimic the downstream effect by abolishing the lumen-positive potential

transporters.name: Carbonic Anhydrase II and IV
transporters.location: CA II in the cytoplasm and CA IV anchored to the apical membrane of the proximal tubule (CA I lives in the red cell)
transporters.function: CA IV splits luminal H2CO3 to CO2 and water so the CO2 can diffuse in; CA II rebuilds HCO3- inside the cell and regenerates the H+ that NHE3 exports
transporters.regulation: Zinc-dependent and bidirectional, catalyzing the reaction in whichever direction the gradient runs
transporters.inhibitor: Sulfonamides — acetazolamide inhibits both isoforms, which is why bicarbonate reabsorption collapses

transporters.name: Delayed Rectifier K+ Channel
transporters.location: All cardiac myocytes
transporters.function: Opposes calcium entry during the phase 2 plateau and then dominates phase 3 repolarization, setting action potential duration
transporters.regulation: Balanced against L-type calcium current during the plateau
transporters.inhibitor: Class III antiarrhythmics, which prolong action potential duration and therefore the effective refractory period

transporters.name: ENaC (Epithelial Na+ Channel)
transporters.location: Apical membrane of principal cells in the late DCT, connecting tubule and cortical collecting duct
transporters.function: Sodium entry here leaves the lumen electrically negative, and that lumen-negative potential is the key determinant of potassium secretion through ROMK
transporters.regulation: Aldosterone raises its expression, as does any upstream diuretic that increases distal sodium delivery
transporters.inhibitor: Amiloride and triamterene directly; spironolactone and eplerenone by blocking its aldosterone-driven expression

transporters.name: Fast Na+ Channel (I_Na)
transporters.location: Atrial, ventricular and His-Purkinje myocytes — everywhere except the SA and AV nodes
transporters.function: Carries phase 0 of the fast-response action potential, driving an upstroke faster than 100 V/s once threshold near -55 mV is reached
transporters.regulation: Has two gates, and its recovery from inactivation is what sets the effective refractory period in fast fibers
transporters.inhibitor: Class I antiarrhythmics; also blocked by tricyclic antidepressants, which is why they widen the QRS

transporters.name: GLUT1 / GLUT2
transporters.location: Basolateral membrane of proximal tubule cells
transporters.function: Facilitated-diffusion channels that release reabsorbed glucose into the interstitium — sodium-independent, and the exit step that keeps intracellular glucose from backing up
transporters.regulation: Passive, following the concentration gradient created by apical SGLT uptake
transporters.inhibitor: Not a clinical drug target

transporters.name: H+-ATPase (proton pump)
transporters.location: Apical membrane of type A (alpha) intercalated cells in the collecting duct
transporters.function: Actively secretes protons against a steep gradient, generating new bicarbonate — this is the step that titrates urinary buffers and can drive urine pH down to its floor of 4.4
transporters.regulation: Inserted acutely in respiratory acidosis; stimulated by angiotensin II and aldosterone
transporters.inhibitor: Its expression falls under mineralocorticoid receptor blockade, which is why K+-sparing agents alkalinize the urine

transporters.name: H+/K+ ATPase
transporters.location: Apical membrane of type A (alpha) intercalated cells in the collecting duct
transporters.function: Secretes H+ into the lumen while reabsorbing K+ against its gradient, which is how the kidney claws back potassium during depletion
transporters.regulation: Upregulated in potassium depletion and by aldosterone
transporters.inhibitor: Its activity during K+ depletion is what couples hypokalemia to metabolic alkalosis

transporters.name: HCN Channel (Funny Current, I_f)
transporters.location: SA node, and to a lesser degree AV node and His-Purkinje tissue
transporters.function: The main driver of phase 4 spontaneous depolarization — a non-selective cation current carrying Na+ and K+ that generates automaticity
transporters.regulation: Opens on hyperpolarization below about -65 mV and is directly modulated by cyclic nucleotides, so sympathetic stimulation steepens the phase 4 slope and vagal tone flattens it
transporters.inhibitor: Ivabradine, which slows heart rate without touching contractility

transporters.name: I_K1 (Inward Rectifier K+ Channel)
transporters.location: Working atrial and ventricular myocardium
transporters.function: Holds the resting membrane potential near -90 mV during phase 4 and contributes to phase 3 repolarization
transporters.regulation: Its progressive closure during late phase 4 contributes to pacemaker depolarization in nodal tissue
transporters.inhibitor: Not a therapeutic target; hyperkalemia alters its behavior and produces the peaked T wave

transporters.name: I_KACh (Acetylcholine-activated K+ Channel)
transporters.location: SA node, atria and AV node
transporters.function: Opening it hyperpolarizes the pacemaker cell, moving the maximum diastolic potential further from threshold and slowing the rate
transporters.regulation: Activated by vagal acetylcholine at M2 receptors through the G-protein beta-gamma subunit
transporters.inhibitor: Atropine, by blocking the muscarinic receptor upstream

transporters.name: I_to (Transient Outward K+ Current)
transporters.location: Fast-response cardiac myocytes
transporters.function: Produces phase 1, the brief notch of early repolarization immediately after the sodium upstroke
transporters.regulation: Density varies across the ventricular wall, which is part of why epicardium and endocardium repolarize differently
transporters.inhibitor: Not a clinical target

transporters.name: K-ATP Channel (vascular smooth muscle)
transporters.location: Plasma membrane of arteriolar smooth muscle cells
transporters.function: Opening it lets potassium leave, hyperpolarizing the cell so voltage-gated calcium channels stay shut and the arteriole cannot contract
transporters.regulation: Opened by minoxidil sulfate, the active metabolite of minoxidil; closed by sulfonylureas in the pancreatic beta cell isoform
transporters.inhibitor: Sulfonylureas act on the beta-cell isoform; the vascular channel is opened, not blocked, by minoxidil

transporters.name: KCC (K+/Cl- cotransporter)
transporters.location: Apical membrane of principal cells and basolateral membrane of proximal tubule cells
transporters.function: An electrically neutral exit route that moves potassium out with chloride, working alongside ROMK to set potassium secretion
transporters.regulation: Driven by the chloride gradient rather than by membrane voltage
transporters.inhibitor: Not a clinical drug target

transporters.name: L-type Calcium Channel
transporters.location: Vascular smooth muscle, cardiac myocytes, and SA and AV nodal tissue
transporters.function: A slow, high-threshold channel that admits extracellular calcium and triggers calcium-induced calcium release; in smooth muscle the calcium-calmodulin complex activates MLCK, phosphorylating myosin light chains to produce contraction
transporters.regulation: Blockers bind the pore-forming alpha-1 subunit from the inner side of the membrane and prefer open and inactivated states, so the block deepens with stimulation frequency
transporters.inhibitor: Verapamil and diltiazem (heart and vessels), and the dihydropyridines (arteriolar smooth muscle)

transporters.name: MATE1 / MATE2-K
transporters.location: Apical membrane of the proximal straight tubule
transporters.function: The exit step of organic cation secretion, using the H+ gradient to push cations into tubular fluid
transporters.regulation: Depends on the luminal proton gradient set up by NHE3
transporters.inhibitor: Cimetidine, and drugs competing for the same carrier

transporters.name: Megalin-Cubilin Endocytosis
transporters.location: Apical clathrin-coated pits of the proximal tubule
transporters.function: Receptor-mediated endocytosis that recovers 96-99% of filtered albumin plus low-molecular-weight proteins and peptide hormones, digesting them in lysosomes and returning amino acids basolaterally
transporters.regulation: Requires ATP and microtubule-associated movement, so it fails when the tubule is injured
transporters.inhibitor: Metabolic inhibitors and cytochalasin B — which is why tubular injury alone can cause proteinuria with a normal glomerulus

transporters.name: Na+/Ca2+ Exchanger (NCX)
transporters.location: Sarcolemma of cardiac myocytes
transporters.function: Extrudes 1 Ca2+ in exchange for 3 Na+ entering, so the net charge movement is depolarizing; it is a main route of calcium removal during relaxation
transporters.regulation: Runs in reverse when intracellular sodium is high — the mechanism behind digoxin's inotropy and its toxicity
transporters.inhibitor: Indirectly by digoxin, which raises intracellular sodium by blocking the Na+/K+ ATPase

transporters.name: Na+/K+ ATPase
transporters.location: Basolateral membrane of every sodium-reabsorbing tubular cell
transporters.function: Pumps 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP, keeping intracellular sodium low so that every apical sodium entry step — NHE3, SGLT, NKCC2, NCC, ENaC — has a downhill gradient to work with
transporters.regulation: Aldosterone raises both its activity and its numbers in principal cells
transporters.inhibitor: Digoxin in the cardiomyocyte isoform; hypokalemia leaves fewer K+ ions competing with digoxin at the pump

transporters.name: NaPi Cotransporters
transporters.location: Apical membrane of the proximal tubule
transporters.function: Reabsorb 80-95% of filtered phosphate — essentially all of it happens here, with almost nothing recovered downstream
transporters.regulation: PTH removes the transporter from the membrane, producing phosphaturia; FGF23 does the same
transporters.inhibitor: PTH indirectly, by internalizing the carrier

transporters.name: NBCe1 (Na+/HCO3- cotransporter)
transporters.location: Basolateral membrane of the proximal tubule
transporters.function: The exit door for reclaimed bicarbonate — it carries the HCO3- rebuilt inside the cell by carbonic anhydrase II back into the blood, completing reabsorption of the 4,320 mmol filtered each day
transporters.regulation: Upregulated along with NHE3 in chronic respiratory acidosis
transporters.inhibitor: Not directly blocked; the whole pathway stalls when carbonic anhydrase is inhibited

transporters.name: NCC (Na+-Cl- cotransporter)
transporters.location: Apical membrane of the distal convoluted tubule
transporters.function: Reabsorbs 5-10% of the filtered sodium load in a water-impermeable segment, so it dilutes tubular fluid without touching the medullary gradient and concentrating ability stays intact
transporters.regulation: Upregulated during chronic loop diuretic use as part of the distal nephron remodeling that produces diuretic resistance
transporters.inhibitor: Thiazides — hydrochlorothiazide and chlorthalidone

transporters.name: NHE3 (Na+/H+ exchanger)
transporters.location: Apical membrane of the proximal tubule
transporters.function: Moves sodium in as H+ goes out to titrate filtered bicarbonate, driving reabsorption of 65-70% of filtered sodium and 80-90% of filtered bicarbonate
transporters.regulation: Stimulated by angiotensin II; stalls when carbonic anhydrase cannot regenerate intracellular H+
transporters.inhibitor: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors indirectly, by starving it of the H+ it needs to export

transporters.name: NKCC1
transporters.location: Stria vascularis of the inner ear
transporters.function: Sustains the endolymph potassium balance that normal hearing and balance depend on
transporters.regulation: Constitutively active and unrelated to renal sodium handling
transporters.inhibitor: Loop diuretics — the off-target hit that produces ototoxicity, worst with ethacrynic acid

transporters.name: NKCC2 (Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter)
transporters.location: Apical membrane of the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle
transporters.function: Reabsorbs about 25% of the filtered sodium load without water, simultaneously diluting tubular fluid and building the hypertonic medullary interstitium
transporters.regulation: Vasopressin raises its activity, and luminal K+ recycling through ROMK keeps it supplied with potassium
transporters.inhibitor: Loop diuretics — furosemide, torsemide, bumetanide, ethacrynic acid

transporters.name: OCT2
transporters.location: Basolateral membrane of the proximal straight tubule (S3)
transporters.function: The entry step of the organic base secretory system, drawing organic cations out of blood driven by the inside-negative membrane potential
transporters.regulation: Paired with apical MATE1, MATE2-K and MDR1 for exit; handles dopamine, epinephrine, norepinephrine and histamine
transporters.inhibitor: Competition from cimetidine and other cationic drugs; blocking it stops amiloride and triamterene from ever reaching their luminal target

transporters.name: Organic Anion Transporters (OATs)
transporters.location: Basolateral then apical membranes of the proximal tubule cell
transporters.function: Secrete highly protein-bound drugs from blood into tubular fluid — the only route by which a diuretic too albumin-bound to be filtered reaches its luminal target
transporters.regulation: Competitive, so any organic anion in the blood competes for the same carrier
transporters.inhibitor: Probenecid and NSAIDs, producing a blunted diuretic response at a normal serum drug level

transporters.name: Pendrin (Cl-/HCO3- exchanger)
transporters.location: Apical membrane of type B (beta) intercalated cells in the collecting duct
transporters.function: Secretes bicarbonate into the lumen while reclaiming chloride — the reverse of the alpha cell, and the route by which the kidney corrects a metabolic alkalosis
transporters.regulation: The proportion of beta cells rises in metabolic alkalosis, and alpha cells can convert to beta cells
transporters.inhibitor: None clinically

transporters.name: PepT1 / PepT2
transporters.location: Apical membrane of the proximal tubule — PepT1 in S1-S2, PepT2 in S3
transporters.function: H+-coupled cotransport of 2-5 residue peptides that resisted brush-border hydrolysis, recovering 99% of filtered oligopeptides
transporters.regulation: PepT1 is low-affinity and high-capacity; PepT2 is high-affinity and low-capacity, mirroring the SGLT2/SGLT1 arrangement
transporters.inhibitor: Not a clinical drug target, though it carries beta-lactam antibiotics

transporters.name: RhBG / RhCG (ammonia gas channels)
transporters.location: Medullary collecting duct cells
transporters.function: Move NH3 into the lumen, where secreted H+ traps it as NH4+ — diffusion trapping, the mechanism behind 40 of the 70 mmol of daily net acid excretion
transporters.regulation: Ammoniagenesis from glutamine rises in chronic metabolic acidosis and in hypokalemia
transporters.inhibitor: None; hyperkalemia competes with NH4+ in the medulla and blunts the pathway

transporters.name: ROMK
transporters.location: Apical membrane of principal cells in the collecting duct and of thick ascending limb cells
transporters.function: Secretes potassium down the lumen-negative gradient in the collecting duct, and recycles potassium back into the lumen in the TAL to keep NKCC2 running
transporters.regulation: Aldosterone raises its activity, and secretion climbs with distal sodium delivery and tubular flow
transporters.inhibitor: Blocked indirectly by ENaC inhibitors and MR antagonists, which collapse the driving gradient

transporters.name: Ryanodine Receptor
transporters.location: Sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane of cardiac myocytes
transporters.function: The calcium release channel of calcium-induced calcium release — a small L-type calcium entry triggers a large SR calcium release that actually drives contraction
transporters.regulation: Opened by calcium entering through L-type channels during phase 2
transporters.inhibitor: Ryanodine experimentally; dantrolene acts on the skeletal muscle isoform

transporters.name: SERCA
transporters.location: Sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane of cardiac myocytes
transporters.function: An ATP-driven pump that reloads the SR with calcium, ending contraction and setting up the next beat
transporters.regulation: Released from phospholamban inhibition when PKA phosphorylates it during beta-1 stimulation, which speeds relaxation (lusitropy)
transporters.inhibitor: Not clinically blocked

transporters.name: SGLT1
transporters.location: Apical membrane of the S3 segment of the proximal straight tubule
transporters.function: A low-capacity, high-affinity carrier moving 2 Na+ per glucose, which gives it the steepest apical gradient and lets it scavenge whatever SGLT2 missed
transporters.regulation: Positioned late in the tubule where luminal glucose is already low, so it works as the mop-up transporter
transporters.inhibitor: Weakly by SGLT2 inhibitors; it is also the main intestinal glucose transporter

transporters.name: SGLT2
transporters.location: Apical membrane of the S1 segment of the proximal convoluted tubule
transporters.function: A high-capacity, low-affinity carrier moving 1 Na+ with 1 glucose, responsible for about 90% of glucose reabsorption
transporters.regulation: Powered indirectly by the sodium gradient the basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase maintains; saturates once the filtered load exceeds the transport maximum
transporters.inhibitor: SGLT2 inhibitors, the -flozin glucuretics approved for type 2 diabetes and heart failure

transporters.name: T-type Calcium Channel
transporters.location: SA and AV nodal tissue
transporters.function: Contributes to late phase 4 depolarization, helping carry the pacemaker potential up to threshold
transporters.regulation: Transient and low-threshold, opening at more negative potentials than the L-type channel
transporters.inhibitor: Not selectively targeted by the standard calcium channel blockers

transporters.name: TRPM6
transporters.location: Apical membrane of the distal convoluted tubule
transporters.function: The regulated magnesium entry pathway of the DCT
transporters.regulation: Downregulated by the DCT remodeling that follows chronic thiazide exposure
transporters.inhibitor: Chronic thiazide therapy indirectly, producing hypomagnesemia

transporters.name: TRPV5
transporters.location: Apical membrane of the distal convoluted tubule
transporters.function: The entry step for regulated calcium reabsorption, which is why thiazides lower urinary calcium and reduce stone recurrence
transporters.regulation: Driven by the basolateral Na+/Ca2+ exchanger NCX1 (3 Na+ in, 1 Ca2+ out) and fine-tuned by PMCA1b
transporters.inhibitor: Not directly blocked — thiazides raise its activity by lowering intracellular sodium

transporters.name: URAT1
transporters.location: Apical membrane of the proximal tubule, alongside OAT4 and OAT10
transporters.function: Reabsorbs filtered urate; because reabsorption dominates over secretion, only about 10% of the filtered urate load is finally excreted
transporters.regulation: Volume depletion enhances proximal fluid reabsorption and drags more urate with it, which is exactly how diuretics raise plasma urate
transporters.inhibitor: Probenecid, which blocks reabsorption and is therefore uricosuric

transporters.name: UT-A1 / UT-A3 (Urea Transporters)
transporters.location: Apical (UT-A1) and basolateral (UT-A3) membranes of the medullary collecting duct
transporters.function: Reabsorb about 50% of luminal urea transcellularly, depositing it in the medullary interstitium where it contributes much of the osmotic gradient that concentrates urine
transporters.regulation: Vasopressin increases their activity, coupling urea recycling to water conservation
transporters.inhibitor: None clinically; at low urine flow only about 15% of filtered urea escapes, which is why BUN climbs in dehydration

transporters.name: UT-A2
transporters.location: Thin limbs of the loop of Henle
transporters.function: Secretes urea back into the tubular lumen, restoring luminal urea after the proximal tubule reabsorbed roughly half of it paracellularly
transporters.regulation: Part of the urea recycling loop that sustains the medullary gradient
transporters.inhibitor: None

transporters.name: V1 Receptor
transporters.location: Vascular smooth muscle
transporters.function: Mediates the pressor arm of vasopressin — raising intracellular calcium for sustained vasoconstriction and higher blood pressure, entirely separate from water handling
transporters.regulation: Engaged at higher vasopressin concentrations than V2, which is why the hormone becomes a pressor only in severe volume depletion
transporters.inhibitor: V1 antagonists; vasopressin is used deliberately at these receptors in septic shock

transporters.name: V2 Receptor
transporters.location: Basolateral membrane of collecting duct principal cells
transporters.function: A GPCR that signals through adenylate cyclase and cAMP to drive both AQP2 transcription and its insertion into the luminal membrane — the single control point for final urine concentration
transporters.regulation: Activated by arginine vasopressin released from the posterior pituitary in response to rising plasma osmolality sensed at circumventricular osmoreceptors
transporters.inhibitor: Vaptans; caffeine potentiates the pathway as a phosphodiesterase inhibitor

formulas.name: Accessory Muscle Recruitment
formulas.equation: Abdominals at ~40 L/min, sternocleidomastoid and serratus at ~50 L/min, spinal erectors and trapezius at ~100 L/min
formulas.meaning: The diaphragm and intercostals carry resting breathing; each further muscle group joins only at a defined minute ventilation, which is why accessory muscle use is a bedside marker of respiratory distress
formulas.normalValue: Resting minute ventilation is only about 7.5 L/min

formulas.name: Alveolar Ventilation
formulas.equation: VA = (VT - VD) x RR
formulas.meaning: The only ventilation that actually participates in gas exchange, which is why rapid shallow breathing can raise minute ventilation while lowering alveolar ventilation

formulas.name: ATR to Cobb Correlation
formulas.equation: An angle of trunk rotation of 7 degrees corresponds roughly to a 20-degree Cobb angle
formulas.meaning: The two scales are not interchangeable and carry different risks of progression, so the referral note must say which was measured
formulas.normalValue: Refer at ATR 7 degrees, or ATR 5 degrees when BMI is at or above the 85th percentile

formulas.name: Atrial Kick
formulas.equation: About 10 mL of a 140 mL end-diastolic volume, up to 20% at most
formulas.meaning: Most atrial blood reaches the ventricle passively during atrial diastole, not during atrial systole — so losing the kick matters only when the ventricle is already stiff or the rate is high
formulas.normalValue: Its loss is what makes new atrial fibrillation symptomatic

formulas.name: Bicarbonate Reabsorption by Segment
formulas.equation: PCT 80%, thick ascending limb 10%, DCT 6%, medullary collecting duct 4%, urine 0.01%
formulas.meaning: Nearly all bicarbonate handling is reclamation in the proximal tubule; the distal nephron contributes little volume but does the regulated fine-tuning
formulas.normalValue: Minimum achievable urinary pH is 4.4 — free protons alone would require a pH of 1.3, which is why buffers are obligatory

formulas.name: Blood Pressure
formulas.equation: BP = Cardiac Output x Peripheral Vascular Resistance
formulas.meaning: Every antihypertensive drug works by lowering one of these two terms, which is why the drug classes sort onto four control sites: resistance arterioles, capacitance venules, the heart and the kidneys
formulas.normalValue: Under 120/80 mm Hg; stage 1 is 130-139 systolic or 80-89 diastolic, stage 2 is 140/90 or above

formulas.name: Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN)
formulas.equation: BUN reflects urea, the primary nitrogenous end product of amino acid catabolism
formulas.meaning: Urea is made in the liver urea cycle, which detoxifies about 95% of ammonium; it makes up roughly half of all urinary solute and doubles as a tool for water regulation
formulas.normalValue: 7-18 mg/dL, with plasma urea 2.5-6 mM — an unusually wide tolerable range

formulas.name: Blood Velocity
formulas.equation: v = Q / A, where A = pi x r^2
formulas.meaning: Velocity is inversely proportional to total cross-sectional area, so blood races through the aorta and crawls through the capillaries — while total flow stays constant everywhere in the circuit
formulas.normalValue: About 1,752 cm/min in the aorta versus 2.2 cm/min in the capillary bed

formulas.name: Bohr Effect (Curve Shifts)
formulas.equation: Right shift: high PCO2, low pH, high temperature, high 2,3-DPG. Left shift: the reverse
formulas.meaning: A right shift raises P50 to about 40 mmHg so oxygen unloads more easily in exercising tissue; a left shift drops it to about 12.5 mmHg, favoring loading in the lung
formulas.normalValue: Applies to adult hemoglobin only — HbF does not interact with 2,3-BPG, which is how the fetus outcompetes maternal blood

formulas.name: Bohr-Enghoff Equation
formulas.equation: VD/VT = (PACO2 - PECO2) / PACO2
formulas.meaning: Estimates the dead space fraction from the difference between alveolar and mixed expired CO2, with arterial PaCO2 substituted for alveolar PACO2 in practice
formulas.normalValue: Fowler's nitrogen method gives the anatomic value directly, about 150 mL of a 500 mL tidal volume

formulas.name: BUN:Creatinine Ratio
formulas.equation: BUN : Creatinine
formulas.meaning: Separates pre-renal failure from intrinsic disease — hypoperfusion drives sodium and water retention, urea follows the water back into the blood while creatinine does not
formulas.normalValue: Above 20:1 indicates a pre-renal pattern from dehydration, heart failure or arterial insult

formulas.name: Calcium Handling by Segment
formulas.equation: PCT 65% paracellular, TAL 25% paracellular, DCT 8% transcellular
formulas.meaning: Bulk calcium recovery is passive and unregulated; the DCT handles only 8% but through TRPV5/TRPV6 it is the regulatory site where PTH and thiazides act
formulas.normalValue: 99% of body calcium is stored in bone as hydroxyapatite

formulas.name: Carbon Monoxide Affinity
formulas.equation: CO binds the heme oxygen site with 210-250 times the affinity of oxygen
formulas.meaning: Competitive displacement forms carboxyhemoglobin, and because CO never accumulates a dissolved partial pressure it stays diffusion-limited and keeps loading
formulas.normalValue: Clearance takes about 5 hours on room air, 1.5 hours on saturated oxygen, and 20 minutes at 3 atmospheres hyperbaric

formulas.name: Cardiac Conduction Velocities
formulas.equation: Purkinje 2-4 m/s > His and bundle branches 2 m/s > atria and ventricles 0.5-1 m/s > AV node 0.01-0.05 m/s
formulas.meaning: The AV node is deliberately the slowest link, creating the delay that lets the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract
formulas.normalValue: The SA node itself conducts at only about 0.01 m/s

formulas.name: Cardiac Cycle Timing
formulas.equation: One beat lasts 0.8-0.9 s at 60-100 bpm; two-thirds diastole and one-third systole at rest
formulas.meaning: Atrial systole takes about 100 ms against roughly 800 ms of atrial diastole, and the AV nodal delay of more than 0.1 s exists so the atria can load the ventricles first
formulas.normalValue: With exertion diastole shortens far more than systole, which is why tachycardia compromises filling and coronary perfusion

formulas.name: Cardiac Equilibrium Potentials
formulas.equation: E_K about -96 mV, E_Na about +52 mV, E_Ca about +134 mV
formulas.meaning: Each phase of the action potential drives membrane voltage toward the equilibrium potential of whichever ion is conducting, which is why phase 0 shoots positive and phase 3 returns negative
formulas.normalValue: Resting membrane potential about -90 mV, set by I_K1

formulas.name: Cardiac Output
formulas.equation: CO = Stroke Volume x Heart Rate
formulas.meaning: The volume of blood the heart ejects per minute, and the term that beta blockers and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers attack
formulas.normalValue: About 5 L/min at rest

formulas.name: Central Venous Pressure
formulas.equation: CVP = pressure in the thoracic vena cava near the right atrium
formulas.meaning: The filling pressure of the right heart and the practical measure of preload, obtained invasively by catheter
formulas.normalValue: 0-7 mmHg

formulas.name: Clearance
formulas.equation: Cx = (Ux x V) / Px
formulas.meaning: The volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance per minute; comparing it to GFR tells you what the tubule did — equal means neither secreted nor reabsorbed, higher means net secretion, lower means net reabsorption
formulas.normalValue: Inulin clearance equals GFR exactly, which is why it is the gold standard marker

formulas.name: CO2 Transport Fractions
formulas.equation: Bicarbonate over 80%, carbaminohemoglobin 5-10%, dissolved 5-10%
formulas.meaning: CO2 enters the red cell, carbonic anhydrase makes carbonic acid, which dissociates to bicarbonate and H+; the bicarbonate leaves through band 3 in exchange for chloride
formulas.normalValue: Dissolved CO2 = 40 mmHg x 0.07 = 2.8 mL per 100 mL blood

formulas.name: Countercurrent Single Effect and Multiplication
formulas.equation: 200 mOsm single effect, multiplied to about 900 mOsm from cortex to papilla
formulas.meaning: Active NaCl transport out of the water-impermeable ascending limb creates a 200 mOsm gradient at any one level, and countercurrent geometry stacks that difference down the medulla
formulas.normalValue: Urea contributes about half the total osmolality of the deepest inner medulla

formulas.name: Daily Acid-Base Budget
formulas.equation: HCO3- filtered and reabsorbed 4,320 mmol/day; CO2 expired ~15,000 mmol/day; urinary H+ ~70 mmol/day
formulas.meaning: The scale gap is the whole point — plasma H+ is measured in nanomoles while filtered bicarbonate is measured in millimoles, so losing even a little filtered bicarbonate is catastrophic
formulas.normalValue: Arterial pH 7.37-7.42, equal to about 40 nEq/L of H+

formulas.name: Daily Water Balance
formulas.equation: Intake 2500 mL/day = output 2500 mL/day
formulas.meaning: Inputs are ingested fluid 1200, water in food 1000 and aerobic metabolism 300; outputs are urine 1500, skin and sweat 550, exhaled air 350 and feces 100 — and only the kidney adjusts to match intake
formulas.normalValue: Sweat regulates core temperature, not water balance

formulas.name: Dalton's Law
formulas.equation: Px = (PB - PH2O) x F
formulas.meaning: Partial pressure is the total pressure times that gas's fraction, corrected for the water vapor the airway adds — which is why humidification alone costs 10 mmHg of oxygen tension
formulas.normalValue: Tracheal PO2 = (760 - 47) x 0.21 = 150 mmHg; PH2O is 47 mmHg at 37 C

formulas.name: Dead Space
formulas.equation: Physiologic dead space = anatomic + alveolar dead space
formulas.meaning: Ventilation without perfusion — the anatomic portion is the conducting airways from nose to terminal bronchioles, and the alveolar portion is alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused
formulas.normalValue: Anatomic dead space about 150 mL; it increases with age

formulas.name: Dead Space Ventilation (V/Q = infinity)
formulas.equation: Ventilation present, perfusion absent — wasted ventilation
formulas.meaning: The alveolus holds inspired values of 150/0 because no blood arrives to exchange with; the classic cause is pulmonary embolism
formulas.normalValue: Compensations are bronchoconstriction toward the unperfused unit and hypoxic vasoconstriction away from the unventilated one

formulas.name: Determinants of Pacemaker Rate
formulas.equation: Rate = distance / speed, where distance is maximum diastolic potential to threshold and speed is the phase 4 slope
formulas.meaning: Vagal stimulation attacks all three levers at once — it hyperpolarizes through I_KACh while reducing I_f and I_Ca to flatten the slope, which is why acetylcholine is such a powerful brake
formulas.normalValue: A flatter slope, a more negative maximum diastolic potential, or a less negative threshold all slow the rate

formulas.name: Diffusion vs Perfusion Limitation
formulas.equation: Perfusion-limited: equilibrates within 1/3 of transit. Diffusion-limited: a gradient persists the whole way
formulas.meaning: Carbon monoxide is always diffusion-limited because it binds hemoglobin instantly and never accumulates a dissolved partial pressure, so the gradient never closes; oxygen and CO2 are normally perfusion-limited
formulas.normalValue: Capillary transit falls from 0.75 s at rest to 0.25 s at maximal exercise, and oxygen still equilibrates in a healthy lung

formulas.name: Dynamic Airway Collapse in Emphysema
formulas.equation: Large airway transmural pressure = airway pressure - intrapleural pressure
formulas.meaning: Normally the large airway sits at +25 against an intrapleural +20, giving a +5 that keeps it open; in emphysema the airway pressure falls to +15 against the same +20, so transmural pressure turns negative and the airway collapses on expiration
formulas.normalValue: This is why emphysema patients purse their lips — it raises airway pressure and keeps transmural pressure positive

formulas.name: ECG Paper Calibration
formulas.equation: 25 mm/sec paper speed, 10 mm/mV amplitude
formulas.meaning: The horizontal axis is time and the vertical axis is voltage, which is why every interval can be read straight off the grid
formulas.normalValue: 1 small box = 0.04 s, 1 large box = 5 small boxes = 0.2 s; the calibration box is 2 big boxes tall by 1 wide

formulas.name: ECG Rate Estimation
formulas.equation: 300, 150, 100, 75, 60, 50 — counting large boxes between R waves
formulas.meaning: The lecturer's preferred method for regular rhythms; for irregular rhythms count QRS complexes across the whole 10-second strip and multiply by 6
formulas.normalValue: Bradycardia below 60, normal 60-100, tachycardia above 100 bpm

formulas.name: Ejection Fraction
formulas.equation: EF = (EDV - ESV) x 100 / EDV = SV x 100 / EDV
formulas.meaning: The fraction of the end-diastolic volume actually ejected — the standard non-invasive measure of systolic function, obtained by transthoracic echocardiography
formulas.normalValue: Normally 55-70%; a reduced value defines HFrEF

formulas.name: Every V/Q Defect Causes Both
formulas.equation: Any V/Q mismatch produces hypoxemia AND hypercapnia
formulas.meaning: Inefficient exchange strands oxygen outside the blood and carbon dioxide inside it at the same time, in either direction of mismatch
formulas.normalValue: Left-to-right shunts (ASD, PDA) typically do not cause hypoxemia; right-to-left shunts (VSD, Eisenmenger) always do

formulas.name: Excretion
formulas.equation: Excretion = Filtration - Reabsorption + Secretion
formulas.meaning: The master balance sheet of the nephron: what leaves in the urine is what was filtered, minus what was taken back, plus what was added along the tubule
formulas.normalValue: Of 173 L filtered daily, 99% is reabsorbed and about 1.73 L is excreted

formulas.name: Fast vs Slow Response Action Potentials
formulas.equation: Fast response phase 0 = Na+ current; slow response phase 0 = L-type Ca2+ current
formulas.meaning: Only the SA and AV nodes use the slow response, which is precisely why calcium channel blockers act on nodal tissue while sodium channel blockers act on working myocardium and Purkinje fibers
formulas.normalValue: Upstroke velocity over 100 V/s for fast fibers versus about 10 V/s for slow

formulas.name: FEV1/FVC Ratio
formulas.equation: FEV1 / FVC
formulas.meaning: The single number that separates obstruction from restriction — obstruction drops it because FEV1 falls far more than FVC, while restriction preserves or raises it because stiff lungs empty fast
formulas.normalValue: About 80% (70% on the guideline cut-off), falling with age; roughly 42% in COPD and 90% in fibrosis

formulas.name: Fick Principle
formulas.equation: CO = O2 consumption / (arterial O2 - venous O2)
formulas.meaning: A laboratory route to cardiac output that needs no stroke volume measurement — with the trap that pulmonary vein oxygen is the arterial value and pulmonary artery oxygen is the venous value
formulas.normalValue: Gives the same answer as CO = SV x HR, about 5 L/min

formulas.name: Fick's Law of Diffusion
formulas.equation: Vx = D x A x dP / dx
formulas.meaning: Transfer rate rises with the diffusion constant, alveolar surface area and the pressure gradient, and falls with membrane thickness — naming exactly how each lung disease impairs gas exchange
formulas.normalValue: D for CO2 is about 50 times that for O2; fibrosis and edema raise dx, emphysema lowers A

formulas.name: Filtered Load
formulas.equation: Filtered load = GFR x plasma concentration
formulas.meaning: How much of a substance arrives at the tubule per minute; glucosuria appears the moment the filtered load exceeds the reabsorptive capacity of SGLT2
formulas.normalValue: About 125 mg/min for glucose at a normal plasma level

formulas.name: Filtration Fraction
formulas.equation: FF = GFR / RPF
formulas.meaning: The proportion of arriving plasma that gets filtered; it rises in dehydration and renal artery stenosis where GFR is defended as RPF falls, and drops in glomerular disease where GFR falls while RPF holds
formulas.normalValue: About 20%

formulas.name: Fractional Excretion of Urea
formulas.equation: FE_urea = 15% at minimal urine flow, over 65% at maximal flow
formulas.meaning: ADH raises both water and urea permeability in the inner medullary collecting duct, so antidiuresis traps urea in the medulla to help build the gradient
formulas.normalValue: Luminal urea reaches 8-10 times the plasma concentration during antidiuresis

formulas.name: Fractional Shortening
formulas.equation: FS = (LVIDd - LVIDs) x 100 / LVIDd
formulas.meaning: The same idea as ejection fraction but measured from linear chamber dimensions rather than volumes
formulas.normalValue: An echocardiographic alternative when volumes are hard to trace

formulas.name: Frank-Starling Law
formulas.equation: Stroke volume rises as end-diastolic volume rises
formulas.meaning: Greater passive stretch produces greater force of contraction, so the ventricle ejects whatever extra volume returns to it — on the pressure-volume loop only EDV moves, not ESV
formulas.normalValue: The curve shifts up and left in exercise and with positive inotropes, and down and right in heart failure

formulas.name: Free Water Clearance
formulas.equation: V = C_osm + C_H2O, so C_H2O = V - C_osm
formulas.meaning: Splits urine flow into the isosmotic volume and the pure water added or subtracted; a positive value means the kidney is dumping free water, a negative value means it is conserving it
formulas.normalValue: Positive when urine is below 300 mOsm, zero when isosmotic, negative when above 300 mOsm

formulas.name: Functional Residual Capacity
formulas.equation: FRC = RV + ERV
formulas.meaning: The relaxed volume of the lung at the end of a quiet breath, where inward elastic recoil exactly balances outward chest wall recoil
formulas.normalValue: About 2,200 mL; it falls when supine, in obesity, in ascites and in pregnancy, and rises in obstructive disease

formulas.name: General Gas Law and Boyle's Law
formulas.equation: PV = nRT; P1V1 = P2V2 at constant temperature
formulas.meaning: Boyle's law is inspiration and expiration in one line — the rib cage expands, pressure falls, air enters; BTPS versus STPD is why lung volumes must state their conditions
formulas.normalValue: BTPS is 37 C, ambient pressure, saturated with water vapor; STPD is 0 C, 760 mmHg, dry

formulas.name: Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
formulas.equation: GFR = Kf x [(P_GC - P_BS) - (pi_GC - pi_BS)]
formulas.meaning: The volume of plasma filtered into Bowman space per minute — the single best indicator of kidney function, and the product of the filtration coefficient and the net Starling pressure
formulas.normalValue: About 120 mL/min, which is 20% of renal plasma flow and filters roughly 173 L per day

formulas.name: Glucose Threshold and Transport Maximum
formulas.equation: Threshold = 200 mg/dL; Tm = ~400 mg/min
formulas.meaning: Glucose is 100% filtered and over 99% reabsorbed until the SGLTs saturate; the threshold is where glucose first appears in urine, and the Tm is where every carrier is fully occupied
formulas.normalValue: Plasma glucose 100 mg/dL — half the threshold — which is why healthy people never spill glucose

formulas.name: Haldane Effect
formulas.equation: Deoxyhemoglobin binds CO2 and H+ more readily than oxyhemoglobin
formulas.meaning: In an exercising muscle three things reinforce each other: the curve right-shifts so oxygen comes off, the resulting deoxyhemoglobin carries more CO2, and that same deoxyhemoglobin buffers the H+ the bicarbonate reaction just made. All three reverse in the lung
formulas.normalValue: CO2 binds at a site distinct from the oxygen site, so the two are not competitive

formulas.name: Heart Rate Ceiling for Cardiac Output
formulas.equation: Cardiac output rises with heart rate up to 180-200 bpm, then falls
formulas.meaning: Faster rates shorten diastole and cut stroke volume, but up to that ceiling the rate increase more than compensates; beyond it both stroke volume and output collapse
formulas.normalValue: Subendocardial left ventricle is perfused only during diastole, which is why tachycardia also starves the coronaries

formulas.name: Helium Dilution
formulas.equation: C1 x V1 = C2 x (V1 + V2)
formulas.meaning: Helium is not absorbed across the alveolar membrane, so the dilution of a known starting concentration reports the unknown lung volume it mixed into
formulas.normalValue: A worked example gives FRC 3,050 mL and RV 1,850 mL

formulas.name: Henry's Law
formulas.equation: Cx = Px x solubility
formulas.meaning: Only gas free in solution exerts a partial pressure — protein-bound gas is invisible to it, which is the whole explanation for why a normal PO2 does not guarantee normal oxygen content
formulas.normalValue: Oxygen is mostly hemoglobin-bound with a small dissolved fraction; CO2 is majority soluble, and both dissolved CO2 and bicarbonate count toward PCO2

formulas.name: Hypoxic Pulmonary Vasoconstriction
formulas.equation: Triggered when alveolar PO2 falls below 70 mmHg
formulas.meaning: The pulmonary circulation does the opposite of every other capillary bed — it constricts when hypoxic, diverting blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli, which is protective in pneumonia
formulas.normalValue: Focal hypoxia shifts flow harmlessly; global hypoxia at altitude raises vascular resistance and drives right heart failure

formulas.name: Indicator Dilution Cardiac Output
formulas.equation: CO = (mg dye x 60) / (average concentration per mL x curve duration in seconds)
formulas.meaning: Cardiogreen injected into a large vein travels through the right heart, lungs and left heart, and the shape of the peripheral concentration curve reports the output
formulas.normalValue: A deeper, delayed and longer curve means a reduced cardiac output; recirculation makes the tail rise again

formulas.name: Intrapleural Fluid Balance
formulas.equation: Hydrostatic -5 inward, oncotic +5 outward, with the oncotic forces cancelling
formulas.meaning: About 10 mL of pleural fluid provides cohesion and lubrication, drained by lymphatics — when that drainage fails the result is a pleural effusion
formulas.normalValue: Atmospheric 760 mmHg against intrapleural 756 mmHg, a 4 mmHg difference at rest

formulas.name: Intrinsic Heart Rate
formulas.equation: Intrinsic HR (both autonomic limbs blocked) is about 100 bpm; resting HR is about 70 bpm
formulas.meaning: Because the heart runs slower at rest than when denervated, parasympathetic tone must be dominant at rest
formulas.normalValue: Both intrinsic heart rate and maximum heart rate (220 - age) decline with age

formulas.name: Intrinsic Pacemaker Rates
formulas.equation: SA node 60-100/min; AV node 40-60/min
formulas.meaning: The SA node is dominant and defines bradycardia below 60 and tachycardia above 100; the AV node takes over as an escape pacemaker at a slower intrinsic rate
formulas.normalValue: Conduction velocity order: Purkinje > atria > ventricles > AV node

formulas.name: Laplace's Law
formulas.equation: Wall tension = (transmural pressure x radius) / (2 x wall thickness)
formulas.meaning: Wall tension climbs with radius, which is why an aneurysm that starts dilating keeps dilating and why a thin-walled dilated ventricle works under punishing tension
formulas.normalValue: Compliance, stiffness and wall thickness are three separate properties — do not conflate them

formulas.name: Lobes, Fissures and Segments
formulas.equation: Right lung: 3 lobes, 10 segments, minor and major fissures. Left lung: 2 lobes, 8 segments, major fissure only
formulas.meaning: The lingula belongs to the left upper lobe, not to a separate middle lobe, and it is what abuts the left heart border
formulas.normalValue: Right hemidiaphragm is seen entire; the left is effaced where the heart sits on it

formulas.name: Lung Compliance
formulas.equation: Compliance = change in volume per unit change in pressure; elastance is its inverse
formulas.meaning: Emphysema destroys elastic fibers so compliance rises and recoil falls — inspiration is easy, expiration is hard; fibrosis lays down extra fibers so compliance falls and recoil rises — inspiration is hard, expiration is easy
formulas.normalValue: FRC is higher than normal in emphysema and lower than normal in fibrosis

formulas.name: Magnesium Handling by Segment
formulas.equation: Proximal tubule 15%, thick ascending limb 70%, DCT 10%
formulas.meaning: Unlike every other ion, magnesium is reabsorbed mostly in the TAL — which is why loop diuretics cause clinically significant hypomagnesemia and thiazides cause it only after chronic DCT remodeling
formulas.normalValue: Reabsorption rises with volume contraction, PTH and alkalosis, and falls with hypercalcemia through the CaSR

formulas.name: Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP)
formulas.equation: MAP = (SBP + 2 x DBP) / 3
formulas.meaning: The time-weighted average driving pressure for organ perfusion, weighted toward diastole because the heart spends more of each cycle there
formulas.normalValue: 70-105 mmHg systemically, falling to roughly 50-60 mmHg by the afferent arteriole

formulas.name: Minute Ventilation
formulas.equation: VE = VT x RR
formulas.meaning: Total air moved per minute, including the portion wasted in the conducting airways
formulas.normalValue: 500 mL x 15/min = 7.5 L/min; respiratory rate 12-18/min in adults

formulas.name: Mixed Venous Oxygen Saturation (SVO2)
formulas.equation: SVO2 = oxygen saturation of venous blood returning to the right heart
formulas.meaning: A read-out of how much oxygen the tissues extracted: high SVR slows capillary flow so extraction rises and SVO2 falls, while low SVR speeds flow so extraction falls and SVO2 rises
formulas.normalValue: Resuscitation target above 70%; a low SVR with a high SVO2 occurs in distributive shock and nowhere else

formulas.name: Net Acid Excretion
formulas.equation: Net acid excretion = titratable acid + NH4+ - excreted HCO3-
formulas.meaning: Reabsorbing filtered bicarbonate only returns the body to zero; new base is generated only by titrating a non-bicarbonate buffer such as phosphate, creatinine, urate or glutamine-derived ammonia
formulas.normalValue: About 70 mmol/day — 40 as NH4+ and 30 as titratable acid — matching the daily nonvolatile acid load

formulas.name: Net Filtration Pressure
formulas.equation: NFP = P_GC - P_BS - pi_GC = 60 - 15 - 29
formulas.meaning: The balance of Starling forces across the glomerular capillary; only glomerular hydrostatic pressure favors filtration, while Bowman hydrostatic pressure and capillary oncotic pressure oppose it
formulas.normalValue: +16 mmHg, directed out of the capillary into Bowman space

formulas.name: Nitric Oxide Signaling Cascade
formulas.equation: ACh at M3 -> Ca2+/calmodulin -> eNOS -> L-arginine to NO -> guanylate cyclase -> cGMP -> PKG -> relaxation
formulas.meaning: Nitric oxide is made in the endothelial cell but acts in the smooth muscle cell next door; shear stress activates the same pathway, which is why laminar flow is protective
formulas.normalValue: PDE-5 terminates the signal by degrading cGMP — sildenafil blocks that step rather than making new NO

formulas.name: Normal Chamber Pressures
formulas.equation: LV 100-140 / 3-12; aorta systolic = LV systolic, diastolic ~80; LA mean 2-10; RA mean 2-8 mmHg
formulas.meaning: The pressure map that drives every valve: valves are entirely passive and open or close only because a gradient reverses
formulas.normalValue: Right-sided pressures sit below their left-sided counterparts, and LV and RV outputs equalize over minutes

formulas.name: Normal ECG Intervals
formulas.equation: PR 120-200 ms; QRS < 120 ms; QT < half the R-R interval
formulas.meaning: The three interval judgments that anchor every ECG read — AV nodal conduction, ventricular depolarization, and total ventricular systole
formulas.normalValue: 1 small box = 0.04 s, 1 large box = 0.2 s; QT 0.36-0.44 s

formulas.name: Normal Electrical Axis
formulas.equation: -30 to +60 degrees, assessed with leads I and aVF
formulas.meaning: The mean direction of ventricular depolarization, which points down and to the left because the left ventricle is thicker; I and aVF are used because they are perpendicular
formulas.normalValue: Both leads upright is normal; I up with aVF down is left axis deviation, I down with aVF up is right axis deviation

formulas.name: Obligatory Solute Load
formulas.equation: ~600 mOsm/day of solute must be excreted
formulas.meaning: Because that solute load is fixed, urine osmolality and urine flow are inversely tied — you cannot concentrate maximally and produce a large volume at the same time
formulas.normalValue: Urine osmolality ranges 40-1200 mOsm/kg, setting a minimum obligatory urine volume of about 0.5 L/day

formulas.name: Obstructive vs Restrictive PFT Pattern
formulas.equation: Obstructive: FEV1 down hard, ratio down, RV and FRC up. Restrictive: FVC down hard, ratio normal or up, RV and FRC down
formulas.meaning: Obstruction is a problem of getting air out, so volume accumulates; restriction is a problem of getting air in, so every volume falls together
formulas.normalValue: Volumes and capacities run 20-25% lower in women

formulas.name: Ohm's Law (renal flow)
formulas.equation: Q = dP / R
formulas.meaning: Flow through any renal vessel equals the pressure gradient over the resistance, which is why the two arteriolar bottlenecks around the glomerulus control filtration so precisely
formulas.normalValue: A 20% occlusion can drive pressure from 120 to 293 mmHg at constant flow

formulas.name: Oxygen Binding Capacity
formulas.equation: 1 g of hemoglobin binds 1.34 mL O2
formulas.meaning: The maximum oxygen the hemoglobin present can carry, which is why anemia lowers oxygen content while leaving PO2 and saturation completely normal
formulas.normalValue: 15 g/100 mL x 1.34 = about 20.1 mL O2 per 100 mL blood

formulas.name: Oxygen Cascade
formulas.equation: Ambient 160 -> humidified trachea 150 -> alveolar 100 -> systemic artery 100 mmHg
formulas.meaning: Oxygen tension steps down at each stage; alveolar PCO2 of 40 mmHg displaces oxygen at the alveolus, and bronchial and coronary venous drainage shunts the arterial value slightly below end-capillary
formulas.normalValue: Mixed venous PO2 is about 45 mmHg entering the capillary; the A-a difference widens with pathology

formulas.name: Oxygen Content
formulas.equation: CaO2 = (capacity x % saturation) + dissolved O2
formulas.meaning: Total oxygen carried in all forms — about 98% bound to hemoglobin and 2% dissolved; the dissolved fraction alone supplies 15 mL/min against a 250 mL/min demand, a 13-fold shortfall
formulas.normalValue: Dissolved O2 = 100 mmHg x 0.003 = 0.3 mL per 100 mL blood

formulas.name: Oxygen Delivery
formulas.equation: DO2 = cardiac output x oxygen content
formulas.meaning: The quantity that actually matters at the tissue — it can fall from anemia, hypoxemia or low cardiac output, and treating the wrong one does nothing
formulas.normalValue: Requires roughly 250 mL O2 per minute at rest

formulas.name: P50 and the Dissociation Curve
formulas.equation: P50 = the PO2 at which hemoglobin is 50% saturated
formulas.meaning: The sigmoidal shape comes from positive cooperativity — saturated hemoglobin holds tightly while unsaturated hemoglobin releases easily, so the plateau protects loading and the steep limb favors unloading
formulas.normalValue: Unshifted P50 is about 25 mmHg; at PO2 50 mmHg hemoglobin is still about 85% saturated

formulas.name: Pacemaker Hierarchy
formulas.equation: SA node 60-100 bpm, AV node 40-60 bpm, His-Purkinje 20-40 bpm
