formulas.meaning: The fastest site suppresses the slower ones by overdrive suppression; an escape rhythm surfaces only when the sites above it fail or vagal tone is overwhelming
formulas.normalValue: Escape beats at 20-40 bpm indicate the ventricle is pacing itself

formulas.name: PAH Clearance
formulas.equation: C_PAH = effective renal plasma flow
formulas.meaning: PAH is both filtered and actively secreted, so essentially all of it is removed in a single pass — clearing it measures the plasma actually delivered to the kidney

formulas.name: Perfusion Threshold
formulas.equation: MAP must stay above 60 mmHg
formulas.meaning: Below this floor, tissue perfusion fails no matter what the systolic number reads — which is why mean pressure, not systolic, is the resuscitation target
formulas.normalValue: MAP = (2 x diastolic + systolic) / 3, about 93 mmHg for a 120/80 reading

formulas.name: Plasma Urate
formulas.equation: Urate is the end product of purine catabolism via xanthine oxidase
formulas.meaning: Filtered, then both reabsorbed and secreted in the proximal tubule, with reabsorption dominant
formulas.normalValue: 3-7 mg/dL (0.2-0.4 mM); only about 10% of the filtered load is excreted

formulas.name: Poiseuille's Equation
formulas.equation: Q = (dP x pi x r^4) / (8 x L x viscosity)
formulas.meaning: Radius is raised to the fourth power, so doubling the radius of a vessel or an IV catheter multiplies flow sixteenfold — which is why arterioles, with their adjustable radius, are the body's flow-control valves
formulas.normalValue: Rising viscosity or vessel length both reduce flow; anemia lowers viscosity, raising flow and cardiac output

formulas.name: Potassium Distribution
formulas.equation: 98% intracellular, 2% extracellular
formulas.meaning: Because so little potassium lives outside cells, a 1% shift out of the intracellular pool changes extracellular potassium by about 50% — which is why transcellular shifts, not total body stores, drive acute hyperkalemia
formulas.normalValue: Plasma 3.5-5.0 mM; about 75% of total body potassium sits in muscle

formulas.name: Potassium Handling by Segment
formulas.equation: PCT 80% reabsorbed, TAL 10% reabsorbed, distal secretory system sets the output
formulas.meaning: Urinary potassium is decided almost entirely by secretion in the DCT, connecting tubule and collecting duct, not by how much was reabsorbed upstream
formulas.normalValue: Filtered load about 810 mmol/day; excretion ranges from 1-3% of it on a low-potassium diet to over 150% of it on a high-potassium diet

formulas.name: Pressure-Volume Loop Landmarks
formulas.equation: EDV ~120 mL, ESV ~50 mL, stroke volume ~70 mL — the width of the loop
formulas.meaning: Traversed counterclockwise: filling, isovolumetric contraction, rapid and reduced ejection, then isovolumetric relaxation; the EDPVR describes passive stiffness and the ESPVR describes contractility
formulas.normalValue: A stiff hypertrophied ventricle steepens the EDPVR; a failing ventricle shifts the ESPVR right

formulas.name: Pressures Across One Breath
formulas.equation: Intrapleural runs -5 to -8 to -5; alveolar runs 0 to -1 to 0 to +1 to 0
formulas.meaning: Atmospheric pressure is always the zero reference, and alveolar pressure is the only one that ever turns positive — that positive value is what pushes air out
formulas.normalValue: Loss of positive alveolar pressure means obstruction; loss of negative alveolar pressure means restriction

formulas.name: Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension Threshold
formulas.equation: Mean pulmonary artery pressure > 20 mmHg at rest
formulas.meaning: The diagnostic cut-off for pulmonary arterial hypertension, a disease of endothelial dysfunction with too little nitric oxide and too much endothelin
formulas.normalValue: Treated by pushing both levers — bosentan to block endothelin, sildenafil to preserve the NO signal

formulas.name: Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure (PCWP)
formulas.equation: PCWP = left atrial pressure, measured by a Swan-Ganz catheter
formulas.meaning: The left-sided filling pressure, and the single measurement that splits obstructive shock into its pulmonary form (low PCWP) and its structural form (high PCWP)
formulas.normalValue: Low in hypovolemic and distributive shock, high in cardiogenic shock

formulas.name: Pulmonary Vascular Resistance vs Lung Volume
formulas.equation: Extra-alveolar vessels have highest resistance at low volume; alveolar capillaries have highest resistance at high volume
formulas.meaning: The two curves oppose each other, so total pulmonary vascular resistance reaches its minimum exactly at functional residual capacity
formulas.normalValue: Both circuits carry about 6 L/min, but the pulmonary side runs at far lower pressure with thinner, more compliant vessels

formulas.name: Pulse Pressure
formulas.equation: PP = Systolic BP - Diastolic BP
formulas.meaning: A direct reflection of stroke volume and arterial compliance: aortic stenosis and arterial calcification narrow it, while hyperthyroidism and lying supine widen it
formulas.normalValue: 30-40 mmHg

formulas.name: Radiographic Density Scale
formulas.equation: Air < fat < soft tissue/fluid < calcium < bone < contrast < metal
formulas.meaning: Density determines x-ray absorption and therefore film appearance, from air at maximum transmission (darkest) to metal at maximum absorption (whitest) — and pus, blood and simple fluid are all the same soft-tissue density
formulas.normalValue: A chest x-ray delivers about 0.1 mSv, roughly 10 days of the 3 mSv annual US background

formulas.name: Renal Ammoniagenesis
formulas.equation: Glutamine to alpha-ketoglutarate yields 2 NH4+ plus new HCO3-
formulas.meaning: The proximal tubule makes both the buffer and the new base from one substrate; NH4+ then substitutes for K+ on NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb and is recycled into the medulla
formulas.normalValue: About 40 mmol/day of NH4+ excretion, rising sharply in chronic metabolic acidosis

formulas.name: Renal Blood Flow (RBF)
formulas.equation: RBF = RPF / (1 - Hct)
formulas.meaning: Total blood reaching both kidneys each minute, delivering oxygen and nutrients; a high hematocrit raises viscosity and resistance and therefore lowers it
formulas.normalValue: About 1 L/min, roughly 20% of cardiac output, to organs that are only 0.5% of body weight

formulas.name: Renal Plasma Flow (RPF)
formulas.equation: RPF = RBF x (1 - Hct)
formulas.meaning: The cell-free plasma delivered per minute — the only part of renal blood flow that can actually be filtered
formulas.normalValue: 600-650 mL/min; estimated clinically as the clearance of PAH, which is cleared in a single pass

formulas.name: Scoliosis Management Thresholds
formulas.equation: 11-19 deg observe; 20-24 deg follow closely; 25-39 deg brace; 40-49 deg brace and consider surgery above 45; 50 deg or more operate
formulas.meaning: Bracing prevents progression rather than correcting the curve, and only works while growth remains (Risser 0-2, Sanders 1-3)
formulas.normalValue: A curve of 50 degrees or more at maturity worsens about 1 degree per year for life

formulas.name: Scoliosis Severity by Cobb Angle
formulas.equation: Mild 10-15 deg, moderate 20-45 deg, moderately severe 45-50 deg, severe over 50 deg
formulas.meaning: Severity is defined purely by the Cobb angle, and above 50 degrees the curve begins to affect systemic function
formulas.normalValue: Respiratory function suffers in thoracic curves over 50 degrees, cardiovascular function over 75 degrees

formulas.name: Serum Calcium Fractions
formulas.equation: 45% free ionized, 40% protein-bound, 15% in diffusible complexes
formulas.meaning: Only the ionized and complexed fractions are filterable; the albumin-bound fraction never reaches the tubule, which is why total calcium must be corrected for albumin
formulas.normalValue: Acidosis displaces calcium from albumin and raises ionized calcium; alkalosis lowers it and mimics hypocalcemia

formulas.name: Shock Thresholds
formulas.equation: Systolic BP < 90 mmHg, or MAP < 65 mmHg
formulas.meaning: The pressure floor below which tissue perfusion is presumed inadequate and shock is declared, whatever the underlying mechanism
formulas.normalValue: Resuscitation targets are MAP above 65 mmHg and SVO2 above 70%

formulas.name: Shunt (V/Q = 0)
formulas.equation: Ventilation absent, perfusion normal — wasted perfusion
formulas.meaning: Blood passes unventilated alveoli and leaves with mixed venous values of 40/46 because no exchange occurred; a right-to-left shunt always causes hypoxemia and cannot be corrected by breathing oxygen
formulas.normalValue: Physiologic shunt is about 2% of cardiac output; a shunt fraction QS/QT above 2% is pathologic

formulas.name: Stroke Volume Determinants
formulas.equation: SV rises with preload and contractility, and falls with afterload
formulas.meaning: Preload is end-diastolic volume set by central venous pressure; afterload is the resistance the ventricle ejects against, which is why aortic stenosis cuts stroke volume
formulas.normalValue: About 70 mL per beat, giving a cardiac output near 5 L/min at rest

formulas.name: Systemic Vascular Resistance (Poiseuille)
formulas.equation: R = 8Ln / (pi x r^4)
formulas.meaning: Resistance depends on vessel radius to the fourth power, which is why arteriolar tone — not vessel length or blood viscosity — is what actually sets afterload
formulas.normalValue: Rises in hypovolemic, cardiogenic and obstructive shock; falls in distributive shock

formulas.name: Technical Assessment (P-I-P-R)
formulas.equation: Projection, Inspiration, Penetration, Rotation
formulas.meaning: Four checks before reading any chest film — projection from the label, inspiration by counting 9-10 posterior ribs, penetration by just seeing the thoracic disc spaces, rotation by equidistant clavicular heads
formulas.normalValue: Each failed check produces its own predictable false finding

formulas.name: TF/P Osmolality Along the Nephron
formulas.equation: Proximal tubule 1.0, descending limb rises, thick ascending limb falls below 1.0, DCT stays hypo-osmotic
formulas.meaning: Fluid leaving the DCT is hypo-osmotic in every state, thirsty or not, because the water-impermeable thick ascending limb strips NaCl regardless; whether urine ends up dilute or concentrated is decided only downstream in the ADH-sensitive segments
formulas.normalValue: Plasma osmolality about 300 mOsm/kg

formulas.name: The 99% / 1% Principle
formulas.equation: 99% of the filtered load is reabsorbed; regulation happens in the final 1%
formulas.meaning: The kidney keeps GFR and distal sodium delivery deliberately constant so the distal nephron can act as a fine adjustable valve under ADH and aldosterone control
formulas.normalValue: 173 L filtered per day yields about 1.73 L of urine

formulas.name: The Four Acid-Base Disturbances
formulas.equation: Metabolic: HCO3- primary. Respiratory: pCO2 primary.
formulas.meaning: Metabolic acidosis lowers HCO3- and triggers hyperventilation; metabolic alkalosis raises it and triggers hypoventilation; respiratory disorders move pCO2 first and the kidney answers by adjusting bicarbonate reabsorption over days
formulas.normalValue: Normal values: pCO2 40 mmHg, pH 7.4, HCO3- 24 mEq/L

formulas.name: The Seven Phases of the Cardiac Cycle
formulas.equation: Atrial systole, isovolumetric contraction, rapid ejection, reduced ejection, isovolumetric relaxation, rapid filling, reduced filling
formulas.meaning: The two isovolumetric phases are the only times all four valves are shut, and they are exactly the flat segments of the ventricular volume curve — if volume is changing, a valve is open
formulas.normalValue: S1 opens isovolumetric contraction; S2 opens isovolumetric relaxation

formulas.name: The Three Autonomic Tropies
formulas.equation: Chronotropic = rate; dromotropic = conduction; inotropic = contractility
formulas.meaning: Sympathetic stimulation increases all three, vagal stimulation decreases all three — the vocabulary for every autonomic effect on the heart
formulas.normalValue: Vagal effects are strongest on the SA and AV nodes; sympathetic effects reach the ventricular myocardium as well

formulas.name: Total Body Water
formulas.equation: TBW = 60% of body weight; 2/3 intracellular, 1/3 extracellular
formulas.meaning: The compartment map behind every fluid problem — the ECF splits again into interstitial fluid and plasma, and because the Na+/K+ ATPase holds intracellular sodium steady, any change in body sodium plays out in the ECF
formulas.normalValue: About 42 L in a 70 kg adult: 28 L intracellular and 14 L extracellular

formulas.name: Total Lung Capacity
formulas.equation: TLC = IC + FRC = VC + RV
formulas.meaning: Anchor everything to functional residual capacity, the level the trace returns to after every normal breath — add inspiratory capacity to reach TLC, subtract expiratory reserve volume and only residual volume is left

formulas.name: Total Peripheral Resistance
formulas.equation: TPR = (MAP - CVP) / CO
formulas.meaning: The resistance of the whole systemic vasculature, set primarily by adjustable arteriolar radius under local (heat, cold) and extrinsic (sympathetic, hormonal) control
formulas.normalValue: Resistance arises from friction between blood and the endothelium; a 95% coronary blockage raises it enough to cause infarction

formulas.name: Transepithelial Voltage (Vte) Along the Nephron
formulas.equation: PCT S1 -3 mV, PCT S3 +3 mV, TAL +6 mV, DCT -24 to -14 mV, CCT -74 mV
formulas.meaning: The electrical map that explains paracellular transport: the lumen-positive TAL drives calcium and magnesium reabsorption, while the strongly lumen-negative collecting tubule drives potassium secretion
formulas.normalValue: Loop diuretics abolish the +6 mV of the TAL; ENaC blockers collapse the -74 mV of the CCT

formulas.name: Transmural Pressure
formulas.equation: Transmural = pressure inside a compartment - pressure outside it
formulas.meaning: At every stage of the breathing cycle transmural pressure is positive and directed outward, and that is what holds the lung open — not the sign of the intrapleural pressure by itself
formulas.normalValue: +5 at rest, +5.5 during inspiration, +8 at peak inspiration, +7.5 during expiration

formulas.name: Transpulmonary Pressure
formulas.equation: Ptp = PA - Ppl
formulas.meaning: The distending pressure holding the lung open — it is what keeps the alveoli from collapsing and is largest at end-inspiration
formulas.normalValue: +5 at FRC, +7 at end-inspiration, +6 at mid-expiration

formulas.name: Urea Excretion
formulas.equation: About 50% of the filtered urea load is excreted at normal urine flow
formulas.meaning: Urea is 100% filtered, roughly half reabsorbed paracellularly in the proximal tubule, secreted back in the thin limbs, then half reabsorbed again in the medullary collecting duct
formulas.normalValue: Falls to about 15% excreted at low urine flow (BUN rises) and up to 70% at high flow (IV fluids lower BUN)

formulas.name: Ventilation-Perfusion Ratio
formulas.equation: V/Q = alveolar ventilation / pulmonary blood flow
formulas.meaning: The whole lung averages 0.8 — ventilation running at 80% of perfusion — but gravity splits it: the apex reaches about 3 because perfusion drops more than ventilation, while the base falls to about 0.6 because perfusion rises more than ventilation
formulas.normalValue: Targets are PaO2 100 mmHg and PaCO2 40 mmHg; the middle zone at 0.8 is the ideal match

formulas.name: Ventricular Wall Stress
formulas.equation: Wall stress = (P x r) / h
formulas.meaning: The primary determinant of myocardial oxygen consumption — dilation raises the radius and thinning lowers wall thickness, so both drive demand up
formulas.normalValue: An efficient heart has a small radius and an adequately thick wall; a big floppy ventricle is metabolically expensive

formulas.name: Why Spirometry Cannot Measure RV
formulas.equation: Spirometry measures only voluntarily moved air
formulas.meaning: Residual volume cannot be blown out, so it is unmeasurable by spirometry — and therefore so are the two capacities that contain it, FRC and TLC
formulas.normalValue: RV or FRC must first come from plethysmography, nitrogen washout or helium dilution

correlates.name: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
correlates.presentation: Focal dilation of the abdominal aorta.
correlates.pathophysiology: In an aneurysm the radius of the aorta increases; by the Laplace law (T = P x r / 2 x wall thickness), wall tension rises compared with a normal-caliber vessel at the same transmural pressure.

correlates.name: ACE Inhibitor Cough
correlates.presentation: persistent dry, non-productive cough starting after the drug is begun. Not dangerous - but bothersome enough to end therapy.
correlates.pathophysiology: accumulation of bradykinin, substance P, and probably prostaglandins in the lungs, irritating the airway (Slide 38).
correlates.treatment: switch to an ARB; incidence with ARBs is low but not zero.

correlates.name: ACE Inhibitor-Associated Angioedema
correlates.pathophysiology: ACE inhibition prevents degradation of vasoactive peptides, producing non-pitting swelling of the lips, tongue and airway.
correlates.treatment: stop the ACE inhibitor and transition to an ARB.

correlates.name: ACE Inhibitor-Induced Angioedema
correlates.presentation: swelling of lips, tongue, face, or airway - rare but potentially fatal.
correlates.pathophysiology: bradykinin and substance P are pro-inflammatory vasoactive peptides; accumulation causes vasodilation and vessel edema (Slides 38-39).
correlates.treatment: stop the drug. Angioedema of any cause is an absolute contraindication to all RAS inhibitors (Slide 40).

correlates.name: Acute Altitude Sickness
correlates.presentation: Most frequently reported are headache, fatigue, dizziness, nausea, palpitations and insomnia.
correlates.pathophysiology: Decreased atmospheric pressure lowers the oxygen available in inspired air, which lowers alveolar PO2 and then arterial PO2. The same hypoxia drives pulmonary hypoxic vasoconstriction.
correlates.treatment: Acetazolamide, which inhibits carbonic anhydrase. With the enzyme blocked, that arm of the bicarbonate buffer system cannot be converted to water and CO2 and blown off, which counterbalances the respiratory alkalosis hyperventilation would otherwise produce.

correlates.name: Acute Mountain Sickness (the Aspen vignette)
correlates.presentation: Throbbing headache, fatigue, nausea, shortness of breath, lightheadedness, difficulty focusing; worse on day two and with further ascent.
correlates.pathophysiology: Ascent lowers inspired PO2; hyperventilation lowers PaCO2 and raises blood pH into respiratory alkalosis, and renal compensation is too slow to help in the first days.
correlates.treatment: A carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (acetazolamide) started before the trip; ibuprofen only blunted the headache.

correlates.name: Acute Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)
correlates.presentation: ST elevation in two or more anatomically contiguous leads - leads that belong to the same coronary artery. V1 and V2 are contiguous (both LAD); leads I and II are not (I is LCx/lateral, II is RCA/inferior).
correlates.pathophysiology: Atherosclerotic plaque buildup that ruptures, triggering thrombus formation and occlusion of a coronary artery. Ischemic myocardium fails to repolarize normally, producing ST-segment shift in the leads overlying the affected wall.

correlates.name: Acute Tubular Necrosis (Medullary Ischemia)
correlates.presentation: Ischemic tubular injury in low-perfusion states (later lectures).
correlates.pathophysiology: Only 5-10% of renal blood flow reaches the medulla via the vasa recta — a deliberately low-flow design that keeps the medulla salty but hypoxia-prone.

correlates.name: Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS)
correlates.pathophysiology: hereditary predisposition, multifactorial; association with hypokyphosis (a thoracic spine flattened or lordotic where kyphosis is expected), a possible CNS defect, increased calmodulin (Slide 18).

correlates.name: Allergic Rhinitis
correlates.presentation: itchy, red, watery eyes and a stuffy, runny nose, present for more than a year alongside the episodic lower-airway symptoms.
correlates.pathophysiology: the same allergic process acting on the upper airway mucosa rather than on bronchiolar smooth muscle; it accompanies asthma in the lecture's case (Slide 10).

correlates.name: Anaphylactic Shock
correlates.presentation: throat and tongue swelling, coughing and wheezing, stridor, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, hives, urticaria, tachycardia, lethargy.
correlates.pathophysiology: an antigen-antibody reaction drives mast cells in the periphery and basophils in the blood to release histamine and histamine-like substances.
correlates.treatment: intramuscular epinephrine is the most important treatment; add normal saline for hypotension, oxygen, and albuterol for bronchospasm persisting after epinephrine (Slide 30).

correlates.name: Anaphylaxis
correlates.presentation: The lecturer's vignette - 25-year-old woman, sudden dyspnea, itchy rash and nausea after a seafood meal; pulse 125/min, respirations 24/min, O2 saturation 97%, BP 82/68; erythematous patches and wheals with mild lip swelling but no tongue or uvular swelling.
correlates.pathophysiology: Allergen exposure produces a surge of histamine (mast cells) and bradykinin, both of which increase NO production in endothelial cells. Widespread vasodilation drops the blood pressure.
correlates.treatment: IM epinephrine, first line. It activates alpha-adrenergic receptors on vascular smooth muscle, causing vasoconstriction that restores blood pressure. Patients with severe allergy carry an auto-injector (EpiPen).

correlates.name: Anemia (High-Output State)
correlates.presentation: A 22-year-old medical student with 3 months of fatigue and sleepiness, a mid-systolic murmur, and higher-than-normal cardiac output. The murmur is generated by the increased heart rate and cardiac output.
correlates.pathophysiology: Fewer red cells → decreased viscosity → increased flow (Poiseuille). With less oxygen-carrying capacity, the body compensates with increased heart rate and increased cardiac output.

correlates.name: Apparent Cardiomegaly on a Portable Film
correlates.presentation: the same patient imaged the same day has a normal cardiac silhouette on the PA film and an enlarged-looking heart on the AP film (Slide 21).
correlates.pathophysiology: projectional magnification, not disease — an anterior heart, a long heart-to-cassette distance, and a diverging beam.

correlates.name: Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess (Licorice)
correlates.presentation: A state of apparent mineralocorticoid excess (slide: hypertension, hypokalemia, low renin, low aldosterone).
correlates.pathophysiology: Eating a lot of licorice inhibits 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, the enzyme that normally inactivates cortisol at the mineralocorticoid receptor. Cortisol then activates MR, mimicking aldosterone excess.

correlates.name: ARDS with Atelectasis: Refractory Hypoxemia
correlates.presentation: Severe hypoxemia; SaO2 82% despite 100% oxygen via non-rebreather mask.
correlates.pathophysiology: Fluid-filled, collapsed alveoli are perfused but not ventilated - a large acquired physiologic right-to-left shunt.

correlates.name: Aristolochic Acid Nephropathy (Acute Kidney Injury)
correlates.presentation: Acute distress, nausea, dehydration, deep bilateral flank pain, oliguria (~0.5 L/day), urinalysis with marked hematuria, proteinuria, and glycosuria with normal plasma glucose.
correlates.pathophysiology: Aristolochic acid, a highly toxic compound in lookalike plants contaminating herbal teas, directly injures the kidney and causes acute kidney injury.

correlates.name: Arteriovenous (AV) Fistula
correlates.pathophysiology: An abnormal direct connection between an artery and a vein that lets arterial blood bypass the capillary bed.

correlates.name: Ascites due to Hepatic Cirrhosis
correlates.pathophysiology: Portal hypertension raises hydrostatic pressure and transudes fluid into the peritoneum, lowering effective circulating volume.
correlates.treatment: Spironolactone is first-line, because the patient is in a state of secondary hyperaldosteronism and the drug attacks that directly. It may be given with furosemide, but furosemide is not used alone here.

correlates.name: Asthma
correlates.presentation: episodic cough, wheeze, shortness of breath and chest tightness; in the acute severe attack, shortness of breath with chest pain and a wheezing cough.
correlates.pathophysiology: the smooth muscle fibers wrapped around the bronchioles and terminal bronchioles undergo undue contraction, closing off airways and impeding airflow (Slide 14).
correlates.treatment: beta-2 agonists - albuterol, epinephrine, isoproterenol - to reverse the constriction (Slide 8).

correlates.name: Asystole
correlates.treatment: If the patient is unresponsive they are in cardiac arrest and need immediate resuscitation.

correlates.name: Atherosclerosis: VSMC, the Fibrous Cap, and Plaque Rupture
correlates.presentation: A ruptured fibrous cap with an overlying occluding thrombus — the acute coronary event.
correlates.pathophysiology: As plaque progresses, medial VSMCs lose the contractile phenotype and become synthetic.

correlates.name: Atrial Fibrillation (and the AV Node as a Protective Filter)
correlates.presentation: The resulting ventricular rate is far slower than the atrial rate, typically 100-150 bpm during AF.
correlates.pathophysiology: During atrial fibrillation the atrial rate is 400-600 bpm. Because the AV node conducts slowly and has a long refractory period, many atrial impulses are blocked within the node.

correlates.name: AV Block (Heart Block)
correlates.presentation: PR interval >200 ms. Degrees range from first through third; third-degree (complete) block shows complete atrioventricular dissociation, with the ventricles escaping at a rate unrelated to the atria.
correlates.pathophysiology: impaired conduction through the AV node or the infranodal system. Because the PR interval is the electrical time spent traversing the AV node, nodal disease lengthens it.

correlates.name: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
correlates.pathophysiology: alpha-1 receptors in the smooth muscle of the bladder neck and prostate hold the outlet constricted.
correlates.treatment: an alpha-1 blocker relaxes that smooth muscle and improves urine flow (Slide 12).

correlates.name: Beta Blocker Withdrawal Syndrome
correlates.presentation: nervousness, tachycardia, increased blood pressure (potentially higher than before treatment ever started), increased intensity of angina, and increased risk of sudden death…
correlates.pathophysiology: chronic blockade causes upregulation or supersensitivity of beta adrenoceptors - more receptors expressed on the plasma membrane. Abrupt discontinuation exposes that enlarged pool to circulating norepinephrine and epinephrine (Slide 54).
correlates.treatment: never stop a beta blocker abruptly - taper gradually over a week or more, depending on how long the patient has been treated and the patient's age .

correlates.name: Birth Strain and Infant Cranial Dysfunction
correlates.presentation: Mechanical cranial problems in infants — largely membranous in origin.
correlates.pathophysiology: In babies the cranial bones are soft with no formed articulations, so the membranes carry the functional role of maintaining shape and stability; abnormal motion from a birth strain then drives abnormal sutural/structural development.
correlates.treatment: At birth, often a treatment or two; by age 10 the abnormally developed structure is nearly impossible to reverse.

correlates.name: Bundle Branch Block (Left or Right)
correlates.presentation: Although normal His and bundle branch activation is invisible on the ECG, bundle branch block CAN be diagnosed on the ECG - because it alters the ventricular activation sequence, and the ventricular activation sequence is what the QRS displays.
correlates.pathophysiology: Loss of conduction down one bundle branch forces the affected ventricle to be activated late, by slow cell-to-cell muscle conduction from the contralateral ventricle rather than by the fast Purkinje network.

correlates.name: CAI-Induced Hyperchloremic Metabolic Acidosis
correlates.presentation: Usually a laboratory finding - mild acidosis with a raised serum chloride and a normal anion gap. Alkaline urine.
correlates.pathophysiology: Carbonic anhydrase inhibition causes massive bicarbonate loss in the urine. Continued loss lowers plasma bicarbonate, the key blood buffer, so arterial pH falls. Chloride is reabsorbed in its place to maintain electroneutrality, raising serum chloride.
correlates.treatment: Usually none; it is mild, and in altitude illness it is the therapeutic goal. Stop the drug if it is not.

correlates.name: Calcific Aortic Stenosis
correlates.presentation: A 73-year-old man in the ER with exertional dyspnea, syncope and chest pain. Poorly managed hypercholesterolemia and an 11-year history of hypertension.
correlates.pathophysiology: The obstructed aortic valve cannot open and close fully, so left ventricular pressure must climb very high to eject across it.
correlates.treatment: Aortic valve repair or replacement, depending on the patient's condition.

correlates.name: Calcium Nephrolithiasis from Idiopathic Hypercalciuria
correlates.pathophysiology: Excess urinary calcium supersaturates the urine with calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate, seeding recurrent stones.
correlates.treatment: A thiazide reduces urinary calcium by the DCT mechanism above, lowering supersaturation and reducing recurrence in selected patients. Never the only measure - combine with increased fluid intake, dietary modification, weight loss and drug therapy.

correlates.name: Carbon Monoxide Poisoning
correlates.presentation: The lecture's example patient was lucky — the exposure lasted only long enough to saturate about 50% of hemoglobin with CO. Anything more would produce a state not consistent with survival.
correlates.pathophysiology: CO competitively binds the same heme site as oxygen with 210-250x the affinity, forming carboxyhemoglobin and taking those binding sites out of service.
correlates.treatment: Regular air, about 5 hours; air saturated with O2, about 1.5 hours (raising the concentration gradient to drive CO off the binding sites); hyperbaric chamber at 3 atmospheres, about 20 minutes in extreme cases.

correlates.name: Carbon Monoxide Uptake
correlates.pathophysiology: CO dissolves well in blood, but as it enters the bloodstream it is taken up by hemoglobin "like a magnet," immediately and essentially completely.

correlates.name: Cardiac Events While Shovelling Snow
correlates.presentation: underlying cardiovascular disease is unmasked at once; emergency departments go to "all hands on deck" during a snowstorm.
correlates.pathophysiology: the lecturer's "perfect storm" of simultaneous stressors - cold-induced vasoconstriction raising blood pressure; strenuous cardiovascular work; heavy lifting that is effectively isometric weight training, imposing afterload…
correlates.treatment: counsel patients of uncertain cardiovascular status not to shovel snow .

correlates.name: Cardiac Tamponade
correlates.presentation: Restricted heart function after chest trauma or pericardial effusion.
correlates.pathophysiology: The pericardium is dense connective tissue that cannot acutely stretch. Traumatic injury to the heart (or pericarditis) leaking blood/fluid into the pericardial sac compresses the heart and restricts dilation/filling.

correlates.name: Cardiogenic Pulmonary Edema
correlates.presentation: Impaired gas exchange, because fluid in the alveolus lengthens the diffusion distance that O2 and CO2 must cross.
correlates.pathophysiology: Left-sided heart dysfunction raises left atrial pressure. Blood returning through the pulmonary vein cannot clear the left atrium and ventricle, so back pressure is transmitted into the pulmonary capillaries.

correlates.name: Carotid Sinus Hypersensitivity Syndrome
correlates.presentation: Syncope or pre-syncopal episodes triggered by trivial mechanical stimulation of the neck — buttoning a shirt, shaving, or brushing hair.
correlates.pathophysiology: The baroreceptor system becomes hypersensitive — receptors are accidentally hyper-stimulated by ordinary neck pressure, constantly signaling that blood pressure has changed. Frequently associated with arteriosclerotic changes in the carotid sinus.

correlates.name: Case Study Opened in This Lecture (diagnosis deferred to Part II)
correlates.presentation: 73-year-old man in the ER with exertional dyspnea, syncope and chest pain; poorly managed hypercholesterolemia and an 11-year history of hypertension.

correlates.name: Cauda Equina Syndrome
correlates.presentation: The S2-S4 findings above, with or without leg weakness.
correlates.pathophysiology: Compression of the lumbosacral roots below the conus - classically a large central disc herniation, but also degenerative central stenosis, epidural hematoma, tumor, infection…
correlates.treatment: Urgent surgical decompression.

correlates.name: Chronic Adrenal Insufficiency (Addison Disease)
correlates.presentation: Metabolic acidosis from acid retention, called life-threatening on the slide.
correlates.pathophysiology: Loss of glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid drive removes the stimulus for proximal Na+/H+ exchange and collecting duct H+ secretion, so acid is retained.
correlates.treatment: Corticosteroid replacement restores acid secretion.

correlates.name: Chronic Hypertension (Sodium-Driven Volume Expansion)
correlates.pathophysiology: Retaining sodium forces water retention (osmolality must be held constant), expanding ECF and plasma volume, raising venous return, preload, stroke volume, cardiac output — and therefore blood pressure (the Slide 17-18 practice question, answer D).
correlates.treatment: This is the physiologic basis for recommending a low-sodium diet to hypertensive patients.

correlates.name: Chronic Hypokalemia
correlates.presentation: Muscle weakness progressing to paralysis, respiratory failure when respiratory muscles are involved, abdominal distension from smooth-muscle failure, vasoconstriction with hypertension.
correlates.pathophysiology: A fall in extracellular [K+] hyperpolarizes membranes and shifts acid-base handling; hypokalemia produces intracellular acidosis with extracellular alkalosis (Slide 10).

correlates.name: Chronic Kidney Disease
correlates.presentation: Know the CKD stages for exams — questions give symptomatology and expect stage 2 vs. stage 4. GFR calculators (kidney.org, MDCalc) linked for rotations.
correlates.pathophysiology: Progressive, permanent nephron loss, staged by eGFR.

correlates.name: Claudication and Statin-Associated Muscle Symptoms
correlates.presentation: claudication - calf pain on walking that forces the patient to stop; watching a peripheral arterial disease patient on a treadmill is diagnostic in itself.

correlates.name: Clonidine Withdrawal (Rebound Hypertension)
correlates.presentation: rebound hypertension with headache, apprehension, tremors, abdominal pain, sweating and tachycardia - a catalogue of sympathetic effects.
correlates.pathophysiology: sympathetic outflow has been suppressed for months. Abrupt discontinuation releases a catecholamine surge (Slide 21).
correlates.treatment: never stop abruptly; taper gradually.

correlates.name: Conditions That Impair Diaphragm Function
correlates.presentation: a fall in FRC is the shared signature. Recall FRC = RV + ERV.
correlates.pathophysiology: paradoxical movement, ascites, pregnancy, and obesity all oppose or splint diaphragmatic descent (Slide 17). The resting balance point of the lung-chest wall system shifts and functional residual capacity decreases.

correlates.name: Congenital (Infant) Torticollis
correlates.presentation: Dislikes turning to one side (decreased right rotation), head sidebent toward the tight muscle; flattening from always lying on the same side.
correlates.pathophysiology: SCM spasm; CN XI (spinal accessory) innervates the SCM and exits the jugular foramen — a precarious junction of occipital condylar parts and petrous temporal bone (occipitomastoid, OM, suture)…
correlates.treatment: OMM to the SCM and cranial findings; by the third visit the spasm had decreased, the torticollis resolved, and the baby turned comfortably both ways.

correlates.name: Congenital Left-to-Right Shunts (ASD, PDA)
correlates.presentation: Typically no hypoxemia. It appears only when the defect is large enough to compromise left ventricular efficiency.
correlates.pathophysiology: Oxygenated blood recirculates into the pulmonary circuit down a pressure gradient; blood delivered to the systemic circulation stays fully oxygenated.
correlates.treatment: Congenital, and the lecturer stresses that these need to be fixed right away.

correlates.name: Congenital Long QT Syndrome and Torsades de Pointes
correlates.presentation: may be silent until syncope or arrest; the family history is the clue - sudden cardiac death in relatives.
correlates.pathophysiology: prolonged ventricular repolarization from a congenital channelopathy, an electrolyte imbalance, or a drug (Slide 12).

correlates.name: Congenital Scoliosis
correlates.presentation: second most common category; 75 percent are progressive.
correlates.pathophysiology: vertebral malformation present at birth - hemivertebrae, wedge vertebrae, failure of segmentation (unilateral bar, bilateral fusion), fused ribs (Slide 20).

correlates.name: Congestive Heart Failure (Renal Volume-Defense Maladaptation)
correlates.presentation: Dyspnea, pitting edema of the lower extremities, ascites, pulmonary edema (crackles); labs may show hyponatremia (e.g., 128 mEq/L in the opening case).
correlates.pathophysiology: Weak pump → low cardiac output → low effective circulating volume despite high total ECF. Renal sensors perceive hypovolemia → chronic RAAS, sympathetic, and non-osmotic ADH activation → sodium and water retention → worsening congestion.
correlates.treatment: Calm the kidney's over-firing signals (see the drug table below).

correlates.name: Congestive Heart Failure and the Kidney
correlates.pathophysiology: Chronic low perfusion drives chronic sympathetic activation → sustained renal vasoconstriction and reduced renal blood flow.

correlates.name: COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease)
correlates.presentation: easily fatigued, frequent respiratory infections, use of accessory muscles to breathe, orthopnea, thin appearance, wheezing, pursed-lip breathing, chronic cough, barrel-shaped chest (classic), dyspnea, prolonged expiratory time, digital clubbing.
correlates.treatment: bronchodilator (albuterol) with repeat spirometry to demonstrate reversible airway obstruction.

correlates.name: COPD and Pulmonary Rehabilitation
correlates.presentation: exertional dyspnea graded +1 to +4; at +3 to +4, often with desaturation toward 90%, stop the test and record the heart rate (lecturer's example: 125 bpm).
correlates.treatment: pulmonary rehab trains up to that heart rate, then backs off.

correlates.name: Coronary Artery Blockage (Myocardial Ischemia)
correlates.presentation: Ischemia — a decrease in blood flow to the myocardium; can progress to heart infarct.
correlates.pathophysiology: A 95% blockage of a coronary artery dramatically increases resistance in that segment; by Q = delta P / R, flow falls.
correlates.treatment: Stent implantation restored the vessel diameter and thereby the flow.

correlates.name: COVID-19 (and Long COVID) Hypoxemia
correlates.presentation: Decreased PaO2 with an increased A-a gradient, placing it in the diffusion-barrier group.
correlates.pathophysiology: Infection causes inflammation leading to pulmonary flooding — an edema. Unlike fibrosis, this is a liquid barrier rather than a tissue barrier, but the effect is identical: increased diffusion distance for gases.
correlates.treatment: Supplemental oxygen is helpful — it maximizes the diffusion pressure of oxygen into the system.

correlates.name: COVID-19 Endotheliopathy
correlates.pathophysiology: SARS-CoV-2 triggers inflammatory cytokines (cytokine storm) and directly injures the endothelium, producing endothelial activation and inflammation. NO production falls while inflammation and vasoconstriction rise.

correlates.name: Cranial Nerve Entrapment (Component of Cranial Somatic Dysfunction)
correlates.presentation: Dysfunction of the affected nerve's territory (the lecture stays conceptual; specific syndromes come later).
correlates.pathophysiology: Cranial nerves pierce the dura on the way to their targets; strain in the dura or in a cranial bone can affect how the nerves perform and function.
correlates.treatment: Cranial diagnosis and treatment directed at the sutural restriction or dural strain (course objectives list sutural restriction, nerve entrapment, dural restriction, and venous congestion as components of cranial somatic dysfunction).

correlates.name: Cranial Nerve Entrapment Screened in OCF
correlates.pathophysiology: Cranial nerves are vulnerable where they cross a suture, a foramen or a dural attachment; a strain pattern there tensions the nerve or its dural sleeve. Localize the deficit to the bone that houses the nerve (table above).
correlates.treatment: BMT for the strain pattern, V-spread and directing the tide for the restricted suture, condylar decompression for CN XII and torticollis [[CV21]].

correlates.name: Craniosynostosis
correlates.presentation: Mimics positional plagiocephaly — the must-not-miss differential.
correlates.pathophysiology: Early closure of a cranial suture, also producing a misshaped head.
correlates.treatment: Referral to pediatric neurosurgery.

correlates.name: Crankshaft Phenomenon
correlates.presentation: progressive severe alignment deformity, rotational and in the sagittal plane, after an apparently successful fusion.
correlates.pathophysiology: after posterior spinal fusion in a child with growth remaining, the posterior column is tethered while the anterior spine keeps growing, twisting the spine around the fusion mass (Slides 17, 80).
correlates.treatment: combined anterior and posterior fusion, removing anterior growth potential.

correlates.name: Crush Injury, Rhabdomyolysis and Hemolysis
correlates.presentation: With skeletal muscle damage or hemolytic activity, plasma potassium is one of the first labs to check.
correlates.pathophysiology: Because ~75% of body potassium is stored in muscle, massive muscle damage dumps K+ into the ECF; hemolysis adds red-cell K+ to plasma.

correlates.name: Cushing Reflex (Cushing Response)
correlates.presentation: The Cushing triad — hypertension, bradycardia, and respiratory depression.
correlates.pathophysiology: The CNS ischemic response above, driven by increased intracranial pressure: cerebral arterioles are constricted → cerebral blood flow falls → ischemia with increased PCO2 and decreased pH → sympathetic activation → systemic hypertension.

correlates.name: Cyanide Poisoning
correlates.presentation: O2 content of blood is fine and PaO2 is unaffected, yet the patient is profoundly hypoxic — the defect is at the mitochondrion, not in transport.
correlates.pathophysiology: Cyanide disables protein complexes of the electron transport chain, so the tissue cannot utilize the oxygen delivered to it.

correlates.name: Decompensated Heart Failure
correlates.presentation: Shortness of breath, chest discomfort or pain, and swelling of the legs (when decompensated).
correlates.pathophysiology: The pump fails, so cardiac output decreases. Less blood reaches the tissues; renal artery perfusion falls, which decreases GFR and activates the renin-angiotensin system, causing compensatory vasoconstriction.

correlates.name: Deep Vein Thrombosis
correlates.presentation: Swelling, redness, warmth and pain.
correlates.pathophysiology: Endothelial dysfunction predisposes to thrombus formation as one leg of Virchow's triad.

correlates.name: Dehydration in Hot, Dry Environments
correlates.presentation: Progressive thirst, light-headedness, palpitations and dark concentrated urine, in a person who reports never having sweated.
correlates.pathophysiology: Insensible loss through skin and airway is unregulated and rises with heat, exercise and fever. In dry air sweat evaporates before it is felt, so the sensible cue that normally drives drinking is absent while losses continue.

correlates.name: Diabetes Insipidus
correlates.presentation: Water loss (dilute, high-volume urine) and hypernatremia.
correlates.pathophysiology: Too little ADH, or an ineffective ADH response, leaves the collecting duct impermeable to water.

correlates.name: Diabetic Cardiomyopathy and Low Cardiac Tissue T3 (NYITCOM Research)
correlates.pathophysiology: In all animal models studied in the Gerdes lab, cardiac tissue T3 is below normal even when serum T3 is normal — and T3 is an important regulator of microvascular blood flow.

correlates.name: Diabetic Nephropathy
correlates.presentation: Fatigue, bilateral pitting edema, hypertension, proteinuria WITHOUT hematuria, urine albumin 78 mg/g, creatinine 1.8, BUN 32, HbA1c 9.4%.
correlates.pathophysiology: Chronic hyperglycemia damages the glomeruli.
correlates.treatment: Tight BP and glucose control; SGLT2 inhibitor and/or ACE inhibitor/ARB; exercise, smoking cessation, low-sodium diet. Monitor eGFR, creatinine, electrolytes, urine albumin. Avoid nephrotoxic NSAIDs; counsel on dialysis/transplant. Goal: slow the declining GFR.

correlates.name: Diabetic Vascular Disease
correlates.presentation: In this model the ROS stain is the readout; clinically the same process is the endothelial dysfunction of diabetes.
correlates.pathophysiology: Slide 6 shows arteries from pre-diabetic and diabetic rats stained red for reactive oxygen species (ROS). A healthy VSMC does not generate ROS — it only contracts and relaxes — so the stain itself marks a switched, unhealthy phenotype.

correlates.name: Digitalis Glycoside Toxicity (Foxglove)
correlates.presentation: Loss of volume regulation with cell expansion and lysis.
correlates.pathophysiology: Digitalis glycosides — alkaloids from Digitalis purpurea (foxglove) — block the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Without osmotic work to exclude NaCl, Gibbs-Donnan forces win: water enters, cells swell and burst.

correlates.name: Digoxin (Digitalis) and Contractility
correlates.presentation: increased Ca²⁺ available for contraction → positive inotropy (increased cardiac contractility).
correlates.pathophysiology: Digoxin inhibits the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, raising intracellular Na⁺. The elevated intracellular Na⁺ drives the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger into reverse mode (pumps Na⁺ out, brings Ca²⁺ in), increasing intracellular Ca²⁺.

correlates.name: Digoxin Toxicity from a Verapamil Interaction
correlates.pathophysiology: P-glycoprotein normally pumps digoxin out of the systemic circulation into the gut and into the renal tubule. Verapamil blocks P-gp, so less digoxin is removed at both sites and plasma levels climb (Slide 25).
correlates.treatment: avoid the combination; if it is used, monitor digoxin levels closely.

correlates.name: Dihydropyridine-Induced Peripheral Edema
correlates.presentation: pitting edema, worst in the lower extremities and feet because of gravity.
correlates.pathophysiology: vasodilation produces pre-capillary (arteriolar) dilation with post-capillary reflex constriction, raising capillary hydrostatic pressure and permeability, so fluid redistributes into the interstitium (Slide 22).
correlates.treatment: dose reduction or a change of agent.

correlates.name: Dilated Cardiomyopathy (Pericardial Adaptation)
correlates.presentation: Massively dilated hearts, as seen in gross anatomy donors who died of dilated cardiomyopathy.
correlates.pathophysiology: Chronic, slowly progressive cardiac enlargement; the chamber dilates by myocyte lengthening (series sarcomere addition).

correlates.name: Diuretic Resistance / Refractory Edema (Diuretic Braking Phenomenon)
correlates.pathophysiology: Edema refractory to typically effective doses of loop diuretic. Three mechanism families: compensatory tubular adaptations, renal hemodynamics, and pharmacokinetic mechanisms.
correlates.treatment: Step 1 - exclude excessive salt intake and drug interactions. Step 2 - check adherence and increase the loop diuretic dose.

correlates.name: Duane Retraction Syndrome (DRS)
correlates.presentation: Decreased abduction of one eye (here the right) since birth; vision problems.
correlates.pathophysiology: Congenital absence or poor development of the abducens nuclei with aberrant innervation, classically limiting abduction (lateral rectus, CN VI).
correlates.treatment: Corrective lenses or eye muscle surgery improve head position but do not normalize horizontal motility. This patient had a right lateral strain (non-physiologic); after OMM her lateral gaze was more symmetric, written up as a poster.

correlates.name: Dyspnea in Left-Sided Heart Failure (J Receptor Activation)
correlates.presentation: Dyspnea, with rapid shallow breathing; activation also causes bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion, all defensive responses meant to protect the delicate alveolar structures.
correlates.pathophysiology: Left-sided failure backs pressure up into the pulmonary circulation and produces pulmonary edema. The excess fluid stretches the alveolar walls and ducts where the juxtacapillary (J) receptors sit, activating them.

correlates.name: Emphysema
correlates.presentation: the same functional endpoint as fibrosis — a diffusion-limited exchange with hypoxemia.
correlates.pathophysiology: destruction of cells rather than fibrotic thickening. The alveolar surface area A shrinks, so gases have "less opportunity" to cross; Vx and DL fall.

correlates.name: Exercise- and Heat-Associated Hypokalemia (Hot Yoga Scenario)
correlates.presentation: Light-headedness and palpitations described as "funny heartbeats" or skipped beats.
correlates.pathophysiology: Excessive sweating causes K+ loss in sweat, dropping plasma [K+] (Slide 29). Only ~2% of total-body K+ sits in the ECF, so small absolute losses move the plasma level substantially.
correlates.treatment: Oral K+ repletion (bananas, coconut water), with relief within about 5 minutes.

correlates.name: Exercise-Associated Dehydration (Hot Yoga Scenario)
correlates.presentation: Loose clothing (acute weight loss), atypically prominent superficial veins, intense thirst.
correlates.pathophysiology: Vigorous exercise plus excessive sweating produces a body water deficit, altering fluid compartment volumes.

correlates.name: Exertional (Stable) Angina
correlates.pathophysiology: fixed coronary obstruction; ischemia appears when demand rises.
correlates.treatment: beta blockers are first-line; a BB plus a DHP CCB is more effective than either agent alone (Slide 20). Non-DHP CCBs are used for patients who do not tolerate a beta blocker, because of their negative inotropic and chronotropic effects.

correlates.name: Facilitated Segment (Segmental Facilitation)
correlates.presentation: A tender, tense, restricted segment; the lecturer's example is segmental facilitation adding to a patient's tachycardia.
correlates.pathophysiology: Nociceptor activity from ligaments and joint capsules produces local tension at the segment, limiting motion and altering position; the same nociceptive drive can add to systemic problems.
correlates.treatment: Positioning to ease turns down the nociceptors; the nervous system responds to the point of balanced tension by resetting tissue tension to baseline and reducing facilitation.

correlates.name: Familial Hypercholesterolemia
correlates.presentation: The reason for a one-time lipid panel at ages 9-11 (Slide 27). In adults, an LDL greater than 190 is itself a high-risk category (Slide 30).
correlates.pathophysiology: Inherited severe elevation of LDL cholesterol, present from childhood rather than acquired through diet.
correlates.treatment: LDL greater than 190 mandates a statin regardless of any calculated risk score.

correlates.name: Fetal RAS Inhibitor Toxicity
correlates.pathophysiology: fetal renal function depends on angiotensin II; RAS blockade produces fetal hypotension and anuria with depressed renal function (Slide 40).
correlates.treatment: prevention only. Absolutely contraindicated in all trimesters, for every RAS inhibitor - period, the end .

correlates.name: First-Degree AV Block
correlates.pathophysiology: Delayed conduction through the AV node; every impulse still gets through.

correlates.name: First-Dose Effect (Alpha Blocker Orthostatic Hypotension)
correlates.presentation: dizziness or syncope on standing, most prominent with the first dose or a dose increase; it tends to subside as blood pressure normalizes but may persist.
correlates.pathophysiology: loss of alpha-1 mediated venoconstriction on standing lets blood pool in the legs, so cerebral perfusion falls (Slide 11).
correlates.treatment: make the first dose small and give it at bedtime so the peak concentration falls during sleep; add a diuretic to counter the sodium and water retention.

correlates.name: Foreign Body Aspiration
correlates.presentation: Sudden choking or coughing followed by unilateral wheeze, decreased breath sounds, and reduced expansion on the affected side.
correlates.pathophysiology: The right mainstem bronchus is shorter, wider, and more vertical than the left, so gravity and airflow carry aspirated material preferentially down the right side (Slide 9).

correlates.name: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease as an Airway Trigger
correlates.pathophysiology: excess stomach acid reaches the respiratory tree, damages and irritates the mucosa, and that irritation triggers bronchoconstriction through the muscarinic pathway (Slide 9).

correlates.name: Glaucoma (Topical Ophthalmic Beta Blockers)
correlates.pathophysiology: beta receptors of the eye are largely beta-2, located in the ciliary body epithelium and blood vessels (Slide 50).
correlates.treatment: topical beta blockers decrease intraocular pressure, presumably by decreasing production of aqueous humor and/or ocular blood flow, which decreases the ultrafiltration responsible for aqueous production.

correlates.name: Global Hypoxia and the Right Heart
correlates.pathophysiology: Uniform alveolar hypoxia constricts the entire pulmonary bed at once. Redistribution is impossible, so the only net result is a large rise in pulmonary vascular resistance.

correlates.name: Global Hypoxic Vasoconstriction at Altitude
correlates.pathophysiology: At high altitude every alveolus has a low PO2, so hypoxic vasoconstriction is triggered lung-wide instead of regionally. There is no better-ventilated region to divert blood toward.

correlates.name: Glucosuria in Diabetes Mellitus
correlates.pathophysiology: The filtered load of glucose exceeds the kidney's reabsorptive capacity, so glucose appears in the urine.

correlates.name: Goodpasture Syndrome
correlates.presentation: Hemoptysis, fatigue, dark urine, hypertension; RBC casts; crescents in Bowman's space on biopsy.
correlates.pathophysiology: Anti-type 4 collagen antibodies attack the glomerular basement membrane — the MIDDLE layer of the filtration barrier.

correlates.name: Heart Failure and Digoxin
correlates.presentation: Ejection fraction; on the Starling curve, an effective inotrope shifts the failing curve back toward normal.
correlates.pathophysiology: In heart failure the heart becomes weak from causes such as hypertension or myocardial infarction, and contractility is reduced (Slide 21).
correlates.treatment: Cardioactive glycosides such as digoxin inhibit the Na+/K+ ATPase (sodium pump), whose normal ATP-dependent job is K+ in and Na+ out against their electrochemical gradients.

correlates.name: Heart Failure and Exercise Intolerance
correlates.presentation: rapid fatigue and poor tolerance with any exertion; HFpEF patients look stable at rest and decompensate quickly with activity.
correlates.pathophysiology: HFrEF - reduced ejection fraction and systolic dysfunction diminish stroke volume, so cardiac output cannot rise with exertion. HFpEF - ejection fraction normal but diastolic filling impaired, so stroke volume is fixed and cannot be augmented (Slide 51).

correlates.name: Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction (HFpEF)
correlates.presentation: Heart failure of the non-dilated type with preserved ejection fraction.
correlates.pathophysiology: Hypertension drives interstitial fibrosis — collagen (tensile strength of steel) accumulating between myocytes — stiffening the ventricle and impairing relaxation.

correlates.name: Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction
correlates.pathophysiology: neprilysin inhibition raises natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, and substance P, which are natriuretic, vasodilatory, and antiproliferative in their own right.
correlates.treatment: ACE inhibitor, ARB, or the neprilysin inhibitor-ARB combination sacubitril-valsartan (the only one marketed), given with a beta blocker, plus a loop diuretic if fluid control is needed (Slide 36).

correlates.name: Heel Lift Therapy in the Growing Child
correlates.presentation: A growing child with a measured leg length discrepancy who is prescribed lift therapy.
correlates.pathophysiology: Compressive force stimulates bone to grow faster. A lift placed under the shorter leg increases compressive load through that limb, so in a skeletally immature patient it may accelerate growth on the lifted side (Slide 50).
correlates.treatment: Prescribe as in the adult, but monitor carefully and repeatedly - the discrepancy may self-correct as the child grows, and a lift left unchanged can overshoot.

correlates.name: High-Altitude Hypoxemia
correlates.presentation: a healthy lung compensates, since equilibration merely takes longer and still completes within the available transit time.
correlates.pathophysiology: barometric pressure falls with altitude, so by Dalton's law inspired and alveolar PO2 fall with it — down to roughly 50 mmHg at extreme altitude. ΔP in Fick's equation shrinks, slowing equilibration.

correlates.name: Horseshoe Kidney
correlates.presentation: Asymptomatic. It does not hurt the kidneys; you can live a completely normal life and even be an Olympic athlete.
correlates.pathophysiology: The two kidneys are connected (fused) by mistake. As the fused kidney rises, it cannot ascend fully because the inferior mesenteric artery stops it — so it gets stuck low.

correlates.name: Hydralazine-Induced Lupus-Like Syndrome
correlates.presentation: rash (the malar butterfly distribution, Slide 33), arthralgia, myalgia and fever.
correlates.pathophysiology: hydralazine is inactivated by N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2). Slow acetylators carry polymorphisms giving fewer or less active enzymes, so plasma levels run high for a given dose (Slide 25).
correlates.treatment: reversible - it resolves when the drug is withdrawn.

correlates.name: Hydronephrosis
correlates.presentation: Fluid-filled enlargement of one (or both) kidneys with a distended ureter.
correlates.pathophysiology: Urine/fluid accumulates in the urinary tract and cannot drain properly; the fluid backs up into the ureter, which bulges and expands.

correlates.name: Hyperkalemia
correlates.presentation: Initially increased excitability and contraction; with continued firing muscle stops responding, producing flaccid paralysis. Cardiac electrophysiology is disturbed and fatal arrhythmias may follow.
correlates.pathophysiology: Rising extracellular [K+] lowers the [K+]IC/[K+]EC ratio and depolarizes excitable membranes.

correlates.name: Hypertension
correlates.presentation: Usually silent; may present late with headache or bleeding when pressure is already very high.
correlates.pathophysiology: Chronically elevated arterial pressure. Primary hypertension (~90% of cases): no identifiable cause. Secondary hypertension (~10% of cases): a specific identifiable problem, for example in the kidneys.
correlates.treatment: RAAS-blocking drugs (ACE inhibitors, ARBs) are among today's drugs of choice.

correlates.name: Hypertension and L-Type Calcium Channel Blockers
correlates.pathophysiology: Excess vasoconstriction raises peripheral resistance and blood pressure. VSMC contraction depends on extracellular Ca²⁺ entering through voltage-gated L-type channels.
correlates.treatment: Nifedipine, amlodipine, verapamil — all L-type calcium channel blockers. Blocking the channel means the calcium never arrives, so there is no Ca²⁺-calmodulin complex and no contraction.

correlates.name: Hypertension in Pregnancy
correlates.treatment: methyldopa for chronic management (Slide 20); hydralazine, including intravenously, for hypertensive emergency during pregnancy or postpartum (Slide 30).

correlates.name: Hypertension with Diabetes, CKD and Left Ventricular Hypertrophy
correlates.pathophysiology: diabetes, chronic kidney disease and hypertension share a metabolic background and insulin resistance, so they cluster in the same patient . Sustained pressure load produces LVH; diabetic nephropathy raises creatinine.
correlates.treatment: add an ACE inhibitor. It improves remodeling of LVH and slows progression of chronic kidney disease in diabetic nephropathy - the one agent that treats all three problems at once.

correlates.name: Hypertension: Secondary Prevention in Practice
correlates.treatment: Diet, exercise, and medication started before the stroke or MI. Here the patient is on hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily but did not take it the day of the visit — an immediate candidate explanation for the 140/90.

correlates.name: Hypertensive Crisis in a Patient with Endothelial Dysfunction
correlates.pathophysiology: In diabetes the endothelium is dysfunctional and produces less nitric oxide, so endothelium-dependent vasodilators lose potency. Sodium nitroprusside bypasses the endothelium entirely by donating NO straight to the VSMC.
correlates.treatment: Sodium nitroprusside, a very potent vasodilator used in the emergency department for hypertensive crisis.

correlates.name: Hypertensive Emergency
correlates.pathophysiology: severe blood pressure elevation requiring controlled, titratable reduction; overshoot must be avoided because an abrupt fall provokes a sympathetic reflex.
correlates.treatment: nicardipine or clevidipine by slow I.V. infusion (Slide 19). A DHP CCB is combined with labetalol or esmolol to prevent reflex tachycardia.

correlates.name: Hypertensive Hypertrophy with Reduced Capillary Reserve
correlates.presentation: Chest pain (angina) on exertion from inadequate myocardial blood flow, with decreased exercise capacity.
correlates.pathophysiology: Systemic hypertension raises LV workload; myocytes enlarge in diameter and push capillaries apart. Capillary density drops from ~4,000 to ~2,500/mm² while resting perfusion rises from ~1/4 to ~1/2 of capillaries.

correlates.name: Hypertensive Nephrosclerosis
correlates.pathophysiology: chronically increased pressure narrows the afferent and efferent arterioles, which reduces glomerular blood flow and produces glomerular and tubular ischemia, then nephrosclerosis and fibrosis.

correlates.name: Hypertensive Urgency
correlates.presentation: SBP 180 or more or DBP 120 or more, without signs or symptoms of acute end-organ damage. Confirm the absence: no headache, no chest pain, unremarkable labs, and a normal fundus with no hemorrhages or papilledema.
correlates.treatment: still treat - short-acting oral agent first, then transition to long-acting.

correlates.name: Hyperthyroidism and Thyroid Storm
correlates.presentation: palpitations, tachycardia, tremulousness, anxiety, heat intolerance. Thyroid storm can cause supraventricular tachycardia and sudden death.
correlates.pathophysiology: hyperthyroidism raises basal metabolic rate and enhances organ sensitivity to catecholamines, associated with an increased number of beta adrenergic receptors (Slide 49).
correlates.treatment: beta blockers ameliorate the symptoms and control pulse rate, hypertension, and atrial fibrillation.

correlates.name: Hypoglycemia Unawareness in an Insulin-Treated Patient
correlates.presentation: the patient does not recognize that he or she is dropping into hypoglycemia.
correlates.pathophysiology: two hits (Slide 52). Beta-2 blockade blocks the hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis that would raise blood sugar, and beta blockade blunts the adrenergic warning symptoms - tremor, tachycardia, nervousness.

correlates.name: Hypokalemia
correlates.pathophysiology: Low extracellular K⁺ makes Vm more negative (would lower excitability), but the dominant effect is decreased K⁺ conductance — fewer K⁺ channels open, slowing repolarization and prolonging AP duration.

correlates.name: Hypokalemic Alkalosis
correlates.presentation: Low plasma K+ with a rising bicarbonate.
correlates.pathophysiology: K+ depletion increases density and activity of the apical H+/K+ ATPase in type A intercalated cells. That enhances K+ reabsorption, but every K+ reclaimed costs a secreted proton, so H+ secretion accelerates in parallel.

correlates.name: Hypomagnesemia
correlates.presentation: Predominantly neurological disturbances (tetany, especially with hypocalcemia), cardiac arrhythmias, increased peripheral vascular resistance.
correlates.pathophysiology: Abnormal loss - GI malabsorption, diarrhea, diuretics, renal disease. Loop diuretics remove the lumen-positive Vte that drives 70% of Mg++ reabsorption in the tALH.
correlates.treatment: Magnesium supplementation - an inexpensive supplement for blood pressure issues because it vasodilates and promotes flow.

correlates.name: Hypovolemic Hemorrhagic Shock (Bleeding Peptic Ulcer)
correlates.presentation: BP 90/40 (low), pulse elevated, respirations 28/min, lethargy, cold extremities; remains hypotensive despite a slow blood transfusion.
correlates.pathophysiology: A 65-year-old man with peptic ulcer disease presents with nausea, melena (blood in feces), and faintness — GI blood loss causing hypovolemia.

correlates.name: Hypovolemic Shock
correlates.presentation: Hypotension with the hallmark compensatory hemodynamic pattern — decreased preload, decreased CO, but increased SVR from intense vasoconstriction, very typical of bleeding.
correlates.pathophysiology: Loss of blood volume (hemorrhage/accident, major burns, dehydration) → decreased preload (decreased venous return) → decreased stroke volume → decreased cardiac output → decreased BP → tissue hypoperfusion.
correlates.treatment: Give volume: restoring volume raises stroke volume, cardiac output, and blood pressure, reperfusing the tissues.

correlates.name: Iliolumbar Ligament Strain and Its Referred Pain Pattern
correlates.presentation: Referred pain from the ipsilateral lumbosacral region into the lateral gluteal region and down the lateral thigh, which may extend into the groin, and into the testicle or labia on that side (Slide 10).
correlates.pathophysiology: Postural imbalance such as Short Leg Syndrome holds the innominate in a rotated position, placing sustained stress on the iliolumbar ligament; over time the ligament can calcify (Slide 9).
correlates.treatment: OMT for the pelvic and lumbar somatic dysfunction plus correction of the underlying postural asymmetry, including lift therapy when indicated.

correlates.name: Imperforate Anus
correlates.presentation: A newborn who cannot defecate — failure to pass meconium. Within a day the parents realize something is wrong if it was missed at birth.
correlates.pathophysiology: Dysfunction of the urorectal septum, which normally forms the sphincters and the opening of the anus into the cloacal region. If it fails, the anus is not open.

correlates.name: In-Stent Restenosis
correlates.presentation: Recurrent ischemic symptoms weeks to months after stenting, with a re-occluded lumen.
correlates.pathophysiology: A stent holds the lumen open but the metal damages the endothelium. Less endothelium means less nitric oxide, and NO is both a vasodilator and an anti-proliferative brake on the underlying VSMC.

correlates.name: Infant Cranial Molding (Parallelogram Head)
correlates.presentation: The classic parallelogram-shaped head of a baby.
correlates.pathophysiology: Strain residing within the bone itself — a distortion of bone shape — rather than between bones at a joint.
correlates.treatment: Molding — the balanced-tension approach applied to the shape of the bone itself.

correlates.name: Infantile Idiopathic Scoliosis and Early-Onset Disease
correlates.pathophysiology: possibly supine and slight side-lying positioning, letting gravity cause plastic deformation of the immature thorax (Slide 15).
correlates.treatment: ideal treatment is prevention by lying infants prone - the opposite of the back-to-sleep recommendation - otherwise well-fitting orthoses and casting early in skeletal growth.

correlates.name: Juvenile Idiopathic Scoliosis
correlates.presentation: onset 4 to 10 years; more progressive than adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (Slide 17).
correlates.treatment: progression of 5 to 7 degrees indicates bracing; non-operative success is variable.

correlates.name: Liddle Syndrome (Pseudoaldosteronism)
correlates.presentation: Hypertension with hypokalemia in a young patient.
correlates.pathophysiology: Rare autosomal dominant gain-of-function mutation in the genes regulating ENaC, producing far more channels than normal. Unregulated sodium reabsorption creates a strong lumen-negative potential, driving potassium and hydrogen secretion.
correlates.treatment: ENaC inhibitor plus sodium restriction, which manages both the hypertension and the hypokalemia.

correlates.name: Lifelong Resistance Training and Aortic Valve Narrowing
correlates.pathophysiology: repeated Valsalva-driven pressure overload produces concentric hypertrophy - wall thickens, chamber shrinks, stroke volume falls - and the valves face that same constant pressure.

correlates.name: Lobar Pneumonia Localized by the Silhouette Sign
correlates.presentation: in the lecturer's case the right heart border is crisp but the left heart border cannot be seen — the patient has a lingular pneumonia.
correlates.pathophysiology: alveoli fill with pus, blood, or fluid, all of which are soft tissue density. Consolidated lung now matches the density of the structure it touches and the interface disappears.

correlates.name: Loop (High-Ceiling) Diuretics
correlates.pathophysiology: NKCC in the thick ascending limb is the target of the loop diuretic class. Blocking it stops Na+, K+ and Cl- reabsorption and abolishes the lumen-positive Vte, so paracellular reabsorption of K+, Ca++ and Mg++ fails as well.

correlates.name: Loop Diuretic Ototoxicity
correlates.pathophysiology: Loop diuretics inhibit NKCC1 in the inner ear, disrupting the endolymph potassium balance that normal hearing depends on. The result is disturbance of hearing and balance.
correlates.treatment: Recognize, reduce dose or rate, avoid stacking ototoxic agents.

correlates.name: Loop Diuretic-Induced Hypokalemic Metabolic Alkalosis
correlates.presentation: Hypokalemia with a rising serum bicarbonate; muscle weakness, cramps, arrhythmia risk.
correlates.pathophysiology: Four converging mechanisms. (1) Strong natriuresis delivers a large sodium load to the principal cells, driving ENaC-mediated K+ wasting and, in parallel, aldosterone-regulated H+ secretion.
correlates.treatment: Potassium repletion, chloride/volume repletion, or a potassium-sparing strategy. Acetazolamide is an adjunct that gets at the cause by inducing a countervailing metabolic acidosis.

correlates.name: Lumbar Disc Herniation with Radiculopathy
correlates.presentation: Axial back pain, referred posterior thigh pain, or true radicular leg pain. Posture may show a trunk side shift that unloads the disc.
correlates.pathophysiology: As above - inflammatory nucleus reaches or breaches the innervated outer annulus, and root pain follows either mechanical compression or chemical inflammation.
correlates.treatment: Therapy and manipulation first; MRI and surgical referral for true or progressive weakness.

correlates.name: Lumbar Spinal Stenosis with Neurogenic Claudication
correlates.presentation: Leg pain on walking at a predictable distance, relieved by sitting. The shopping cart sign - leaning forward on a cart or walker - relieves it the same way, by flexing the lumbar spine.
correlates.pathophysiology: Degenerative narrowing of the foramen and central canal. Walking cycles the lumbar spine into repeated extension, and extension of an already narrow foramen provokes symptoms.
correlates.treatment: Therapy and manipulation; MRI and referral if leg symptoms do not improve.

correlates.name: Lymphatic Failure and Perivascular Edema
correlates.pathophysiology: When lymphatic clearance falls behind filtration, the perivascular potential space around the bronchovascular bundle fills with fluid - edema.

correlates.name: Mannitol-Induced Pulmonary Edema
correlates.presentation: A 65-year-old man treated with IV mannitol for traumatic brain injury improves neurologically, then hours later develops dyspnea, crackles, falling oxygen saturation and bilateral pulmonary edema on imaging (Slide 46).
correlates.pathophysiology: Mannitol stays extracellular and raises plasma osmolality; water is pulled from the intracellular to the interstitial to the intravascular compartment, rapidly expanding plasma volume.

correlates.name: Maxillary Sinusitis
correlates.presentation: Most common site of sinusitis of all the paranasal sinuses.
correlates.pathophysiology: The maxillary sinus ostium sits high on the medial sidewall of the sinus, so drainage is inherently poor; the sinus depends on a mechanical "pump" generated by motion between the maxilla and the zygoma.
correlates.treatment: Zygomatic (maxillary) lift to restore zygoma-maxilla motion and the sinus pump; the frontal lift and nasion spread address frontal/ethmoid sinus drainage.

correlates.name: Medullary Ischemic Injury from Hypoperfusion
correlates.presentation: Falling urine output after any drop in cardiac output or renal perfusion; cell death and tissue damage appear relatively quickly.
correlates.pathophysiology: The medulla operates at a baseline oxygen tension far below the cortex because medullary blood flow, vascular permeability and vascular volume are all low by design - the same arrangement that lets solutes accumulate. There is no reserve to give up.

correlates.name: Metastatic Disease of the Spine
correlates.presentation: The pain has a different feel - patients do not describe positional modifiers. It is a deep, creepy pain at night in bed that does not change with position.
correlates.pathophysiology: The spine is a common site of metastasis.

correlates.name: Methemoglobinemia (Slide 6)
correlates.presentation: Fatigue and a bluish tint to the skin.
correlates.pathophysiology: The central iron atom of heme is oxidized from the normal Fe2+ to Fe3+. Ferric heme is unable to bind oxygen.

correlates.name: Microvascular Ischemia in "Non-Ischemic" Heart Disease
correlates.presentation: Traditionally required PET scanning with radioisotopes, so it was rarely measured and is underreported; newer non-radioactive technology is rapidly moving toward clinical use, which is why reports are increasing.
correlates.pathophysiology: Impaired microvascular blood flow despite patent epicardial coronary arteries.

correlates.name: Myocardial Infarction (Histologic Appearance)
correlates.presentation: Histologically, an infarct is an area that is all fibrotic with NO myocytes — myocytes are missing where they should be.
correlates.pathophysiology: Infarction kills myocytes; because adult myocytes cannot proliferate, the dead muscle is replaced by collagen (replacement fibrosis).

correlates.name: Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome
correlates.presentation: the lecture's radiograph shows a normally aerated right lung and a completely opaque, collapsed left lung (Slide 16).
correlates.pathophysiology: mostly premature infants born with insufficient surfactant; Laplace collapsing forces go unopposed and alveoli close.
correlates.treatment: antenatal steroid injections to the mother aid lung maturation and surfactant production. Otherwise nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP) applies positive pressure to hold the alveoli open; no surgery is required.

correlates.name: Nephrotic Syndrome
correlates.presentation: Appearance of large proteins — notably albumin — in the urine.
correlates.pathophysiology: Defects in or damage to the slit diaphragm's integral membrane proteins (nephrin, NEPH1/Kirrel1, podocin) make the glomerular filtration barrier leaky.

correlates.name: Neurogenic Shock
correlates.presentation: like septic and anaphylactic shock - hypotension, wide pulse pressure, warm skin - except there is no tachycardia.
correlates.pathophysiology: dysregulation of the autonomic nervous system causing loss of sympathetic tone with an unopposed parasympathetic response, so the vasculature cannot constrict and the heart cannot mount a reflex response.
correlates.treatment: fluid resuscitation and vasoactive support (Slide 34).

correlates.name: Neuromuscular and Acquired Scoliosis
correlates.presentation: ask whether the curve disappears with forward flexion or lying down. If it does, the curve comes from below - a leg length discrepancy - rather than from the spine; if not, consider primary postural scoliosis.
correlates.pathophysiology: the two most common neuromuscular causes are leg length discrepancy and neurofibromatosis (Slide 22).

correlates.name: Nitroprusside Cyanide Toxicity
correlates.pathophysiology: cyanide is part of the nitroprusside molecule, released when red blood cells take the drug up. Detoxification by rhodanese needs a sulfur donor and saturates; a large or prolonged infusion exhausts the sulfur supply and cyanide accumulates (Slide 24).
correlates.treatment: two antidote strategies (Slide 32) - sodium nitrite followed by sodium thiosulfate, supplying the sulfur donor that lets cyanide metabolism continue; or hydroxocobalamin, which binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin, nontoxic vitamin B12.

correlates.name: Non-Physiologic Right-to-Left Shunt (Eisenmenger Syndrome and Others)
correlates.presentation: Hypoxemia that persists on supplemental oxygen.
correlates.pathophysiology: A septal defect lets oxygen-poor right-heart blood mix directly into oxygen-rich blood returning from the lungs, which is then ejected into the aorta.

correlates.name: NSAID-Induced Acute Kidney Injury
correlates.presentation: Acute kidney injury in a volume-depleted patient taking NSAIDs.
correlates.pathophysiology: NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis. In a volume-depleted patient with angiotensin II acting, losing the prostaglandin afferent dilation leaves unopposed afferent constriction → GFR crashes.

correlates.name: NSAID-Induced Blood Pressure Elevation
correlates.presentation: an apparently non-responsive hypertensive whose medication list includes a chronic NSAID - here, ibuprofen taken for osteoarthritis.
correlates.pathophysiology: NSAIDs raise blood pressure and antagonize the mechanism by which antihypertensives work, blunting the response to therapy .
correlates.treatment: counsel on NSAID use and substitute an analgesic that does not raise blood pressure, e.g. acetaminophen (Tylenol Extra Strength) or another headache agent.

correlates.name: Nutcracker Syndrome
