correlates.presentation: Hematuria, left flank pain, pelvic pressure/pain, pelvic varicose veins, varicocele.
correlates.pathophysiology: Very rare compression disorder — the longer left renal vein is squeezed between the abdominal aorta and superior mesenteric artery as it crosses to the left kidney.

correlates.name: Obesity (and abdominal loading generally)
correlates.pathophysiology: Mass load of adipose tissue surrounding the ribcage and abdomen, plus elevated intra-abdominal pressure transmitted to the chest.

correlates.name: Obstructive Lung Disease (Asthma, Chronic Bronchitis)
correlates.presentation: increased residual volume and increased FRC - both of which represent air left in the lung after expiration (Slide 35).
correlates.pathophysiology: airways are partially obstructed, so the lung loses the ability to develop the positive alveolar pressure needed to drive air out; air is retained after expiration.
correlates.treatment: not covered here beyond mechanics; the lecture notes that in asthma expiration becomes an active process, with the abdominals contracting exactly as in exercise (Slide 16).

correlates.name: Obstructive Shock: Pulmonary Embolism, Tension Pneumothorax, Cardiac Tamponade
correlates.presentation: all three share narrow pulse pressure, cool clammy extremities and poor capillary refill.
correlates.pathophysiology: PE and tension pneumothorax obstruct flow through the pulmonary circulation, so the RV strains against a high afterload and the LV is starved of preload.
correlates.treatment: fluid resuscitation plus relieving the obstruction - remove the embolus, decompress the pericardium or pleural space (Slide 34).

correlates.name: Obstructive Sleep Apnea
correlates.presentation: polysomnography.
correlates.pathophysiology: disordered breathing during sleep; a recognized secondary cause of hypertension.

correlates.name: Occipitomastoid Suture Restriction and Jugular Foramen Compromise
correlates.presentation: Vagal (CN X) effects dominate - cardiac symptoms with heart rate and blood pressure changes, respiratory complaints including asthma, and GI symptoms such as GERD and nausea. Infantile colic belongs here as well.
correlates.pathophysiology: The OM suture lies between the occiput and the temporal, and the jugular foramen sits immediately at that junction.
correlates.treatment: V-spread with directing the tide, restricted side first, then recheck and usually treat the contralateral suture.

correlates.name: Oligohydramnios
correlates.presentation: Without the protective fluid, the embryo/fetus sticks to the wall of the uterus and gets deformed — feet, arms, and sometimes the face are molded against the wall, and the deformation is permanent ("you're born this way").
correlates.pathophysiology: Too little amniotic fluid (oligo- = a little). Amniotic fluid is essentially the baby's urine — the fetus pees it out, swallows it, and recirculates it continuously as it grows.

correlates.name: Olmesartan Sprue-Like Enteropathy
correlates.presentation: severe chronic diarrhea and weight loss.
correlates.pathophysiology: a drug-specific effect unique to olmesartan, not a class effect of the ARBs (Slide 38).
correlates.treatment: discontinue olmesartan.

correlates.name: Open-Angle Glaucoma
correlates.pathophysiology: Bicarbonate formed in the ciliary epithelium is required for aqueous humor production. Carbonic anhydrase inhibition reduces bicarbonate formation, so aqueous humor secretion falls and intraocular pressure drops, relieving pressure on the optic nerve.
correlates.treatment: Systemic acetazolamide or topical dorzolamide/brinzolamide eye drops.

correlates.name: Pediatric Nervous System and Learning Problems
correlates.presentation: Learning disabilities in children and a range of "nervous-system-type" problems.
correlates.pathophysiology: Distortion of the cranial container can interfere with the function of the sensitive, tightly packed brain.

correlates.name: Pelvic Kidney
correlates.presentation: Sits low, next to the bladder. It functions normally — you would not know you had one unless it showed up on an X-ray.
correlates.pathophysiology: A kidney that fails to rise during its normal ascent.

correlates.name: Pheochromocytoma
correlates.presentation: hypertension and sweating from excessive catecholamine release.
correlates.pathophysiology: a tumor of the adrenal medulla secreting norepinephrine (mainly) and epinephrine, episodically or continuously.
correlates.treatment: phenoxybenzamine perioperatively; because it is an irreversible blocker the blockade outlasts the drug (duration >=3 days). Surgery is definitive.

correlates.name: Piriformis Syndrome
correlates.presentation: Typically no actual back pain - deep buttock pain radiating down the posterior thigh to the back of the knee. Supine, the leg often rests in passive external rotation, which slackens the muscle and unloads the nerve. Gait is antalgic or normal.
correlates.pathophysiology: The piriformis pressing on the sciatic nerve. Active contraction makes it bulge against the nerve; internal rotation of the hip stretches it taut against the nerve. Either is a provocative maneuver.

correlates.name: Plagiocephaly and Brachycephaly
correlates.pathophysiology: Moldable infant bones deform under sustained positional pressure. Plagiocephaly = asymmetrical distortion (one side flattened); brachycephaly ("flat-head syndrome") = shortened front-to-back (AP) diameter.
correlates.treatment: OMM, or helmet molding therapy — helmets require ~23 hours/day of wear (compliance is difficult) and a recent article showed they do not necessarily improve outcomes. Prospective OMM studies use a validated sensor "hairnet" mapping head asymmetry.

correlates.name: Pleural Effusion
correlates.presentation: chest x-ray showing dramatic fluid collection at the lung base, with hardly any visible air in the affected lower zone (Slide 21).
correlates.pathophysiology: fluid rather than air accumulates in the pleural space. Only an optimal thin film belongs there; excess fluid displaces air from the dependent lung.
correlates.treatment: thoracentesis, also called pleural tapping - a needle is inserted carefully into the pleural cavity and fluid is drained over a good period of time…

correlates.name: Pleural Effusion / Intrapleural Edema
correlates.presentation: the lecturer frames it as edema of the intrapleural space, which compresses lung and impairs expansion.
correlates.pathophysiology: lymphatic drainage of the intrapleural space fails while hydrostatic filtration continues, so fluid accumulates far beyond the normal 10 mL.

correlates.name: Pleural Effusion and Thoracocentesis
correlates.presentation: Aspiration of the fluid for analysis; ultrasound is increasingly used to localize it.
correlates.pathophysiology: Fluid collects by gravity in the costodiaphragmatic recess, the largest region of pleural cavity without lung in it (Slide 26).
correlates.treatment: Pleural tap in the 8th or 9th intercostal space, midaxillary line, just superior to the superior border of the rib (Slide 32).

correlates.name: Pneumothorax
correlates.presentation: the lecturer's settings are stab wounds and trauma, and after cardiothoracic surgery, where air is found in the pleural cavity.
correlates.pathophysiology: air enters the pleural space through rupture or puncture of the lung or chest wall. Pleural pressure becomes less negative, transpulmonary pressure falls toward zero, and unopposed elastic recoil collapses the lung (Slide 21).

correlates.name: Pneumothorax and Loss of Pleural Pressure
correlates.presentation: Failure of ventilation on the affected side.
correlates.pathophysiology: Ventilation depends on the pressure differential between parietal and visceral pleura, not on chest wall mechanics alone.

correlates.name: Polyhydramnios
correlates.presentation: When the water breaks, a gallon or two of fluid comes out — a bad sign that flags the diagnosis.
correlates.pathophysiology: Excess accumulation of amniotic fluid — because the embryo/fetus does not swallow it (or does not swallow enough of it). Maternal diabetes can also cause it.

correlates.name: Positive-Pressure Mechanical Ventilation and Iatrogenic Zone 1
correlates.pathophysiology: The ventilator raises alveolar pressure and therefore lowers transmural pressure - the pressure difference between the inside of the lung and the outside.
correlates.treatment: Settings are calibrated to the individual patient and monitored closely, precisely because of this zone 1 risk (Slide 18).

correlates.name: Post-Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)
correlates.pathophysiology: hemodynamic changes after acute MI drive high RAAS activity, and angiotensin II promotes ventricular remodeling.
correlates.treatment: an ACE inhibitor or ARB improves mortality in randomized trials, especially after ST-elevation MI (Slides 36, 45).

correlates.name: Post-Viral Airway Disease (including Long COVID)
correlates.pathophysiology: viral infection of the airway is one of the depicted triggers of bronchoconstriction (Slide 9).

correlates.name: Posterior Fibular Head Somatic Dysfunction
correlates.presentation: Referenced at the fibular head, but the entire fibula is assessed; after treatment, recheck by shifting the fibula anterior-posterior and superior-inferior, feeling for ease and evenness of motion.
correlates.pathophysiology: Somatic dysfunction of the fibula in which the fibular head rests posteriorly — the more common scenario compared with an anterior fibular head.
correlates.treatment: BLT of the fibula — contacts at the fibular head and lateral malleolus, balance the seesaw motion (anterior pressure at the posterior component moves it anteriorly and slightly superiorly)…

correlates.name: Potassium Disorders on the ECG
correlates.presentation: hyperkalemia raises T wave amplitude and can also widen the QRS; hypokalemia flattens the T wave and brings out a U wave, which looks like an inverted T wave sitting after it.
correlates.pathophysiology: serum potassium sets the repolarization gradient, so it is read off the T wave.

correlates.name: Potassium Disturbances on the ECG
correlates.pathophysiology: Potassium carries phase 3 (repolarization) of the cardiac action potential, so any potassium disturbance shows up in the repolarization structures - the QT interval, the T wave, and if severe enough the QRS complex.

correlates.name: Potassium-Sparing Diuretics (Amiloride, Triamterene)
correlates.presentation: Reduced urinary K+ loss - the mirror image of the kaliuresis produced by diuretics acting upstream.
correlates.pathophysiology: These agents block apical ENaC in principal cells. Without Na+ entry the apical membrane hyperpolarizes, the gradient for K+ exit collapses, and falling intracellular Na+ reduces Na+/K+ ATPase activity.

correlates.name: Pre-Renal Failure (Pre-Renal Azotemia)
correlates.presentation: BUN:creatinine ratio greater than 20:1 with low urine sodium — the kidney works fine, it just is not being fed.
correlates.pathophysiology: An insult to the kidney's blood supply (arterial insult, dehydration, CHF). The kidney senses hypovolemia and sequesters sodium (urine sodium falls); slow tubular flow allows extra urea reabsorption — but creatinine is NOT reabsorbed.

correlates.name: Pregnancy
correlates.pathophysiology: The gravid uterus compresses the diaphragm from below, reducing both FRC and TLC.

correlates.name: Preterm Labor (Tocolysis)
correlates.treatment: nifedipine, for 48 hours only, to suppress premature contractions in preterm labor at 24-34 weeks (Slide 21).

correlates.name: Primary Aldosteronism
correlates.presentation: the triad of hypertension, unexplained hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis.
correlates.pathophysiology: primary mineralocorticoid excess, specifically aldosterone, driving sodium retention with potassium and hydrogen ion loss.

correlates.name: Probenecid and Penicillin G: Blocking the Organic Acid Secretory System
correlates.pathophysiology: penicillin G is an organic anion avidly secreted into the lumen by the OASS, so much of a dose is lost in urine. Probenecid inhibits the organic acid secretory system, blocking that secretion.

correlates.name: Prolonged QT Interval and Torsades de Pointes
correlates.presentation: QT longer than half the R-R interval, or outside 0.36-0.44 s.
correlates.pathophysiology: Delayed ventricular repolarization widens the vulnerable window for a triggered beat.

correlates.name: Proteinuric Chronic Kidney Disease (Diabetic and Non-Diabetic)
correlates.pathophysiology: three layers - lowering systemic blood pressure (which every antihypertensive does), dilating the efferent arteriole to drop intraglomerular pressure (which only RAS inhibitors do), and reducing protein excretion. Other intrarenal mechanisms are likely.
correlates.treatment: ACE inhibitors and ARBs slow progression of both forms (Slide 36).

correlates.name: Psoas Syndrome
correlates.presentation: Back pain via its lumbar attachments and groin and thigh pain via its insertion on the lesser trochanter, looking much like L2-L3 disc pathology.
correlates.pathophysiology: The psoas is not just a hip flexor - it actively stabilizes and moves the lumbar spine. A spectrum from image-confirmable tendonitis or bursitis (athletes doing heavy hip flexion or plyometrics) to a simply tight psoas harboring a trigger point.

correlates.name: Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension
correlates.presentation: Mean pulmonary artery pressure greater than 20 mmHg at rest.
correlates.pathophysiology: Endothelial dysfunction in the pulmonary vasculature goes beyond reduced NO - there is also increased endothelin and elevated ROS, plus reduced prostacyclin, producing pulmonary vasoconstriction.
correlates.treatment: Bosentan, an endothelin-1 receptor antagonist that stops endothelin binding its receptor; and sildenafil (Viagra), a PDE-5 inhibitor that prevents cGMP breakdown and enhances NO-mediated vasodilation.

correlates.name: Pulmonary Embolism and the Dual-Supply Safety Net
correlates.pathophysiology: An embolus occludes a vessel in one circulation and would otherwise starve the downstream territory of blood.

correlates.name: Pulmonary Embolism as Dead Space Ventilation
correlates.presentation: V/Q for that unit is infinity, and its alveolar gas drifts toward ambient values, PO2 150 and PCO2 0.
correlates.pathophysiology: The embolus clogs a pulmonary vessel, so a ventilated alveolus loses its perfusion entirely - alveolar dead space.

correlates.name: Pulmonary Fibrosis
correlates.presentation: hypoxemia and exertional dyspnea; oxygen, already the poorer diffuser, suffers before CO2 does.
correlates.pathophysiology: thickening of the epithelium and basal membrane separating the alveolar space from the capillary raises Δx. Since Δx is the denominator of Fick's equation, Vx falls and DL falls. Pulmonary edema does the same thing by inserting fluid into the path.

correlates.name: RAS Inhibitor Acute Kidney Injury and Hyperkalemia
correlates.pathophysiology: efferent arteriolar dilation drops glomerular capillary pressure. If intrarenal perfusion pressure is already compromised, that further drop causes acute kidney injury.

correlates.name: Raynaud Phenomenon
correlates.treatment: long-acting DHP CCBs. At least a moderate reduction in the intensity of attacks and prevention of tissue loss is achievable in most patients (Slide 21).

correlates.name: Renal Agenesis
correlates.presentation: Unilateral agenesis is surprisingly benign — one kidney is enough. In a baby, the solitary kidney expands and enlarges (hypertrophies) because it does the work of two.
correlates.pathophysiology: A kidney is not formed (agenesis = not developed; the Greek "a-" means "no").

correlates.name: Renal Artery Stenosis
correlates.pathophysiology: Arterial narrowing reduces renal plasma flow while GFR is defended, so filtration fraction RISES.

correlates.name: Renal Artery Stenosis and Fibromuscular Dysplasia
correlates.presentation: an abdominal bruit heard on abdominal auscultation is the exam clue for both.
correlates.pathophysiology: renovascular narrowing lowers renal perfusion, which stimulates renin and drives the RAAS cascade above.

correlates.name: Renal Disease / Renal Failure and K+ Excretion
correlates.pathophysiology: When kidneys lose the capacity to excrete K+, the GI tract tries to pick up the slack by increasing K+ secretion.

correlates.name: Renal Failure
correlates.presentation: Severe acidosis from acid retention.
correlates.pathophysiology: The kidneys are the sole effective route for neutralizing nonvolatile acid; when they fail, titratable buffer and ammonium excretion collapse and de novo bicarbonate generation stops.

correlates.name: Resistant Hypertension
correlates.presentation: blood pressure remaining >= 140/90 despite optimal use of 3 or more antihypertensive medications of different classes, including a diuretic at maximally tolerated dose - or blood pressure controlled only on 4 or more medications…

correlates.name: Restrictive Lung Disease (pulmonary fibrosis, pneumonia, pulmonary edema)
correlates.presentation: FVC decreased more than FEV1, so FEV1/FVC is preserved or elevated (the lecturer's example, 2.8 ÷ 3.1 ≈ 90%); FRC and RV both decreased.
correlates.pathophysiology: reduced lung compliance increases stiffness and limits expansion; the same elastic recoil that resists filling also drives rapid emptying.

correlates.name: Ruptured Chordae Tendineae / Papillary Muscle Dysfunction after Myocardial Infarction
correlates.presentation: the valve leaks severely; the lecturer notes it can leak so far that it produces severe, even lethal cardiac incapacity.
correlates.pathophysiology: low coronary blood flow in MI ruptures a chorda tendinea or paralyzes a papillary muscle. The tethering system fails, so during ventricular contraction the mitral leaflet bulges far backward into the left atrium.

correlates.name: Sacral Insufficiency Fracture
correlates.presentation: Low back and buttock pain in an elderly patient, often without significant trauma.
correlates.pathophysiology: In the elderly the SI joint often fuses/ankyloses while bone quality falls with osteoporosis.

correlates.name: Saphenous Vein Graft in Coronary Bypass Surgery
correlates.pathophysiology: The saphenous vein of the leg is so muscular — already possessing a relatively thick "muscularized" wall from a lifetime of working against gravity — that it is the preferred vein for coronary bypass grafting.

correlates.name: Scoliosis and the Functional vs Structural Curve
correlates.presentation: Asymmetric rib cage on forward bending; may be a full scoliosis or only a type 1 group curve with a subtle hump.
correlates.pathophysiology: Vertebral rotation accompanies lateral curvature, carrying the ribs posteriorly on the convex side and producing the rib hump.
correlates.treatment: Determined by whether the curve is correctable - side-bend the patient toward the convexity; if the hump resolves the curve is functional and responds to OMT, exercise and postural correction, whereas a persistent hump indicates a structural curve.

correlates.name: Septic Shock
correlates.presentation: SIRS = 2 of 4 - temperature > 38 or < 36 C, HR > 90, RR > 20 (or PaCO₂ < 32 mmHg), WBC > 12,000 or < 4,000 or > 10% immature bands. qSOFA = 2 of 3 - RR > 22, altered mentation, systolic BP < 100 (Slides 26-27).
correlates.pathophysiology: usually gram-negative bacteria acting through the endotoxin lipopolysaccharide (LPS). The lipid A portion binds the pattern-recognition receptor toll-like receptor 4 (TLR-4) on macrophages and B cells, stimulating IL-1, TNF and IL-6.
correlates.treatment: broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within the first hour of diagnosis while awaiting blood cultures - vancomycin plus cefepime or piperacillin.

correlates.name: Severe Scoliosis with Cardiopulmonary Compromise
correlates.presentation: A recent patient with a large scoliosis finally presented because of shortness of breath.
correlates.pathophysiology: Progressive distortion of the thoracic container mechanically impairs cardiac and pulmonary function.

correlates.name: SGLT2 Inhibitors ("Glucuretics") in Type 2 Diabetes and Heart Failure
correlates.pathophysiology: blocking apical SGLT2 in S1, the transporter responsible for most glucose reabsorption, forces glucose into the urine — hence glucuretics.
correlates.treatment: developed for type 2 diabetes mellitus, later found remarkably efficacious in congestive heart failure; approved for both.

correlates.name: Short Leg Syndrome
correlates.presentation: Multiple findings rather than one: unlevel iliac crests, ASIS/PSIS and shoulders; increased lumbar lordosis; asymmetric foot orientation; low back, gluteal, lateral thigh or groin pain; and the iliolumbar referral pattern.
correlates.pathophysiology: An asymmetry at or below the pelvis - a true short bone, a pronated foot, a healed fracture, polio, a hip prosthesis, or innominate somatic dysfunction - unlevels the sacral base.
correlates.treatment: OMT first, then heel lift therapy dosed by L ≤ SBU / (D + C), placed on the side of the lowered sacral base, plus stretching and toning homework. The standing flexion test should become negative when the lift is correct.

correlates.name: SIADH (Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone)
correlates.presentation: Hyponatremia (dilution of serum sodium by retained water).
correlates.pathophysiology: Too much ADH → continuous water retention.

correlates.name: Sickle Cell Anemia in the Pulmonary Bed
correlates.presentation: Respiratory manifestations of the disease follow from obstruction of this bed.
correlates.pathophysiology: Pulmonary capillaries admit red cells essentially one at a time and depend on the cell deforming to fit a ~6 micrometer lumen. A misshapen, rigid cell cannot deform and lodges, obstructing the bed (Slide 21).

correlates.name: Sickle Cell Hemoglobin, HbS (Slide 7)
correlates.presentation: A red cell packed with HbS has a lower oxygen-carrying capacity and destabilizes in shape, especially under oxygen-poor conditions, which wears the hemoglobin out much faster and causes a whole host of downstream problems.
correlates.pathophysiology: A point mutation in the hemoglobin beta chain substitutes valine for glutamic acid, slightly changing the conformation of the molecule.

correlates.name: Sinus Tachycardia and Sinus Bradycardia
correlates.presentation: Normal adult sinus rate is 60-100 bpm (average about 72 bpm). A sinus rate above 100 bpm is sinus tachycardia; below 60 bpm is sinus bradycardia.
correlates.pathophysiology: Both are disorders of the rate of sinus node phase 4 depolarization (or of the distance to threshold). Sympathetic drive steepens phase 4 and speeds the rate; vagal drive hyperpolarizes and flattens phase 4 and slows it.

correlates.name: Situational / Performance Anxiety ("Stage Fright")
correlates.presentation: extreme anxiety or panic in specific situations, with sympathetic manifestations - palpitations, chest tightness, breathlessness, muscular tension, trembling, flushing, sweating, dry mouth (Slide 51).
correlates.treatment: a low dose of propranolol taken about an hour before the performance reliably decreases the somatic manifestations, such as the pounding heart and trembling hands and voice.

correlates.name: Solute-Free Water Infusion Injury
correlates.presentation: Massive tissue damage at the injection site — the cells simply burst.
correlates.pathophysiology: Infusing pure water delivers profoundly hypo-osmolar fluid directly to cells at the infusion site; water rushes in by osmosis.
correlates.treatment: Never infuse solute-free water. When free water is needed, give isotonic 5% dextrose: isotonic on entry, then the glucose is metabolized to CO₂ and water, leaving free water safely diluted throughout the ECF.

correlates.name: Somatic Dysfunction (Ligamentous Articular Strain)
correlates.presentation: A tight, tender, restricted area that often fails to move with breathing (obvious at the ribs, subtle at the ankle); tissue may feel congested or dry and poorly perfused.
correlates.pathophysiology: Strain held in the ligaments and joint capsule (articular surfaces only define the planes of motion).
correlates.treatment: Bring the strained ligaments to a point of balanced tension (indirect or direct) so the natural agencies within the patient make the correction; add respiratory or postural assistance as needed.

correlates.name: Spondylolysis and Isthmic Spondylolisthesis
correlates.presentation: Back pain in a young athlete - high school age. A visible step-off may be seen on the lateral film.
correlates.pathophysiology: Stress fracture through the pars interarticularis, which allows the vertebra above to translate forward.

correlates.name: ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)
correlates.presentation: chest pain, discomfort or pressure - the trigger phrase for "EKG, stat" to rule out acute coronary syndrome.
correlates.pathophysiology: transmural ischemia shifts the injured myocardium's resting potential, lifting the ST segment.

correlates.name: Stable Angina and Cardiac Rehabilitation
correlates.presentation: ST depression or reproducible angina at a definable workload; terminate the test there (Slide 28).
correlates.pathophysiology: fixed coronary obstruction; ischemia appears once myocardial oxygen demand crosses a fixed supply ceiling.
correlates.treatment: cardiac rehab then trains repeatedly up to that heart rate.

correlates.name: Stalled Labor and Ineffective Contractions
correlates.presentation: Labor that has stalled despite ongoing contractions.
correlates.pathophysiology: Ineffective or arrested contractions with widespread fascial and autonomic strain. CV4 is proposed to work through improved CSF contact with the circumventricular organs, including the posterior pituitary, which secretes oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone.
correlates.treatment: CV4 - studies have been done in stalled labor with ineffective contractions, and the technique helps the process proceed.

correlates.name: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
correlates.treatment: nimodipine, which is lipophilic and produces cerebral artery vasodilation, to reduce the incidence and severity of ischemic deficits (Slide 21).

correlates.name: Supraventricular Tachyarrhythmias
correlates.treatment: verapamil and diltiazem in hemodynamically stable patients, to slow automaticity and slow conduction through the AV node, which slows the ventricular response (Slide 21).

correlates.name: Supraventricular Tachycardia (Vagal Maneuver Response)
correlates.presentation: Rapid heart rhythm with palpitations, arriving in the ER needing rate control quickly.
correlates.treatment: Vagal maneuvers — Valsalva or carotid massage — driving the parasympathetic outflow above from the NTS via CN X, slowing AV conduction and the rate.

correlates.name: Temporal Bone Dysfunction - "The Troublemaker of the Head"
correlates.presentation: Difficulty draining the middle ear (otitis media), tinnitus, hearing and balance problems, vertigo; strabismus from CN IV/VI involvement; trigeminal neuralgia; Bell's palsy from CN VII.
correlates.pathophysiology: More cranial nerves relate to the temporal than to any other bone. CN IV and VI run where the temporal and sphenoid meet, alongside the leaves of the tentorium, and can be irritated or compressed when the temporal is severely internally or externally rotated.
correlates.treatment: Diagnose with this hold now; it can also serve as a treatment contact once one or both temporals are found restricted (taught later). Bilateral external rotation of the temporals is exactly the accident to avoid during a CV4.

correlates.name: Tension Headache
correlates.presentation: Bilateral, sharp headaches at the temples, feeling "around the head" (band-like), lasting 1-2 hours, severity 3-8/10, associated with work stress.
correlates.pathophysiology: Stress-associated headache with prominent musculoskeletal contributors — in this patient: forward head carriage, protracted shoulders, paravertebral and trapezius muscle spasm, and cervical/OA somatic dysfunction.
correlates.treatment: OMT plus lifestyle — walking 30 min/day, meditation/prayer for stress, cervical and pectoral stretching, rhomboid strengthening. Antidepressants and biofeedback/CBT are options she declined or cannot access.

correlates.name: Tension Pneumothorax Missed on a Rotated Film
correlates.presentation: the film shows a pneumothorax; the degree of mediastinal shift is the finding that separates simple from tension physiology.
correlates.pathophysiology: air trapped under pressure in the pleural space shifts the mediastinum away from the affected side, obstructing venous return.

correlates.name: The Triple Hit: NSAID + ACE Inhibitor/ARB + Diuretic Acute Kidney Injury
correlates.presentation: The lecture's case - a 75-year-old with hypertension and heart failure on lisinopril and furosemide self-treats knee pain with naproxen and develops dizziness and a sharp rise in serum creatinine.
correlates.pathophysiology: Three simultaneous attacks on glomerular filtration pressure. (1) The NSAID blocks prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilation, so the afferent arteriole constricts and glomerular filtration pressure falls.
correlates.treatment: Stop the NSAID; reassess volume status and diuretic dose.

correlates.name: Thiazide-Induced Hyponatremia
correlates.pathophysiology: NCC inhibition leaves solute in the tubular fluid, so solute-free water cannot be excreted. Concentrating ability is preserved - the medullary gradient is untouched, the collecting duct still answers ADH, AQP2 is inserted, and free water is reabsorbed.

correlates.name: Third-Degree (Complete) AV Block
correlates.pathophysiology: The atria beat without synchronization to the ventricles - conduction from atria to ventricles is completely interrupted.

correlates.name: Tracheoesophageal Fistula (Congenital)
correlates.presentation: A neonatal anomaly; feeds and secretions cross into the airway.
correlates.pathophysiology: Failure of the tracheoesophageal septum to completely separate the respiratory diverticulum from the foregut leaves a persistent connection between the trachea and the esophagus.
correlates.treatment: Surgical correction.

correlates.name: Traumatic Brain Injury / Post-Concussion Syndrome
correlates.presentation: Post-concussion syndromes, head injuries, and problems presenting as nervous system or brain dysfunction (including learning problems).
correlates.pathophysiology: A concussion severe enough to produce traumatic brain injury has a huge impact on the bones and membranes — but there may also be dysfunction of the motility of the brain itself.
correlates.treatment: Treat the bones and membranes to improve function — but if a brain-motility component exists and you cannot identify and treat it, you do not entirely help your patient.

correlates.name: Triple Hit: Thiazide plus MRA plus NSAID
correlates.presentation: A 70-year-old woman on hydrochlorothiazide and spironolactone starts daily OTC naproxen for knee pain; labs show rising creatinine and potassium 5.8 mEq/L (Slide 37).
correlates.pathophysiology: (1) The thiazide reduces effective circulating volume and renal perfusion pressure, so GFR becomes prostaglandin-dependent on afferent dilation.

correlates.name: Tubular Proteinuria (Proximal Tubule Injury)
correlates.presentation: proteinuria on urinalysis. The lecturer's example: people foraging for mushrooms who eat a toxic look-alike, where the pattern of proteinuria helps localize the damage.
correlates.pathophysiology: protein recovery depends on ATP- and microtubule-dependent receptor-mediated endocytosis. Poison that machinery and filtered protein passes into the urine — tubule injury causes proteinuria even without glomerular injury.

correlates.name: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (Case Presentation)
correlates.presentation: polyuria (7.5 L/day vs. a normal 0.8-1.5 L/day), polydipsia, two months of weight loss, fatigue and lethargy, failing schoolwork, and dehydration in a previously healthy 12-year-old athlete.
correlates.pathophysiology: blood sugar exceeds the renal threshold of 200 mg/dL; SGLT2/SGLT1 saturate at Tm; unreabsorbed luminal glucose acts as an osmotic diuretic, and downstream segments have no reserve to reclaim it.

correlates.name: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus and Obesity
correlates.pathophysiology: In T2DM, endothelial cells make less NO and more endothelin-1; endothelin-1 acts on ET-A and ET-B receptors on VSMC, causing vasoconstriction and smooth muscle proliferation. In obesity, NO again falls, impairing vasodilation and favoring vasoconstriction.

correlates.name: Unstable Angina / Acute Coronary Syndrome
correlates.treatment: a DHP CCB only when combined with a beta blocker. A non-DHP may be used only in patients who (1) do not tolerate a beta blocker, (2) do not have left ventricular dysfunction, and (3) show no signs of disturbed AV conduction (Slide 20).

correlates.name: Urea Retention and the Elevated BUN
correlates.presentation: rising BUN above the normal 7-18 mg/dL.
correlates.pathophysiology: urea reabsorption follows water reabsorption and the luminal gradient. Severe dehydration, falling renal blood flow and GFR, or progressive renal disease lower urine flow, raise fractional urea reabsorption, and cause retention.
correlates.treatment: give IV fluids and increase urine flow — less water and urea are reabsorbed, so more urea clears and the BUN falls.

correlates.name: Variant (Vasospastic / Prinzmetal) Angina
correlates.pathophysiology: coronary artery vasospasm rather than fixed obstruction.
correlates.treatment: CCBs are first-line and may be combined with nitroglycerin (Slide 20). CCBs induce coronary vasodilation.

correlates.name: Vasopressin Resistance (AVP-R / Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus), including Lithium-Induced
correlates.presentation: Polyuria and polydipsia despite adequate or high ADH.
correlates.pathophysiology: The collecting duct cannot respond to ADH (vasopressin), so free water is lost and the patient has polyuria. Lithium is a major acquired cause.
correlates.treatment: Discontinue lithium if possible, then thiazide diuretic + low-sodium, low-protein diet (low solute load) + an NSAID.

correlates.name: Vasopressor Complications
correlates.presentation: extravasation at the IV site with vasoconstriction of nearby connective tissue and skin necrosis; hypoperfusion of the extremities, mesenteric organs and kidneys with prolonged use.
correlates.pathophysiology: the same vasoconstriction that raises MAP shrinks the radius of vessels feeding tissue beds, so the drug that treats the shock simultaneously hypoperfuses organs.
correlates.treatment: treat the underlying cause so pressors can be weaned; monitor IV sites and distal perfusion.

correlates.name: Venous Sinus Congestion
correlates.presentation: Listed in the session objectives as a component of cranial somatic dysfunction.
correlates.pathophysiology: Dural venous sinuses are spaces between dural folds; veins and sinuses cannot pump blood, so drainage depends on patent, mobile surroundings. Restriction diminishes flow and favors pooling of venous blood.

correlates.name: Ventricular Escape Rhythm (Escape Beats)
correlates.presentation: A very slow rhythm, in the range of 20-40 bpm from His-Purkinje tissue; under strong vagal stimulation the lecturer specifies a rate under 40 bpm.
correlates.pathophysiology: Failure of both the sinus node and the AV node to generate impulses removes overdrive suppression, unmasking the latent pacemaker channels in the His-Purkinje system.

correlates.name: von Willebrand Disease
correlates.presentation: Prolonged bleeding even after minor injury; the most common genetic bleeding disorder. Autosomal dominant.
correlates.pathophysiology: von Willebrand factor (vWF) is released exclusively by endothelial cells. At an injury site it binds exposed collagen in the damaged wall and bridges platelets to it, and it also binds factor VIII.
correlates.treatment: Desmopressin, which stimulates endothelial cells to release stored vWF and factor VIII.

correlates.name: White Coat Hypertension (White Coat Syndrome)
correlates.presentation: Elevated BP readings in the clinic with normal readings when measured elsewhere.
correlates.pathophysiology: Stress and nervousness triggered by the clinical environment (seeing someone in a white coat) transiently elevate blood pressure during measurement.

correlates.name: Widened Mediastinum After Blunt Trauma
correlates.presentation: a trauma patient imaged supine with a portable AP film, reported as a "wide mediastinum.".
correlates.pathophysiology: a true mediastinal hematoma widens the mediastinal contour, but AP projection and patient rotation both widen it artifactually.

findings.name: Anterior Infarct Pattern
findings.represents: ST elevation across the anterior wall of the left ventricle
findings.territory: Leads V3 and V4 — the left anterior descending artery
findings.association: The LAD is the most commonly occluded artery and this territory can be particularly fatal

findings.name: Aortic Knob
findings.represents: The rounded contour of the distal aortic arch on the frontal film
findings.territory: Always on the left, the uppermost of the three left contour bumps above the pulmonary outflow tract and left ventricle
findings.association: The superior segment of a lower lobe can project as high as the knob — a classic localization trap

findings.name: AP Projection
findings.represents: An anterior-to-posterior beam, used portably in the ICU or trauma bay, usually with the patient supine and the heart far from the cassette
findings.territory: Magnifies both the heart and the anteriorly-placed mediastinum
findings.association: Produces false cardiomegaly (mimicking CHF) and false mediastinal widening (mimicking hematoma) — check the label, not just the scapulae

findings.name: Asystole
findings.represents: A flat line with no electrical activity at all
findings.territory: Whole heart
findings.association: Cardiac arrest if the patient is unresponsive — but check for an unplugged lead if the patient looks well

findings.name: Atrial Fibrillation
findings.represents: Loss of organized atrial depolarization — no true P waves, only fibrillatory waves
findings.territory: Atria, with irregular conduction through the AV node
findings.association: An irregularly irregular rhythm and the most common cause of stroke

findings.name: Carotid Sinus Massage
findings.represents: External pressure on the carotid sinus that the baroreceptors read as a rise in blood pressure
findings.territory: Carotid sinus, afferent CN IX, efferent vagal CN X
findings.association: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity — the elderly man with atherosclerosis who faints while shaving or buttoning a collar

findings.name: Delta Wave
findings.represents: A slurred upstroke at the start of the QRS from pre-excitation through an accessory pathway that bypasses the AV node
findings.territory: Accessory bundle bridging atrium and ventricle
findings.association: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome — a short PR with a widened QRS

findings.name: Inferior Infarct Pattern
findings.represents: ST elevation in the leads that look up at the inferior wall of the heart
findings.territory: Leads II, III and aVF — the right coronary artery, which also supplies the SA and AV nodes
findings.association: The second most common infarct location; watch for bradyarrhythmia and heart block, and expect reciprocal depression in I and aVL

findings.name: JVP 'a' Wave
findings.represents: Atrial contraction — the pressure bump of atrial systole, following the P wave by about 0.1 second
findings.territory: Right atrium, read from the jugular venous pulse
findings.association: Absent in atrial fibrillation; prominent in first-degree AV block; large in right atrial myxoma, pulmonary hypertension and pulmonary stenosis

findings.name: JVP 'c' Wave
findings.represents: Compression of the atrium by the contracting ventricle, appearing just after the peak of the QRS
findings.territory: Right atrium, transmitted from the tricuspid valve bulging backward
findings.association: Marks the start of ventricular systole on the venous tracing

findings.name: JVP 'v' Wave
findings.represents: Passive atrial filling from the great veins while the AV valve is still closed
findings.territory: Right atrium during ventricular systole
findings.association: Becomes giant in tricuspid regurgitation

findings.name: JVP 'x' Descent
findings.represents: Atrial relaxation, when atrial pressure falls after contraction
findings.territory: Right atrium
findings.association: Absent in tricuspid regurgitation, where systolic backflow fills the atrium instead of letting it relax

findings.name: JVP 'y' Descent
findings.represents: The fall in atrial pressure as the AV valve opens and the atrium empties into the ventricle
findings.territory: Right atrium at the onset of ventricular filling
findings.association: Slow in tricuspid stenosis; absent in cardiac tamponade, where the ventricle cannot expand to receive the blood

findings.name: Lateral Infarct Pattern
findings.represents: ST elevation over the lateral wall of the left atrium and ventricle
findings.territory: Leads V5, V6, I and aVL — the left circumflex artery
findings.association: Reciprocal change appears inferiorly in II, III and aVF

findings.name: Left Axis Deviation
findings.represents: A mean electrical vector pushed leftward — lead I upright with aVF negative
findings.territory: Left ventricle
findings.association: Left ventricular hypertrophy, ventricular tachycardia, or an inferior MI

findings.name: Minor (Horizontal) Fissure
findings.represents: The fissure dividing the right upper lobe from the right middle lobe
findings.territory: Right lung only — the left lung has no minor fissure
findings.association: The only fissure visible on both the frontal and lateral films; the major fissure shows on the lateral alone

findings.name: Overpenetration
findings.represents: A film so dark that the lung parenchyma is saturated out
findings.territory: Lung fields
findings.association: Misses nodules and parenchymal disease

findings.name: P Wave
findings.represents: The summation of right and left atrial depolarization, with the left atrium depolarizing slightly later than the right
findings.territory: Atria — assessed in the money leads II, III, aVF and V1
findings.association: A double hump (P mitrale) means one atrium is enlarged or intra-atrial conduction is delayed; a tall P wave means atrial hypertrophy

findings.name: Poor Inspiratory Effort
findings.represents: Fewer than 9-10 posterior ribs visible above the diaphragm
findings.territory: Whole thorax, with the diaphragm riding high against the heart
findings.association: Produces false cardiomegaly by crowding the heart against an elevated diaphragm

findings.name: PR Interval
findings.represents: The time from the onset of atrial depolarization to the onset of ventricular depolarization — essentially conduction time through the AV node
findings.territory: AV node, the deliberate delay between atrial and ventricular contraction
findings.association: Prolonged beyond one large box in first-, second- and third-degree AV block; normal is 120-200 ms

findings.name: QRS Complex
findings.represents: Ventricular depolarization — Q is the first downstroke, R the upstroke, S the second downstroke
findings.territory: Ventricular myocardium and the His-Purkinje system
findings.association: Widened beyond 120 ms by bundle branch or fascicular block, hyperkalemia, tricyclic antidepressants, sodium channel blockers and WPW

findings.name: QT Interval
findings.represents: Depolarization through repolarization — the electrical equivalent of ventricular systole
findings.territory: Whole ventricular myocardium
findings.association: Prolongation from congenital long QT syndrome, electrolyte derangement or the anti-ABCDE drugs risks torsades de pointes; normal is 0.36-0.44 s and under half the R-R interval

findings.name: R Wave Progression
findings.represents: The R wave growing steadily more positive from V1 through V3, with the transition to a dominant R between V3 and V4
findings.territory: Sweeping across the precordium from septum to lateral wall
findings.association: Poor progression is a marker of anterior infarction or lead misplacement; normal progression is a marker of heart health

findings.name: Reciprocal Change (PAILS)
findings.represents: ST depression in leads electrically opposite an area of true ST elevation, confirming the infarct is real
findings.territory: Posterior, Anterior, Inferior, Lateral, Septal — each shows reciprocal change in the next letter of the sequence
findings.association: An inferior STEMI shows reciprocal depression in the lateral leads I and aVL

findings.name: Retrosternal Clear Space
findings.represents: The gas-filled space behind the sternum on the lateral film
findings.territory: Anterior mediastinum, invisible on the frontal film
findings.association: Should be entirely lucent; filling it means an anterior mediastinal mass

findings.name: Right Axis Deviation
findings.represents: A mean electrical vector pushed rightward — lead I negative with aVF upright
findings.territory: Right ventricle
findings.association: Right ventricular hypertrophy or an anterolateral MI

findings.name: Rotation
findings.represents: Clavicular heads that are not equidistant from the spinous process
findings.territory: Mediastinum and aortic contour
findings.association: Exaggerates the aorta into a false aneurysm or tracheal deviation, and under-represents mediastinal shift so a tension pneumothorax is missed

findings.name: S1 Heart Sound
findings.represents: Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the start of isovolumetric contraction
findings.territory: AV valves, timed to the QRS
findings.association: Marks the beginning of systole; all four valves are closed during the phase it opens

findings.name: S2 Heart Sound
findings.represents: Closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves at the start of isovolumetric relaxation
findings.territory: Semilunar valves, timed just after the T wave
findings.association: Marks the beginning of diastole and end-systolic volume

findings.name: S3 Heart Sound
findings.represents: A low-pitched sound during the rapid filling phase, as blood strikes a compliant or overfilled ventricle
findings.territory: Early diastole, just after S2
findings.association: Normal in youth and pregnancy; in an older patient it suggests volume overload and heart failure

findings.name: S4 Heart Sound
findings.represents: Atrial contraction forcing blood into a stiff ventricle during atrial systole
findings.territory: Late diastole, just before S1
findings.association: A stiff, non-compliant ventricle — hypertrophy from long-standing hypertension or aortic stenosis

findings.name: Septal Infarct Pattern
findings.represents: ST elevation over the interventricular septum
findings.territory: Leads V1 and V2 — the left anterior descending artery
findings.association: Often extends into the anterior leads; V1 and V2 are contiguous so two-lead elevation here does meet STEMI criteria

findings.name: Silhouette Sign
findings.represents: Loss of the expected interface between two structures of different density, because a structure is only visible where it abuts something of a different density
findings.territory: The left heart border is left ventricle abutting the lingula; the right heart border is right atrium abutting the medial segment of the right middle lobe
findings.association: Localizes a consolidation to whichever lobe touches the effaced border — the lecturer's first named must-know

findings.name: ST Depression
findings.represents: Subendocardial ischemia — the inner layer, which is farthest from the coronary supply and first to suffer
findings.territory: Often diffuse rather than assigned to one artery
findings.association: Also appears as reciprocal change in the leads opposite a STEMI territory

findings.name: ST Elevation
findings.represents: Transmural ischemia involving all layers of the myocardial wall
findings.territory: Must appear in two or more anatomically contiguous leads to meet STEMI criteria — I and II are not contiguous
findings.association: An emergency requiring immediate catheterization to restore flow

findings.name: ST Segment
findings.represents: The interval when the ventricles are fully depolarized and mechanically contracting, so no net current flows
findings.territory: Localizes the injured wall by which contiguous leads are involved
findings.association: Elevation in two or more contiguous leads defines a STEMI; depression signals subendocardial ischemia

findings.name: T Wave
findings.represents: Ventricular repolarization — the lecturer's line is that potassium lives under the T wave
findings.territory: Ventricular myocardium
findings.association: Peaked and narrow in hyperkalemia; flattened with a following U wave in hypokalemia

findings.name: Third-Degree AV Block
findings.represents: Complete atrioventricular dissociation — P waves march at their own regular rate, unrelated to the QRS complexes
findings.territory: AV node, whose blood supply comes from the right coronary artery
findings.association: Consider an inferior MI as the cause; both atrial and ventricular rates are regular but independent

findings.name: TP Segment
findings.represents: Electrical rest during diastole, from the end of the T wave to the start of the next P wave
findings.territory: The whole heart at rest
findings.association: The true isoelectric reference line — ST elevation and depression are measured against it, not against the PR segment

findings.name: Underpenetration
findings.represents: A whiter film, in which the thoracic disc spaces cannot be made out behind the heart
findings.territory: Retrocardiac space
findings.association: Misses retrocardiac masses and pneumonia hiding behind the cardiac shadow

findings.name: Valsalva Maneuver
findings.represents: Forceful exhalation against a closed airway, raising intrathoracic pressure and stretching the baroreceptors
findings.territory: Carotid sinus and aortic arch, reporting through CN IX and CN X to the nucleus tractus solitarius
findings.association: Used at the bedside to break supraventricular tachycardia by driving a parasympathetic response

omm.name: Adams Forward Bend Test
omm.definition: The screening maneuver in which the patient bends forward so the examiner can see rib asymmetry
omm.findings: Reveals the rib hump produced by vertebral rotation
omm.treatment: Screen around age 10, before the pubertal growth spurt, since children and adolescents with scoliosis are otherwise asymptomatic

omm.name: Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis
omm.definition: The commonest form — idiopathic curves account for 70-90% of all scoliosis — with hereditary contribution, hypokyphosis, raised calmodulin and linkage to chromosomes 17 and 19
omm.findings: Progression risk is highest in girls who are premenarchal, Risser 0, with double, thoracic, or already severe curves
omm.treatment: Observation at 11-19 degrees, bracing from 25 degrees while growth remains, surgery at 50 degrees or more

omm.name: Balanced Ligamentous Tension (BLT)
omm.definition: Positioning an articulation at the point where its ligaments are poised between the normal tension of the free range of motion and the increased tension preceding the strain
omm.findings: Sutherland called it ligamentous articular strain in the spine and membranous articular strain in the cranium; ligaments are the source of all tension, and articular surfaces only define the planes of motion
omm.treatment: The correction comes from within the patient — you hold the balance point and the natural agencies make the change

omm.name: C-Curve vs S-Curve Compensation
omm.definition: A C-scoliotic response makes a single curve at the thoracolumbar junction; an S-scoliotic response curves the thorax one way and the lumbar spine the other
omm.findings: Typical patterns put the sacral base low on the short side with the caudal curve side-bending away; atypical responses tip into the short side and load the opposite side
omm.treatment: Atypical compensations may produce more pain than typical ones, so identify the pattern before dosing a lift

omm.name: Cobb Method
omm.definition: A line along the superior border of the highest vertebra inclined toward the concavity and another along the inferior border of the lowest such vertebra; the curve is the angle where their perpendiculars intersect
omm.findings: Filmed standing, full length C7 to iliac crest, PA rather than AP to spare breast and thyroid — never supine, which removes gravity and underestimates the curve
omm.treatment: Place a block under the shorter leg before the film if there is a leg length discrepancy

omm.name: Condylar Decompression
omm.definition: Release of the occipital condyles, where the occiput articulates with the atlas and the hypoglossal canal transmits CN XII
omm.findings: Check the condyles in an infant with torticollis or feeding difficulty
omm.treatment: Hand placement is the safety step — thenar eminences must sit medial to the OM sutures, because landing on the mastoid processes externally rotates both temporal bones and can provoke extreme reactions

omm.name: Core Link
omm.definition: The dural continuity running from the foramen magnum through attachments at C2-C3, then free, to its anchor at S2
omm.findings: A bound sacrum keeps the head from opening — which is why the sacrum belongs to the cranial mechanism
omm.treatment: Treat the pelvis when the head will not respond after a head injury

omm.name: Cranial Exhalation Phase
omm.definition: The phase in which the transverse diameter narrows while the anteroposterior diameter lengthens and the vertical deepens
omm.findings: Midline bones move into extension and the sphenobasilar junction drops; paired bones internally rotate
omm.treatment: The sacrum nutates (rotates anteriorly) with cranial extension

omm.name: Cranial Inhalation Phase
omm.definition: The phase in which the transverse diameter widens while the anteroposterior and vertical diameters decrease
omm.findings: Midline bones move about transverse axes into flexion and the sphenobasilar junction rises; paired bones externally rotate
omm.treatment: The sacrum counternutates (rotates posteriorly) with cranial flexion, through the core link

omm.name: Direct Action Approach
omm.definition: Engaging the restrictive barrier and adding energy to stir the tissues to action
omm.findings: Matches the barrier rather than overcoming it
omm.treatment: Never force through the barrier — add just enough energy for the tissues to respond

omm.name: Disengagement
omm.definition: A subset of the direct approach in which the two parts are drawn directly apart, bringing tension up
omm.findings: Useful where compression is holding the articulation
omm.treatment: One the lecturer uses frequently; tension is raised until the balance point declares itself

omm.name: Exaggeration Approach
omm.definition: An indirect approach in which the operator exaggerates the lesion, side-bending further into the side-bent side
omm.findings: The most commonly used of the BLT approaches
omm.treatment: Carry the part further into its ease until tension balances, then wait

omm.name: Falx Cerebri
omm.definition: The sagittal-plane dural sheet running from the crista galli of the ethmoid back to the confluence of sinuses at the inion, along the sagittal suture
omm.findings: Attaches to ethmoid, frontal, parietals and occiput, so strain anywhere is transmitted through the whole system
omm.treatment: Balanced membranous tension addresses the membrane rather than the individual bone

omm.name: Fluctuation of the CSF
omm.definition: The to-and-fro action of cerebrospinal fluid that Sutherland called the potency of the Tide — the fundamental principle and the drive of the whole mechanism
omm.findings: Circulation alone is insufficient for cellular exchange: interstitial pressure is negative, so unstirred fluid stagnates
omm.treatment: The goal of treatment is to promote the interchange of fluids, keeping concentration gradients continuously changing at the microcirculation

omm.name: Heel Lift Placement
omm.definition: The lift goes under the heel on the side of the LOWERED sacral base
omm.findings: Rule out a pronated foot (which needs orthotics) and pelvic torsion or shear (which needs OMT) before ordering any lift
omm.treatment: Maximum 1/4 inch inside the shoe and 1/2 inch from heel to floor; anything above that is split between the anterior sole and the posterior heel, because heel-only excess rotates the pelvis away in the transverse plane

omm.name: Heilig's Formula
omm.definition: L is less than or equal to SBU / (D + C), where SBU is the sacral base unleveling, D scores duration since injury and C scores compensation
omm.findings: Duration: 1 for 0-10 years, 2 for 11-29 years, 3 for 30+ years. Compensation: 0 for none, 1 for side-bending and rotation changes, 2 for wedging, facet size change, endplate growths and spurring
omm.treatment: The longer the problem has been present and the more the body has already compensated, the smaller the lift the patient can tolerate

omm.name: Hip Drop Test
omm.definition: A test of lateral lumbar flexion — not of the hip joint — performed with the feet flat 4-6 inches apart while the patient bends one knee
omm.findings: The iliac crest drops on the bent-knee side; the side with the greatest drop is the side of restricted side-bending, and an equal drop scores zero degrees
omm.treatment: Note the group curve nuance — the pelvis drops more easily opposite the natural side-bending position

omm.name: Iliolumbar Ligament Strain
omm.definition: The lateral ligament running from the transverse processes to the ilium, with anterior fibers strained by anterior innominate rotation and posterior fibers by posterior rotation
omm.findings: Refers pain to the lumbosacral region, lateral gluteal area, lateral thigh, groin, and testicle or labia
omm.treatment: Calcification represents functional demand becoming structural change, so address the innominate rotation before it fixes

omm.name: Inferior Vertical Shear
omm.definition: A non-physiologic strain about two transverse axes with both bones rotating posteriorly in the SAME direction, leaving the basisphenoid low
omm.findings: On the vault hold the fingers rotate up toward the ceiling
omm.treatment: Trauma-induced; treat the shear directly

omm.name: Jugular Foramen
omm.definition: The opening at the occipitomastoid junction transmitting cranial nerves IX, X and XI along with the internal jugular vein
omm.findings: Cranial nerves VII and VIII travel through the temporal bone but NOT through the jugular foramen — the classic distractor
omm.treatment: OM suture release for symptoms referable to CN IX, X and XI, including vagally mediated cardiac, respiratory and GI complaints

omm.name: Lateral Shear
omm.definition: A non-physiologic strain about two vertical axes with sphenoid and occiput translating in the SAME direction, producing a parallelogram-shaped head
omm.findings: Index fingers sit on the greater wings and the pinkies displace the opposite way; the side is named for the direction the basisphenoid moved
omm.treatment: Trauma-induced midline disruption requiring direct attention to the shear

omm.name: Molding
omm.definition: An approach for a strain held within a bone — a distortion of the bone's own shape — rather than between two bones at a joint
omm.findings: The classic parallelogram-shaped head of an infant
omm.treatment: The balanced-tension principle applied to the shape of the bone itself

omm.name: Motility vs Mobility
omm.definition: Motility means capable of moving itself, which is what the brain and spinal cord do; mobility means it must be moved, which is what the bones and membranes do
omm.findings: On inhalation the cortical buds coil so the brain becomes shorter and fatter, and the cord lifts like a tadpole's tail; exhalation uncoils it
omm.treatment: Brain motility dysfunction after traumatic brain injury or concussion must be addressed or the patient is not fully helped

omm.name: Muscle Balance of the Innominate
omm.definition: The innominate is balanced between the abdominal muscles pulling it superiorly and the hamstrings pulling it inferiorly from the ischial tuberosity
omm.findings: The vertebral column has its own pair — spinal extensors posteriorly against iliopsoas and rectus femoris anteriorly
omm.treatment: Strengthen the weak and stretch the tense; the Thomas test identifies iliopsoas contracture

omm.name: Naming Cranial Somatic Dysfunction
omm.definition: Cranial dysfunctions are named for the FREEDOM — the direction the mechanism wants to go — never for the barrier
omm.findings: The same naming convention used throughout osteopathic diagnosis
omm.treatment: It is what makes indirect treatment 'toward the name'

omm.name: Natural Agencies
omm.definition: The forces within the patient that perform the correction: respiratory cooperation, the nervous system reset, circulation, and the primary respiratory mechanism
omm.findings: A dysfunctional area often fails to move with breathing; capsule proprioceptors and nociceptors hold the segment facilitated; tension impedes interstitial flow and cellular nutrition
omm.treatment: The stated goal of treatment is to improve the interchange of all body fluids across all interfaces

omm.name: Primary Respiratory Mechanism
omm.definition: The five observed phenomena Sutherland described: motility of the brain and spinal cord, fluctuation of the CSF, mobility of the dural membranes, mobility of the cranial bones, and involuntary mobility of the sacrum between the ilia
omm.findings: Palpable as a rhythmic change in cranial shape at roughly 6-12 cycles per minute — a change in shape, never in volume
omm.treatment: Its presence or absence anywhere in the body is itself diagnostic and serves as an index of overall health

omm.name: Primary vs Secondary Respiration
omm.definition: Primary respiration is the cranial rhythmic impulse with its own inhalation and exhalation phases; secondary respiration is pulmonary breathing
omm.findings: The two are distinct mechanisms and are palpated separately
omm.treatment: Respiratory cooperation from the patient can be used to assist a cranial technique

omm.name: Reciprocal Tension Membrane
omm.definition: The falx cerebri in the sagittal plane and the tentorium cerebelli in the transverse plane, working as one unit whose opposing fiber directions guide and limit cranial bone motion
omm.findings: Because no muscles cross the cranial joints, the motion it produces is entirely involuntary
omm.treatment: Its fulcrum is the falx-tentorium junction at the straight sinus — the still point that supplies the power for the lever

omm.name: Risser Sign
omm.definition: A grading of iliac apophyseal ossification running anterolateral to posteromedial, from grade 0 (none) to grade 5 (full bony fusion)
omm.findings: Grade 1 appears only after peak height velocity; a lower grade means more growth remaining and greater risk of progression
omm.treatment: Bracing works only while growth remains, which is why Risser 0-2 (or Sanders 1-3) is part of every treatment decision

omm.name: SBS Compression
omm.definition: A non-physiologic pattern in which the sphenobasilar synchondrosis is jammed toward the midline with no axis of motion at all
omm.findings: The classic bowling ball feel — dense, heavy, with minimal or absent primary respiratory mechanism
omm.treatment: Decompression of the synchondrosis before any other pattern can be addressed

omm.name: SBS Extension
omm.definition: A physiologic strain about two transverse axes in which the midline bones rotate oppositely and the sphenobasilar synchondrosis drops
omm.findings: On the vault hold the hands approximate and the sense of motion is toward the vertex
omm.treatment: Named for the phase; treated by balancing membranous tension

omm.name: SBS Flexion
omm.definition: A physiologic strain about two transverse axes in which the midline bones rotate in opposite directions and the sphenobasilar synchondrosis rises
omm.findings: On the vault hold the hands spread and the operator's sense is of motion toward the feet
omm.treatment: Named for the phase, not for a side; balance the membranous tension at the point of stillness

omm.name: SBS Sidebending / Rotation
omm.definition: A physiologic strain combining two vertical axes with one anteroposterior axis, so the vertical components move oppositely and the AP components move together
omm.findings: Named for the convexity: the convex side moves down and out while the concave side moves up and in
omm.treatment: Balanced membranous tension into the direction of ease

omm.name: SBS Torsion
omm.definition: A physiologic strain about a single anteroposterior axis running from nasion to opisthion, with sphenoid and occiput rotating in opposite directions
omm.findings: The hands roll in opposite directions on the vault hold, and the side is named for the HIGH greater wing — the index finger that travels cephalad
omm.treatment: Physiologic, so an indirect balanced membranous tension approach follows the ease

omm.name: Scoliometer
omm.definition: Essentially a carpenter's level, used to measure the angle of trunk rotation on a forward-bent patient
omm.findings: Run cephalad to caudad; with a right rib hump the right side lifts and the ball deviates left. Inter-rater error is 2 degrees thoracic and 2.2 lumbar
omm.treatment: Refer at ATR 7 degrees or more, or 5 degrees or more if BMI is at or above the 85th percentile — and always state which method you used

omm.name: Scoliosis
omm.definition: Lateral curvature of the spine in the coronal plane, usually with rotation, measuring 10 degrees or more by the Cobb method — below 10 degrees it is spinal asymmetry with no long-term significance
omm.findings: Named for the side of the convexity; the apical vertebra is the most deviated and rotated and defines the curve location; rotation drives the convex-side ribs posteriorly into a rib hump
omm.treatment: Decided by two numbers only — the Cobb angle and the growth remaining

omm.name: Short Leg Syndrome
omm.definition: A historical misnomer for the triad of sacral base unleveling, compensatory innominate rotation, and a caudal curve side-bending away from the low sacral base — the cause may have nothing to do with leg length
omm.findings: Measured on a standing film for iliac crest heights, femoral head heights, sacral base unleveling and the scoliotic curve, allowing for 2 mm of measurement error and 25% bony distortion
omm.treatment: Treat all somatic dysfunction with OMT before the radiological evaluation, then dose a heel lift

omm.name: Structural vs Functional Curve
omm.definition: A structural curve does not resolve with rotation, side bending or forward bending; a functional curve does
omm.findings: On the Adams forward bend test a functional curve improves with side bending while a structural curve does not; a curve that disappears on forward flexion or lying down points to a cause below the spine
omm.treatment: Functional curves convert to structural through soft tissue shortening, bony change, disc degeneration and fascial fibrosis — which is the argument for treating early

omm.name: Superior Vertical Shear
omm.definition: A non-physiologic strain about two transverse axes in which sphenoid and occiput rotate in the SAME direction, both anteriorly, leaving the basisphenoid high
omm.findings: On the vault hold the fingers rotate down toward the table
omm.treatment: Non-physiologic and usually trauma-induced; the midline is disrupted, so treatment addresses the shear itself

omm.name: Tentorium Cerebelli
omm.definition: The transverse-plane dural sheet spanning the confluence of sinuses, the transverse sinus, the petrous ridge of the temporal bone and the clinoid processes of the sphenoid
omm.findings: Its junction with the falx at the straight sinus is the Sutherland fulcrum
omm.treatment: Balanced membranous tension at the fulcrum, since it guides and limits cranial motion

omm.name: True vs Apparent Leg Length Discrepancy
omm.definition: A true discrepancy is measured fixed landmark to fixed landmark, ASIS to medial malleolus; an apparent discrepancy runs non-fixed to fixed
omm.findings: Exclude a true discrepancy first, then check for pelvic torsion; localize by measuring tibial heights from the feet and femoral lengths from the side with the patient supine and knees bent
omm.treatment: Correct pelvic torsion with OMT before attributing the finding to bone length

omm.name: Vault Hold
omm.definition: The standard diagnostic contact: index fingers on the greater wings of the sphenoid, middle and ring fingers around the ear, and little fingers on the occiput
omm.findings: The vault accommodates to whatever the base is doing, so what the vault reveals is a base strain — the house tells you about the basement
omm.treatment: True articular mobility and the primary dysfunctions live in the cranial base, so base treatment is the more profound
